probes.exEn: The train leaves the station at eight.

items.note: Feminine, so 'to the station' is 'à la gare'; a bus station is 'la gare routière'.
items.ex: On se retrouve devant la gare à huit heures.
items.exEn: We're meeting in front of the station at eight o'clock.

items.note: Masculine; a false friend, it is not a magazine (that is 'le magazine').
items.ex: Le magasin ferme à dix-neuf heures.
items.exEn: The shop closes at 7 pm.

items.note: Masculine, so 'at the restaurant' is 'au restaurant'; the final -t is silent.
items.ex: On dîne au restaurant ce soir.
items.exEn: We're having dinner at the restaurant tonight.

items.note: Feminine (une école); French keeps the article: 'à l'école' where English says 'at school'.
items.ex: Les enfants vont à l'école à pied.
items.exEn: The children walk to school.

items.note: Masculine (un hôpital); the h is silent so 'le' becomes 'l''; plural is 'les hôpitaux'.
items.ex: Ma sœur travaille à l'hôpital.
items.exEn: My sister works at the hospital.

items.note: Feminine; 'à la banque' for 'at the bank' (money only, a river bank is different).
items.ex: Je retire de l'argent à la banque.
items.exEn: I withdraw money at the bank.

items.note: Masculine, so 'in the park' is 'au parc'; the final -c is pronounced.
items.ex: Les enfants jouent au parc.
items.exEn: The children are playing in the park.

items.note: Feminine; French says 'dans la rue' (in the street), not 'sur'.
items.ex: J'habite dans une petite rue calme.
items.exEn: I live on a quiet little street.

items.note: Masculine (un aéroport); vowel start means 'à l'aéroport'.
items.ex: Le taxi va à l'aéroport.
items.exEn: The taxi is going to the airport.

items.note: Masculine; 'au marché' for 'at the market'; most towns have an open-air one on set days.
items.ex: J'achète des légumes au marché le samedi.
items.exEn: I buy vegetables at the market on Saturdays.

items.note: Feminine; shops ending in -erie are feminine (la boucherie, l'épicerie), and so is 'la pharmacie'.
items.ex: J'achète une baguette à la boulangerie.
items.exEn: I buy a baguette at the bakery.

items.note: Feminine; 'la poste' is the post office, while 'le poste' (masculine) means a job or position.
items.ex: Je vais à la poste pour envoyer un colis.
items.exEn: I'm going to the post office to send a parcel.

teaching.rule: To ask the way, start with 'Excusez-moi' or 'Pardon', then 'Où est la gare ?' (Where is the station?) or 'Pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?' (How do I get to the station?). Answers use two verbs: tournez (turn) and continuez (keep going): 'Tournez à gauche', 'Continuez tout droit'. Position words are followed by 'de': 'à côté de la gare', 'en face de l'école'; 'de + le' becomes 'du' (en face du parc).

examples.en: Excuse me, where is the station?
examples.note: Polite opener + 'où est' + the place.

examples.fr: Tournez à droite, puis continuez tout droit.
examples.en: Turn right, then keep going straight.
examples.note: The -ez ending is the polite 'you' form used with strangers.

examples.fr: C'est en face de la banque.
examples.note: 'en face de' needs 'de' before the place.

contrast.note: 'droite' (with -e, sounds 'drwat') is right; 'droit' (no -e, sounds 'drwa') is straight.
'près', 'à côté', 'en face', 'loin' all need 'de' before the place: près de la gare.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers mix up 'à droite' (right) with 'tout droit' (straight) and drop the 'de' after près / à côté / en face / loin.

probes.ex: Continuez tout droit jusqu'au pont.
probes.exEn: Keep going straight to the bridge.

probes.ex: L'hôtel est à côté de la gare.
probes.exEn: The hotel is next to the station.

probes.ex: Tournez à gauche après la pharmacie.
probes.exEn: Turn left after the pharmacy.

items.note: 'la gauche' is the left-hand side; you always keep the 'à' when giving a direction.
items.ex: Tournez à gauche au feu rouge.
items.exEn: Turn left at the traffic light.

items.note: 'droite' ends in -e and the -t is heard ('drwat'); do not confuse with 'tout droit'.
items.ex: La banque est à droite, après le pont.
items.exEn: The bank is on the right, after the bridge.

items.note: No -e on 'droit' and the final -t is silent ('too drwa'); it means keep going in a straight line.
items.ex: Continuez tout droit jusqu'à la place.
items.exEn: Keep going straight ahead to the square.

items.note: Always followed by 'de' + the place; 'de + le' becomes 'du' (près du parc).
items.ex: L'hôtel est près de la gare.
items.exEn: The hotel is near the station.

items.note: The opposite of 'près de'; also needs 'de' before the place.
items.ex: Le parc n'est pas loin de l'école.
items.exEn: The park isn't far from the school.

items.note: Sounds like 'ee-see'; use it for the spot where you are standing.
items.ex: Le bus s'arrête ici.
items.exEn: The bus stops here.

items.note: Points to a place away from you; the hyphen joins 'là' (there) and 'bas' (down/along).
items.ex: Le cinéma est là-bas, au bout de la rue.
items.exEn: The cinema is over there, at the end of the street.

items.note: Literally 'at the side of'; the 'de' is part of the phrase.
items.ex: La poste est à côté de la banque.
items.exEn: The post office is next to the bank.

items.note: 'face' is the front, so 'en face de' means facing / across from; keep the 'de'.
items.ex: Le café est en face de l'église.
items.exEn: The café is opposite the church.

items.note: 'le coin' is the corner; 'au' = à + le, and 'de' links it to the street.
items.ex: La boulangerie est au coin de la rue.
items.exEn: The bakery is at the corner of the street.

items.note: The vous form of 'tourner' used as an instruction to a stranger; with a friend say 'tourne'.
items.ex: Ensuite, tournez à droite.
items.exEn: Then turn right.

items.en: how do I get to (asking the way)
items.note: Literally 'to go to'; French asks the way with this unfinished sentence plus 's'il vous plaît'.
items.ex: Pardon, pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
items.exEn: Excuse me, how do I get to the station, please?

teaching.rule: To say what someone does, use 'être' + the job with NO 'a / an': Je suis médecin, Il est boulanger (never 'je suis un médecin'). Many job words change for a woman: -eur becomes -euse (serveur / serveuse), -er becomes -ère (boulanger / boulangère), -ien becomes -ienne (pharmacien / pharmacienne); some like 'médecin' and 'professeur' stay the same. When you add a comment, switch to 'c'est un / une': C'est un bon médecin.

examples.note: No 'une' after 'je suis'; the -e ending shows the speaker is female.
Plain job statement: 'il est' + job, no article.
Feminine form of 'infirmier': -er becomes -ère.

contrast.note: With je suis / il est / elle est a job takes no article: Je suis professeur.
After 'c'est' you say 'C'est un médecin' or 'C'est un bon médecin'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers add 'un / une' after 'je suis' when naming their job ('je suis un avocat'); say 'je suis avocat', and keep 'un / une' only after 'c'est'.

probes.ex: Je suis infirmière à l'hôpital de Lille.
probes.exEn: I'm a nurse at the Lille hospital.

probes.ex: Le boulanger ouvre à six heures.
probes.exEn: The baker opens at six.

probes.ex: Mon cousin est avocat à Lyon.
probes.exEn: My cousin is a lawyer in Lyon.

items.note: Often shortened to 'le prof / la prof'; the feminine 'la professeure' exists but many women still say 'je suis professeur'.
items.ex: Mon professeur de français est sympa.
items.exEn: My French teacher is nice.

items.note: One form for both men and women ('elle est médecin'); 'le docteur' is the title you use to address them.
items.ex: Elle est médecin dans un hôpital.
items.exEn: She's a doctor in a hospital.

items.note: Masculine form; a female student is 'l'étudiante', and the final -t is only heard in the feminine.
items.ex: Je suis étudiant à l'université.
items.exEn: I'm a student at the university.

items.note: Masculine -eur ending; call him 'Monsieur', never 'garçon', in a modern café.
items.ex: Le serveur apporte l'addition.
items.exEn: The waiter brings the bill.

items.note: The -eur ending becomes -euse for a woman, a pattern shared by vendeuse and coiffeuse.
items.ex: La serveuse est très gentille.
items.exEn: The waitress is very kind.

items.note: Masculine (un ingénieur); the feminine 'ingénieure' is spelled with an extra -e but sounds the same.
items.ex: Mon père est ingénieur chez Renault.
items.exEn: My father is an engineer at Renault.

items.note: Feminine form of 'infirmier' (-er becomes -ère); a male nurse is 'un infirmier'.
items.ex: Ma mère est infirmière.
items.exEn: My mother is a nurse.

items.note: Masculine -er ending; the feminine is 'la boulangère' with a grave accent that opens the vowel.
items.ex: Le boulanger fait du pain tous les matins.
items.exEn: The baker makes bread every morning.

items.note: The same word means avocado; context tells you which. Feminine: l'avocate.
items.ex: Mon frère est avocat à Paris.
items.exEn: My brother is a lawyer in Paris.

items.note: From 'vendre' (to sell); the feminine 'la vendeuse' follows the -eur / -euse pattern.
items.ex: Le vendeur est très gentil.
items.exEn: The salesperson is very kind.

items.note: Masculine; feminine 'la patronne' doubles the -n and you finally hear it.
items.ex: Mon patron est exigeant.
items.exEn: My boss is demanding.

items.note: Literally 'in life'; 'Qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ?' is the normal way to ask someone's job.
items.ex: Qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ?
items.exEn: What do you do for a living?

teaching.rule: Days and months are written in lowercase in French: lundi, janvier. To say 'on Monday' (one time) just say the day on its own: 'Je travaille lundi'. To say 'on Mondays' (every week) add 'le': 'le lundi'. Months take 'en': en janvier, en juillet. Three seasons take 'en' (en été, en automne, en hiver) but spring takes 'au': au printemps.

examples.note: No word for 'on' and no article for a single day.
'en' + month, month in lowercase.

examples.en: In spring the weather is mild.
examples.note: Spring is the odd one out: 'au printemps', not 'en printemps'.

contrast.note: Among the seasons, only 'printemps' takes 'au'; été, automne and hiver take 'en'. This is a seasons-only quirk: months always take 'en' (en janvier, en mars).
'à + day' is a goodbye, not 'on Monday'; for 'on Monday' say just 'lundi'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers capitalise days and months and translate 'on Monday' as 'sur lundi' or 'à lundi'; write 'lundi' in lowercase and use it on its own.

probes.ex: Au printemps, les jardins sont pleins de fleurs.
probes.exEn: In spring the gardens are full of flowers.

probes.ex: Le dimanche, je fais la grasse matinée.
probes.exEn: On Sundays I sleep in.

probes.ex: Les soldes commencent en janvier.
probes.exEn: The sales start in January.

items.note: Lowercase in French; named after the moon (lune). On its own it means 'on Monday'.
items.ex: Je vais chez le médecin lundi.
items.exEn: I'm going to the doctor on Monday.

items.note: Lowercase; named after Mars, like 'Mardi gras' (Fat Tuesday).
items.ex: Le cours de français est mardi soir.
items.exEn: The French class is on Tuesday evening.

items.note: Lowercase; named after Mercury; in France many primary schools have a short day or no school on Wednesday.
items.ex: Les enfants n'ont pas école mercredi après-midi.
items.exEn: The children have no school on Wednesday afternoon.

items.note: Lowercase; named after Jupiter; the 'j' is soft, like the s in 'measure'.
items.ex: J'ai un rendez-vous jeudi matin.
items.exEn: I have an appointment on Thursday morning.

items.note: Lowercase; the -en- is a nasal sound, as in 'vent'.
items.ex: On va au cinéma vendredi soir.
items.exEn: We're going to the cinema on Friday evening.

items.note: Lowercase; from Latin 'sabbati dies'; 'le samedi' means every Saturday, e.g. market day.
items.ex: Il y a un marché samedi matin.
items.exEn: There's a market on Saturday morning.

items.note: Lowercase; 'le dimanche' with the article means every Sunday.
items.ex: Le dimanche, les magasins sont fermés.
items.exEn: On Sundays the shops are closed.

items.note: Borrowed from English but masculine and written with a hyphen; 'ce week-end' means this weekend.
items.ex: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
items.exEn: What are you doing this weekend?

items.note: Lowercase; months take 'en' for 'in': en janvier.
items.ex: Il neige souvent en janvier.
items.exEn: It often snows in January.

items.note: Lowercase; the -ll- is pronounced like a 'y' (zhwee-yeh); le 14 juillet is the national holiday.
items.ex: En juillet, beaucoup de Français sont en vacances.
items.exEn: In July many French people are on holiday.

items.note: Lowercase; dates go number + month with no 'of': le vingt-cinq décembre.
items.ex: Noël est le vingt-cinq décembre.
items.exEn: Christmas is on the twenty-fifth of December.

items.note: Masculine; the only season that takes 'au' (au printemps); the final -ps is silent.
items.ex: Au printemps, les fleurs poussent.
items.exEn: In spring the flowers grow.

items.note: Masculine (un été); 'in summer' is 'en été' with no article.
items.ex: En été, on va à la plage.
items.exEn: In summer we go to the beach.

items.note: Masculine (un automne); the -mn- is said like a single 'n' (oh-tonn).
items.ex: En automne, les feuilles tombent.
items.exEn: In autumn the leaves fall.

items.note: Masculine (un hiver); silent h, so 'l'hiver' and 'en hiver' link the sounds.
items.ex: En hiver, les jours sont courts.
items.exEn: In winter the days are short.

teaching.rule: Adjectives are describing words like big, new or happy. In French they change their ending to match the noun they describe: add -e when the noun is feminine (grand → grande, petit → petite) and -s when it is plural. A handful of very common short adjectives (grand, petit, bon, mauvais, beau, nouveau, vieux, jeune) go BEFORE the noun; nearly every other adjective goes AFTER it, the opposite of English.

examples.note: maison is feminine, so grand takes an -e; the final d is now pronounced.
bon is one of the short adjectives that sit before the noun.
difficile is not in the short list, so it follows the noun; it already ends in -e, so the feminine looks the same.
beau becomes belle in the feminine and belles in the plural; des shrinks to de in front of a plural adjective.

contrast.fr: une voiture rouge (not une rouge voiture)
contrast.note: Colours and most other adjectives come after the noun; only the short beauty-age-goodness-size adjectives go first.

contrast.fr: Elle est grande. (not Elle est grand.)
contrast.note: Agreement also applies after être: the adjective matches the person being described, not just a noun next to it.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers put every adjective before the noun (une rouge voiture); only the short ones like grand, petit, bon, beau, nouveau and vieux go first, the rest follow the noun (une voiture rouge).

probes.ex: un petit café
probes.exEn: a small coffee

probes.ex: Ce sac est trop cher.
probes.exEn: This bag is too expensive.

probes.ex: un vieux château
probes.exEn: an old castle

items.note: Means both big (for things) and tall (for people); goes before the noun and the feminine is grande with the d sounded.
items.ex: Mon frère est très grand.
items.exEn: My brother is very tall.

items.note: Goes before the noun; the feminine petite makes the silent t audible (puh-TEET).
items.ex: J'ai un petit appartement.
items.exEn: I have a small apartment.

items.note: Goes before the noun; the feminine bonne doubles the n, and the vowel stops being nasal.
items.ex: C'est un bon restaurant.
items.exEn: It's a good restaurant.

items.note: Goes before the noun; the final s is silent, and the feminine mauvaise makes it sound like z.
items.ex: C'est un mauvais film.
items.exEn: It's a bad film.

items.note: Goes before the noun; feminine belle, and bel before a masculine noun starting with a vowel (un bel homme).
items.ex: Quel beau jardin !
items.exEn: What a beautiful garden!

items.note: Goes before the noun; feminine nouvelle, and nouvel before a masculine noun starting with a vowel (un nouvel ami).
items.ex: J'ai un nouveau téléphone.
items.exEn: I have a new phone.

items.note: Goes before the noun; feminine vieille, and vieil before a masculine noun starting with a vowel (un vieil homme).
items.ex: C'est un vieux quartier.
items.exEn: It's an old neighbourhood.

items.note: Already ends in -e, so masculine and feminine look and sound the same; goes before the noun.
items.ex: Elle est très jeune.
items.exEn: She is very young.

items.note: Adjectives ending in -eux swap to -euse in the feminine: heureuse; the final x is silent.
items.ex: Je suis heureux de vous voir.
items.exEn: I'm happy to see you.

items.note: Ends in -e, so one form for both genders; like most adjectives it goes after the noun (un exercice facile).
items.ex: Cet exercice est facile.
items.exEn: This exercise is easy.

items.note: Ends in -e, so one form for both genders; goes after the noun (une question difficile).
items.ex: La question est difficile.
items.exEn: The question is difficult.

items.note: Goes after the noun when it means expensive; the feminine is chère. Before a name it means 'dear' (Cher Paul).
items.ex: Ce restaurant est trop cher.
items.exEn: This restaurant is too expensive.

teaching.rule: These are the verbs you will need in almost every conversation. The dictionary form (faire, voir, prendre) is the infinitive, the 'to ...' form; after je, tu, il and so on the ending changes (je fais, tu fais, il fait), and most of these verbs are irregular, so learn each one with its je form. The infinitive stays unchanged after vouloir, pouvoir and devoir: je veux manger, je peux venir, je dois partir.

examples.note: prendre (to take) is the normal verb for ordering food and drink; je prends is its je form.
pouvoir is conjugated (tu peux) and the second verb, venir, stays in the infinitive.
faire covers both 'do' and 'make'; tu fais is its tu form.

contrast.fr: Je veux un thé. (not Je vouloir un thé.)
contrast.note: The first verb after je must be conjugated; the infinitive is only used after another verb (je veux boire un thé).

contrast.fr: Je vois la tour Eiffel. (not Je regarde la tour Eiffel.)
contrast.note: voir is simply seeing with your eyes; regarder is watching or looking at something on purpose, so je regarde la tour Eiffel only if you are deliberately looking at it.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'je suis manger' for 'I am eating' because English uses 'to be' + -ing; French has no such form, so use the plain present: je mange.

probes.ex: Je prends le bus.
probes.exEn: I take the bus.

probes.ex: Tu veux un thé ?
probes.exEn: Do you want a tea?

probes.ex: Il boit du café.
probes.exEn: He drinks coffee.

items.note: One verb for both 'do' and 'make', and the base of many set phrases: faire la cuisine (cook), faire du sport; irregular (je fais, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font).
items.ex: J'aime faire la cuisine.
items.exEn: I like to cook.

items.note: Irregular: je dis, tu dis, il dit, nous disons, vous dites, ils disent; French uses dire for both 'say' and 'tell'.
items.ex: Qu'est-ce que tu dis ?
items.exEn: What are you saying?

items.note: Seeing with your eyes (je vois, nous voyons, ils voient); to watch or look at on purpose you use regarder instead.
items.ex: Je veux voir la mer.
items.exEn: I want to see the sea.

items.note: Irregular (je viens, tu viens, il/elle vient, nous venons, ils viennent); venir de + place means 'to come from'.
items.ex: Elle vient de Lyon.
items.exEn: She comes from Lyon.

items.note: Irregular (je prends, il prend, nous prenons, ils prennent); also the everyday verb for ordering: je prends un café.
items.ex: Je prends le métro.
items.exEn: I take the metro.

items.note: Irregular (je veux, tu veux, il veut, nous voulons, ils veulent); je veux sounds blunt, so when ordering say je voudrais (I would like).
items.ex: Je veux un café.
items.exEn: I want a coffee.

items.note: Irregular (je peux, tu peux, il peut, nous pouvons, ils peuvent); the next verb goes straight after it in the infinitive.
items.ex: Tu peux m'aider ?
items.exEn: Can you help me?

items.note: Irregular (je dois, tu dois, il doit, nous devons, ils doivent); followed directly by an infinitive, no 'to' needed.
items.ex: Je dois partir maintenant.
items.exEn: I have to leave now.

items.note: A regular -er verb (je mange, tu manges, il/elle/on mange); on is the everyday spoken 'we' and takes the il form; nous mangeons keeps the e so the g stays soft.
items.ex: On mange à midi.
items.exEn: We eat at noon.

items.note: Irregular: je bois, tu bois, il boit, but nous buvons, vous buvez, ils boivent.
items.ex: Je bois de l'eau.
items.exEn: I drink water.

items.note: An -er verb whose je, tu, il and ils forms take a grave accent: j'achète, tu achètes, il achète, ils achètent, but nous achetons, vous achetez.
items.ex: Je veux acheter du pain.
items.exEn: I want to buy some bread.

items.note: Irregular (je lis, tu lis, il lit, nous lisons, ils lisent); do not confuse it with rire (to laugh), which differs only by the first sound.
items.ex: Elle aime lire le soir.
items.exEn: She likes to read in the evening.

teaching.rule: The French R is made at the back of the throat, not with the tip of the tongue. Keep the tongue tip down behind your bottom teeth, raise the back of the tongue towards the soft palate and let the air rub through, like a very soft gargle or the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch'. It is strongest at the start of a word (rire), lighter between vowels (Paris) and almost whispered at the end of a word after a consonant (quatre).

examples.note: Two Rs: a clear one at the start, a softer one at the end; neither uses the tongue tip.
Between vowels the R is a light friction; the final s is silent (pa-REE).
After t at the end of a word the R is barely more than a breath: KATR.

contrast.note: The English R curls the tongue tip back; the French one keeps it down and makes the sound in the throat.
For L the tongue tip touches the ridge behind the teeth; for R it stays down, so the two words must sound clearly different.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers curl the tongue tip back for an American-style R (as in 'red'); keep the tip down and make the friction at the back of the throat instead, and do not roll it like Spanish either.

probes.ex: Elle aime rire.
probes.exEn: She likes to laugh.

probes.ex: On va à la mer.
probes.exEn: We are going to the sea.

probes.ex: C'est très bon.
probes.exEn: It's very good.

items.note: Start with the tongue tip down and the back of the tongue raised; the first R is strong, the final one soft. Keep it distinct from lire (to read).
items.ex: Elle aime rire.
items.exEn: She likes to laugh.

items.note: Word-initial R before 'i': make the throat friction first, then slide into a tight 'ee'; the z is silent (REE).
items.ex: Je mange du riz.
items.exEn: I eat rice.

items.note: Final R after a vowel is fully pronounced: finish the word with a short throat rub. It sounds exactly like mère (mother) and maire (mayor).
items.ex: On va à la mer.
items.exEn: We are going to the sea.

items.note: After t the R is a quick, light scrape rather than a full sound; the final s is silent (TREH).
items.ex: C'est très bon.
items.exEn: It's very good.

items.note: Consonant + R at the end of a word: the R is almost whispered and the final -e is silent, so it sounds like KATR.
items.ex: J'ai quatre frères.
items.exEn: I have four brothers.

items.note: The 'vr' cluster: keep the lips touching the teeth for v and let the throat R follow immediately, with no vowel in between (VREH).
items.ex: C'est vrai !
items.exEn: That's true!

items.note: Double rr is the same single throat sound, never a roll; the final -er sounds like 'ay' with no R at all (a-ree-VAY).
items.ex: Le train va arriver.
items.exEn: The train is about to arrive.

items.note: The 'fr' cluster: f then straight into the throat R, and the vowel after it is nasal (FRAHNSS).
items.ex: J'habite en France.
items.exEn: I live in France.

items.note: R between two vowels is light and quick: bu-RO, with rounded lips for both vowels; also means desk.
items.ex: Je travaille au bureau.
items.exEn: I work at the office.

items.note: Word-initial R before the rounded 'oo' vowel: round your lips while the throat friction is still going (ROOT).
items.ex: La route est longue.
items.exEn: The road is long.

items.note: Word-initial R before 'a': open the mouth wide right after the throat friction (ra-PEED); same form for masculine and feminine.
items.ex: Le train est rapide.
items.exEn: The train is fast.

items.note: R at the start before an open 'eh' (the ê) and a v at the end: REHV; the final -e is silent.
items.ex: C'est mon rêve.
items.exEn: It's my dream.

teaching.rule: A nasal vowel is a vowel where the air comes out through your nose and mouth at the same time, and the n or m written after it is NOT pronounced as a separate sound. French has three main ones: 'on' as in bon (lips rounded), 'an/en' as in cent (mouth wide open) and 'in/ain/ein/un' as in vin (lips slightly spread, like a nasal 'eh'). Look for a vowel + n or m at the end of a word or before another consonant; when the n or m is followed by a vowel (bonne, une, voisine), the vowel is normal and you hear the n.

examples.note: Say 'oh' with rounded lips and let the air go through your nose; do not close your mouth for an n at the end.
Open your mouth wide as for 'ah' and let the air go through your nose; 'en' and 'an' spell the same sound.
Spread your lips slightly as for 'eh' and send the air through your nose; 'in', 'ain', 'ein' and 'un' all spell this sound in everyday Paris French.

contrast.note: In bon the vowel is nasal and there is no n sound; in bonne the n is followed by a vowel, so the vowel is plain 'o' and the n is pronounced.
Three different words that differ only by which nasal vowel you make: spread lips (vin), open mouth (vent), rounded lips (vont).

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers finish the word with an English n or ng (saying 'bon' like 'bonn'); the tongue must not touch the roof of the mouth at the end, the nasal sound is in the vowel itself.

probes.ex: Je cours le matin.
probes.exEn: I run in the morning.

probes.ex: Ce train est lent.
probes.exEn: This train is slow.

probes.ex: On traverse le pont.
probes.exEn: We cross the bridge.

items.note: The 'on' nasal: round your lips as for 'oh' and let the air out through your nose; the written n is silent (NOH with nasal resonance).
items.ex: Non, merci.
items.exEn: No, thank you.

items.note: 'on' before a consonant is nasal; the final t is silent, so pont sounds just like the nasal vowel after p (POH).
items.ex: Le pont est très vieux.
items.exEn: The bridge is very old.

items.note: A written m after the vowel works exactly like n: nom and non sound identical, both ending in the nasal 'on' with no closed lips.
items.ex: Quel est votre nom ?
items.exEn: What is your name?

items.note: 'on' + d: make the rounded nasal vowel, then the d; tout le monde (literally 'all the world') means everybody.
items.ex: Tout le monde est là.
items.exEn: Everybody is here.

items.note: The 'an/en' nasal: drop your jaw as for 'ah' and send the air through your nose; the final t is silent (LAH with nasal resonance).
items.ex: Le bus est lent.
items.exEn: The bus is slow.

items.note: 'an' before g is the same open nasal as in lent; langue also means tongue, the body part.
items.ex: Le français est une belle langue.
items.exEn: French is a beautiful language.

items.note: 'en' before d gives the open nasal (a-TAHNDR); a false friend, since attendre means to wait, not to attend.
items.ex: Je vais attendre ici.
items.exEn: I am going to wait here.

items.note: Two different nasals in one word: open-mouth 'an' first, then rounded-lips 'on' (shah-SOH), with no n sound in either.
items.ex: J'aime cette chanson.
items.exEn: I like this song.

items.note: The 'in' nasal: spread your lips slightly as for 'eh' and send the air through your nose (ma-TEH); the n is not pronounced.
items.ex: Je travaille le matin.
items.exEn: I work in the morning.

items.note: 'ain' is spelled differently but is the same nasal as 'in' (TREH with nasal resonance); en retard has the open 'en' nasal.
items.ex: Le train est en retard.
items.exEn: The train is late.

items.note: 'in' at the end of the word is nasal: vwa-ZEH with the air through the nose and no n sound at all.
items.ex: Mon voisin est sympa.
items.exEn: My neighbour (a man) is nice.

items.note: Add -e and the n is now followed by a vowel, so the nasal disappears: vwa-ZEEN with a clear n; the same switch happens in bon/bonne and un/une.
items.ex: Ma voisine est sympa.
items.exEn: My neighbour (a woman) is nice.

teaching.rule: Always open any exchange with bonjour (bonsoir after about 6 pm) before you ask for anything, even in a shop or at a ticket window, and close it with au revoir; skipping these sounds rude in France. Add s'il vous plaît when you ask for something and merci when you get it, and answer merci with de rien. Keep salut and s'il te plaît for friends and people you call tu.

examples.fr: Bonjour, un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
examples.note: Greeting first, then the request, then s'il vous plaît at the end: the standard shop formula.

examples.en: Thank you very much! — You're welcome.
examples.note: de rien (literally 'of nothing') is the everyday reply to thanks.
Leaving a shop: au revoir plus a wish like bonne journée (daytime) or bonne soirée (evening).
salut is only for friends and family; it also works as 'bye'.

contrast.note: salut with a stranger, a shopkeeper or your boss sounds overly familiar; use bonjour with anyone you would call vous.
bonne nuit is only said when someone is going to bed; to greet people in the evening use bonsoir.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers walk up to a counter and start with their request, as they would at home; in France say bonjour first, otherwise the person may not respond warmly or at all.

probes.ex: — Merci ! — De rien.
probes.exEn: — Thanks! — You're welcome.

probes.ex: Bonsoir madame.
probes.exEn: Good evening, madam.

probes.ex: Excusez-moi, vous avez l'heure ?
probes.exEn: Excuse me, do you have the time?

items.note: The default daytime greeting, said to everyone before anything else, from shopkeepers to bus drivers; used until early evening, and normally only once a day to the same person.
items.ex: Bonjour, vous avez une table pour deux ?
items.exEn: Hello, do you have a table for two?

items.note: Replaces bonjour from about 6 pm; used both when arriving and, more formally, when leaving in the evening.
items.ex: Bonsoir, je voudrais réserver une table.
items.exEn: Good evening, I would like to book a table.

items.note: Casual greeting for friends, family and classmates, and also a casual goodbye; never use it with a stranger or someone you call vous.
items.ex: Salut Léa, ça va ?
items.exEn: Hi Léa, how are you?

items.note: Used constantly, even for tiny things like being handed change; to refuse an offer politely say non merci.
items.ex: Merci beaucoup, madame.
items.exEn: Thank you very much, madam.

items.note: Literally 'if it pleases you', with the polite vous; add it at the end of any request to a stranger, waiter or shop assistant.
items.ex: L'addition, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: The bill, please.

items.note: The same formula with te, for one person you call tu: a friend, a family member or a child.
items.ex: Papa, passe-moi le sel, s'il te plaît.
items.exEn: Dad, pass me the salt, please.

items.note: Literally 'of nothing'; the relaxed, everyday reply to merci in any situation.
items.ex: — Merci ! — De rien.
items.exEn: — Thanks! — You're welcome.

items.note: A more formal reply to thanks than de rien, typical from staff or with vous; it also means 'please, go ahead' when you hold a door or offer a seat.
items.ex: — Merci beaucoup, madame. — Je vous en prie.
items.exEn: — Thank you very much, madam. — You're welcome.

items.note: To get a stranger's or a waiter's attention, or to squeeze past someone; uses the vous form, so with a friend say excuse-moi.
items.ex: Excusez-moi, où sont les toilettes ?
items.exEn: Excuse me, where are the toilets?

items.note: Literally 'until seeing again'; the standard goodbye in any situation, said every time you leave a shop or office.
items.ex: Au revoir et bonne journée !
items.exEn: Goodbye and have a good day!

items.note: Literally 'delighted', said when you are introduced to someone; a woman says and writes enchantée.
items.ex: Enchanté, je m'appelle Paul.
items.exEn: Nice to meet you, my name is Paul.

items.note: A quick apology when you bump into someone, or, with rising voice, a request to repeat; for a real apology use désolé (désolée for a woman).
items.ex: Pardon, je n'ai pas compris.
items.exEn: Sorry, I didn't understand.

teaching.rule: Most consonants written at the end of a French word are silent: the t of petit, the s of vous, the p of beaucoup, the d of grand, the x of deux. A plural -s and the verb ending -ent (ils parlent) are silent too. The main exceptions are c, r, f and l (think of the English word CaReFuL), which are usually pronounced: avec, le sel, neuf, finir. But the r of the -er infinitive ending is silent (parler). When a feminine -e follows the consonant, the consonant is no longer last, so you hear it: petit (peu-TI) but petite (peu-TIT).

examples.note: The final t is silent: peu-TI. The word ends on the vowel sound.
The s of ils (before a consonant) and the -ent ending are both silent, so ils parlent sounds exactly like il parle: il-PARL.
c and l are among the final consonants that are usually pronounced: a-VEK, SEL.

contrast.note: In petit the t is last and silent; in petite the -e follows it, so the t is heard. Often this consonant is the only spoken difference between masculine and feminine.
The r of the -er infinitive is silent (par-LÉ); the r of -ir infinitives is pronounced (fi-NIR).

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers pronounce every letter they see, saying the t of petit or the s of vous; stop on the vowel instead. The opposite slip is dropping a final c, r, f or l, which are usually heard: say the c of avec and the l of sel.

probes.ask: How is “beaucoup” pronounced?
probes.ex: Il mange beaucoup.
probes.exEn: He eats a lot.
options: both the c and the p are silent: 'bo-ou'

probes.en: exactly like il chante: the -ent is silent
probes.ask: How does “ils chantent” sound?
probes.ex: Ils chantent bien.
probes.exEn: They sing well.
options: the s of ils is pronounced: 'ils-shant'

probes.ask: How is “le sac” pronounced?
probes.ex: Où est mon sac ?
probes.exEn: Where is my bag?
options: the c is said as s: 'sas'
the c is said as ch: 'sash'

items.note: The final p is silent and eau is a single 'o' sound: bo-KOU. The word ends on the vowel.
items.ex: Il travaille beaucoup.
items.exEn: He works a lot.

items.note: The d is silent but the r before it is heard: TAR. For being late for something, French says en retard instead.
items.ex: Il est tard, je rentre.
items.exEn: It's late, I'm going home.

items.en: too (as in too expensive) / too much
items.note: The p is silent: TRO, with the same o as in beau. Like beaucoup, it ends on the vowel.
items.ex: C'est trop cher.
items.exEn: It's too expensive.

items.note: The t is silent: MO, ending on a round o. Mot rhymes with beau.
items.ex: Je ne connais pas ce mot.
items.exEn: I don't know this word.

items.note: The s is silent: MWA, exactly like moi (me). Only the article and the context tell the two apart.
items.ex: Je pars le mois prochain.
items.exEn: I'm leaving next month.

items.note: In the -er ending of an infinitive the r is silent: par-LÉ, so parler sounds like parlez. The r in the middle (par-) is pronounced.
items.ex: Je voudrais parler à Sophie.
items.exEn: I'd like to speak to Sophie.

items.note: Unlike -er verbs, -ir infinitives keep their final r: shwa-ZIR. The s between two vowels sounds like z.
items.ex: Tu dois choisir une couleur.
items.exEn: You have to choose a colour.

items.note: A final c is usually pronounced: SAK. Think of the English word CaReFuL: c, r, f and l at the end are usually heard.
items.ex: Mon sac est lourd.
items.exEn: My bag is heavy.

items.note: A final l is pronounced: SEL, rhyming with belle.
items.ex: Tu peux me passer le sel ?
items.exEn: Can you pass me the salt?

items.note: The d is silent and au is a single 'o': SHO. The word ends on the vowel.
items.ex: Le café est chaud.
items.exEn: The coffee is hot.

items.note: The added -e means the d is no longer last, so you hear it: SHOD. In many adjectives this consonant is the only spoken difference between masculine and feminine.
items.ex: La soupe est chaude.
items.exEn: The soup is hot (soupe is feminine).

items.note: The verb ending -ent is silent: il-SHANT. Ils chantent sounds exactly like il chante, so only the context tells you it is plural.
items.ex: Ils chantent très bien.
items.exEn: They sing very well.

teaching.rule: French accents are part of the spelling, and four of them matter most for pronunciation. é (accent aigu) is a closed 'ay' sound, shorter than English 'day' and with no glide: le thé, la clé. è (accent grave) and ê (accent circonflexe) are both the open 'eh' of English 'bed': la mère, la fête. ç (cédille) only appears before a, o or u and makes the c sound like s instead of k: ça, le garçon. On à and ù the accent changes nothing in the sound; it only tells words apart in writing (a / à, ou / où). An e with no accent at the end of a word is usually silent, so an accent on a final e tells you to say it: aime ends on the m, aimé ends on 'ay'.

examples.note: é is a tight 'ay' with no glide at the end: TÉ. The h is silent.
è is open, like the e in 'bed': MÈR.
The cedilla makes c sound like s before a: SA. Without it, ca would read 'ka'.

contrast.note: In marche the final e is silent (MARSH); the accent on marché makes the last syllable heard: mar-SHÉ.
é is closed, with the lips spread and the jaw high (ka-FÉ); ê is open, with the jaw lower (FÈT). Mixing them up can change the word.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers treat accents as decoration: they say é, è and ê the same way, or read garçon with a k. Keep é closed ('ay'), è and ê open ('eh' as in 'bed'), and ç always as s.

probes.ask: How are the two é's of “bébé” pronounced?
probes.ex: Le bébé a faim.
probes.exEn: The baby is hungry.
options: both are silent, like a final e
both are an open 'eh', as in 'bed'

probes.ask: How is the è of “la bière” pronounced?
probes.ex: Il boit une bière.
probes.exEn: He's drinking a beer.

probes.ask: How is the ç of “le garçon” pronounced?
probes.ex: Ce garçon est mon frère.
probes.exEn: This boy is my brother.

items.note: é is a closed 'ay' sound with no glide at the end: KLÉ. Without the accent, a final e would be silent.
items.ex: J'ai perdu ma clé.
items.exEn: I've lost my key.

items.note: Two é's, both closed and short: bé-BÉ. Keep the jaw still; English 'bay-bay' glides too much.
items.ex: Le bébé dort.
items.exEn: The baby is sleeping.

items.note: Both é's are closed 'ay' sounds, and the s between two vowels sounds like z: dé-zo-LÉ. A woman writes désolée, which sounds the same.
items.ex: Je suis désolé, je suis en retard.
items.exEn: I'm sorry, I'm late.

items.note: é is a closed 'ay': dé-JA. The grave accent on the final à changes nothing in the sound; it is only spelling.
items.ex: Tu es déjà là ?
items.exEn: You're here already?

items.note: ê sounds like è, an open 'eh' as in 'bed': MÈM. The final e is silent.
items.ex: C'est la même chose.
items.exEn: It's the same thing.

items.note: ê is the open 'eh' of 'bed' and the final e is silent: ÈTR, a single syllable.
items.ex: Je veux être médecin.
items.exEn: I want to be a doctor.

items.note: ê is an open 'eh' and the final t is silent: fo-RÈ. The circumflex often stands for an s that French lost and English kept: forêt / forest, fête / feast.
items.ex: On se promène dans la forêt.
items.exEn: We're walking in the forest.

items.note: è is open, like the e in 'bed': BYÈR. The grave accent tells you not to say a closed é here.
items.ex: Une bière, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: A beer, please.

items.note: è is an open 'eh': PYÈS. Une pièce is any room of a home (a bedroom is une chambre); the word also means a coin and a play.
items.ex: L'appartement a trois pièces.
items.exEn: The flat has three rooms.

items.note: Two different accents, two different sounds: a closed é, then an open è (é-LÈV). Reading both the same way is the classic slip.
items.ex: C'est un bon élève.
items.exEn: He's a good pupil.

items.note: The cedilla makes the c sound like s before o: gar-SON. Without it, co would read 'ko'.
items.ex: Le garçon joue dans le jardin.
items.exEn: The boy is playing in the garden.

items.note: The cedilla makes the c sound like s before o: leu-SON. Without it, co would read 'ko'.
items.ex: Je ne comprends pas cette leçon.
items.exEn: I don't understand this lesson.

teaching.rule: A handful of very short words lose their final vowel when the next word starts with a vowel sound (a vowel or a silent h), and an apostrophe takes its place: je, me, te, se, le, la, ne, de, que, and ce before forms of être (c'est). So je + arrive becomes j'arrive, le + homme becomes l'homme, ne + aime becomes n'aime. Before y, only the pronoun y triggers it (j'y vais, il n'y a pas): it stays le yaourt. Si elides only before il and ils (s'il, s'ils), never before elle. Elision is not casual or optional: it is required in careful speech and in writing, and the two words are said as one.

examples.note: ne + habite becomes n'habite, because the h of habiter is silent and counts as a vowel.
que + elle becomes qu'elle, said as one word: KEL. Que elides before any vowel.
je + aime becomes j'aime, said as one syllable: JÈM.

contrast.note: si drops its i only before il and ils; before elle, on or any other vowel it stays whole.
Most words starting with h behave as if they started with a vowel (l'homme). A small set have an 'aspirated' h that blocks elision: le héros, with a tiny break. Dictionaries mark these words.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers keep both vowels and say 'je arrive', 'le homme' or 'de accord'. These little words never sit in front of a vowel sound: say and write j'arrive, l'homme, d'accord. The opposite slip is eliding si before elle ('s'elle'), which is always wrong.

probes.ask: How is je + arrive written and said?
probes.ex: J'arrive tout de suite !
probes.exEn: I'm coming right away!
options: je arrive, with both vowels said
j'arrive, with a pause after j'

probes.ask: What happens to si before elle?
probes.ex: Si elle vient, on part ensemble.
probes.exEn: If she comes, we'll leave together.

probes.en: the h is 'aspirated': it is not pronounced, but it blocks elision
probes.ask: Why is it “le héros” and not “l'héros”?
probes.ex: C'est le héros du film.
probes.exEn: He's the hero of the film.
options: the h is pronounced, as in English 'hero'
le never elides before a masculine noun
elision happens only before a vowel letter, never before an h

items.note: je + arrive: the e of je drops and the two words are said as one: zha-RIV. Je arrive is never correct.
items.ex: J'arrive à la gare à midi.
items.exEn: I arrive at the station at noon.

items.note: de + accord: da-KOR. Être d'accord means to agree; d'accord on its own means OK.
items.ex: Tu es d'accord avec moi ?
items.exEn: Do you agree with me?

items.note: The h of homme is silent, so le elides exactly as before a vowel: LOM.
items.ex: L'homme attend le bus.
items.exEn: The man is waiting for the bus.

items.note: quelque + un becomes quelqu'un, said as one word with the nasal un at the end: kèl-KUN. It is one of the very few places quelque loses its e.
items.ex: Il y a quelqu'un ?
items.exEn: Is anyone there?

items.note: me + appelle becomes m'appelle, said ma-PÈL. Literally 'I call myself'.
items.ex: Je m'appelle Léa.
items.exEn: My name is Léa.

items.note: ne + aime becomes n'aime: the ne of a negation elides like any other, as in je n'ai pas and ce n'est pas.
items.ex: Il n'aime pas le café.
items.exEn: He doesn't like coffee.

items.note: que + il becomes qu'il, said KIL. Que elides before any vowel: qu'elle, qu'on, qu'un.
items.ex: Je crois qu'il est malade.
items.exEn: I think he's ill.

items.note: si elides only before il and ils: s'il, s'ils. Before elle or on it stays whole: si elle, si on.
items.ex: S'il pleut, on reste à la maison.
items.exEn: If it rains, we'll stay at home.

items.note: te + aime becomes t'aime, said TÈM. Me, te and se all elide before a vowel.
items.ex: Il t'aime, tu sais.
items.exEn: He loves you, you know.

items.note: de + orange becomes d'orange, said in one run with jus: zhu-do-RANJ. De elides before any vowel: un jus d'ananas, une tasse d'eau chaude.
items.ex: Je voudrais un jus d'orange.
items.exEn: I'd like an orange juice.

items.note: de + Italie becomes d'Italie. Compare de Lyon, where de stays whole because Lyon starts with a consonant.
items.ex: Elle vient d'Italie.
items.exEn: She comes from Italy.

items.note: je + écoute becomes j'écoute, said zhé-KOUT. Je keeps its e only before a consonant: je parle, but j'écoute.
items.ex: J'écoute de la musique.
items.exEn: I'm listening to music.

teaching.rule: Where English says 'I am' plus a bodily feeling, French says 'I have' plus a noun: j'ai faim (I'm hungry, literally 'I have hunger'), j'ai soif, j'ai chaud, j'ai froid, j'ai peur. Age works the same way, j'ai trente ans (I'm thirty), and in a full sentence the word ans must be said. So does being right or wrong, avoir raison and avoir tort, and two very common expressions take de before what follows: avoir besoin de (to need) and avoir envie de (to feel like). Conjugate avoir for the subject (j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont) and leave the word after it as it is: it never agrees, so elle a froid, not 'elle a froide'. To say 'very', add très: j'ai très faim.

examples.note: Literally 'I have hunger': faim is a noun, so French uses avoir where English uses 'to be'.
Age is something you have, and in a full sentence ans (years) is required: never just 'il a vingt-cinq'.
Being right is having reason: avoir raison. Its opposite is avoir tort.

contrast.note: For the weather use faire: il fait froid. For a person feeling the cold use avoir: j'ai froid.
avoir tort is for a person who is mistaken; for a statement or an answer that is incorrect, say c'est faux.

teaching.commonMistake: Once avoir is in place, learners still treat the word after it as an adjective and make it agree: 'elle a froide', 'ils ont chauds'; faim, soif, froid, chaud and peur never change here. They also drop ans from an age in a full sentence ('il a trente') and use avoir tort for a wrong answer, which is c'est faux.

probes.ex: Ferme la porte, j'ai froid.
probes.exEn: Close the door, I'm cold.

probes.ex: Écoute-le, il a raison.
probes.exEn: Listen to him, he's right.

probes.ex: Tu as besoin d'aide avec ta valise ?
probes.exEn: Do you need help with your suitcase?

items.note: Hunger is something you have: tu as faim, literally 'you have hunger'. Never 'tu es faim'.
items.ex: Tu as faim ?
items.exEn: Are you hungry?

items.note: Like faim, soif is a noun, so it follows avoir: j'ai soif. Add très for 'very': j'ai très soif.
items.ex: J'ai soif, tu as de l'eau ?
items.exEn: I'm thirsty, do you have any water?

items.note: A person feeling hot is j'ai chaud. Chaud does not change for the speaker, so a woman also says j'ai chaud.
items.ex: Ouvre la fenêtre, j'ai trop chaud.
items.exEn: Open the window, I'm too hot.

items.note: ont is the ils/elles form of avoir. 'Ils sont froids' would describe them as cold to the touch or unfriendly, not as feeling cold.
items.ex: Les enfants ont froid.
items.exEn: The children are cold.

items.note: What you are afraid of follows de, and de + les becomes des: elle a peur des chiens.
items.ex: Elle a peur des araignées.
items.exEn: She's afraid of spiders.

items.note: Literally 'to have reason'. It works for any subject: tu as raison, ils ont raison.
items.ex: Tu as raison, c'est trop cher.
items.exEn: You're right, it's too expensive.

items.note: Use it for a person who is mistaken. For a wrong answer or a false statement, say c'est faux.
items.ex: Je crois que tu as tort.
items.exEn: I think you're wrong.

items.note: The thing you need follows de, which shortens to d' before a vowel: j'ai besoin d'un café.
items.ex: J'ai besoin d'un café.
items.exEn: I need a coffee.

items.note: A softer way to say you want something: j'ai envie d'une glace, or with a verb, j'ai envie de dormir.
items.ex: J'ai envie d'une glace.
items.exEn: I feel like an ice cream.

items.note: à + the body part with le, la or les, not 'my': j'ai mal à la tête, j'ai mal au dos, j'ai mal aux dents.
items.ex: J'ai mal à la tête.
items.exEn: I have a headache.

items.note: Age takes avoir, and the word ans must be said: mon frère a trente ans, never 'mon frère est trente'.
items.ex: Mon frère a trente ans.
items.exEn: My brother is thirty.

items.note: Literally 'to have some luck', with the partitive de la: here chance means luck. A very common reaction to good news.
items.ex: Tu as de la chance !
items.exEn: You're lucky!

teaching.rule: French has two words for 'you'. Use tu when you talk to ONE person you are close to: a friend, a family member, a child, a classmate. Use vous with one person you don't know well, someone older, or anyone serving you or working with you (shopkeeper, waiter, boss), and ALWAYS when you talk to two or more people. The verb changes with it: tu takes an -s ending (tu parles, tu as), vous takes -ez (vous parlez, vous avez; the one exception to learn is vous êtes). When in doubt, say vous: it is never rude, and the other person will offer 'tu' if they want it.

examples.en: Are you coming tonight? (to a friend)
examples.note: One close person, so tu; the verb ends in -s (viens).

examples.fr: Vous avez une table pour deux ?
examples.en: Do you have a table for two? (to a waiter)
examples.note: A stranger doing their job gets vous; the verb ends in -ez (avez).
Even children get vous when there are several of them: vous is the only plural 'you'.

examples.en: Can we use 'tu' with each other?
examples.note: The polite way to switch; wait for the older or more senior person to suggest it.

contrast.en: Hello madam, do you have the time? (wrong register)
contrast.note: Madame signals a stranger, so tu sounds rude here; say 'vous avez l'heure ?'.

contrast.en: Hi Léa, how are you? (too stiff)
contrast.note: Salut and a first name are informal, so vous is odd here; say 'tu vas bien ?'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers default to tu because it feels like plain 'you'; default to vous with anyone you would not call by their first name, and remember that a group is always vous.

probes.en: you (formal, or more than one person)
probes.ex: Vous êtes de Paris ?
probes.exEn: Are you from Paris?

probes.ex: Excusez-moi, vous avez l'heure ?
probes.exEn: Excuse me, do you have the time?

probes.ex: Salut Léa, tu vas bien ?
probes.exEn: Hi Léa, how are you?

items.note: The verb for formal address, a regular -er verb built on vous (je vouvoie, tu vouvoies, il vouvoie); it is what you do with strangers, elders and colleagues you don't know well.
items.ex: Je vouvoie toujours mon patron.
items.exEn: I always address my boss as 'vous'.

items.note: The verb for informal address, built on tu; used with friends, family and children.
items.ex: Tu peux me tutoyer, tu sais.
items.exEn: You can call me 'tu', you know.

items.note: The standard phrase for proposing the switch to informal; the senior or older person usually says it first.
items.ex: On se tutoie ? — Oui, bien sûr !
items.exEn: Shall we use 'tu'? — Yes, of course!

items.note: Masculine noun for the habit of saying vous; it is the normal register at work and in shops.
items.ex: Le vouvoiement est normal au travail.
items.exEn: Using 'vous' is normal at work.

items.en: Where do you live? (to a friend)
items.note: Informal question: tu plus the -s verb ending (habites), with the question word at the end as in casual speech.
items.ex: Tu habites où ? Moi, à Lyon.
items.exEn: Where do you live? Me, in Lyon.

items.en: Where do you live? (to a stranger)
items.note: Same question in the polite register: vous plus the -ez ending (habitez).
items.ex: Et vous, vous habitez où ?
items.exEn: And you, where do you live?

items.en: Do you have the time? (to a friend)
items.note: Casual request to a peer: tu and the short verb form 'as'; note the rising question tone with no 'est-ce que'.
items.ex: Tu as l'heure ? Mon portable est mort.
items.exEn: Do you have the time? My phone is dead.

items.en: Do you have the time? (to a stranger)
items.note: The vous version of the same request, usually opened with 'excusez-moi' when speaking to someone in the street.
items.ex: Excusez-moi, vous avez l'heure ?
items.exEn: Excuse me, do you have the time?

items.en: Can you help me? (to a stranger)
items.note: Polite request with the verb before vous and a hyphen; the -ez ending (pouvez) marks the formal register.
items.ex: Pardon, pouvez-vous m'aider ?
items.exEn: Sorry, can you help me?

items.en: Can you help me? (to a friend)
items.note: Informal request: tu and the -x ending of 'peux' (pouvoir keeps -x instead of -s in the tu form).
items.ex: Tu peux m'aider ? C'est lourd.
items.exEn: Can you help me? It's heavy.

items.en: What would you like? (shop or café)
items.note: The stock phrase a server or shopkeeper uses to a customer; the customer is always vous, so answer with vous too.
items.ex: Bonjour, vous désirez ?
items.exEn: Hello, what would you like?

items.note: Vous for a group: prêts takes plural -s because it describes several people, even if they are all close friends.
items.ex: Allez, vous êtes prêts ? On part !
items.exEn: Come on, are you all ready? We're leaving!

teaching.rule: A French adjective changes its ending to match the noun it describes, whether it sits next to the noun or after être (to be). Start from the masculine form: add -e for a feminine noun (petit / petite), add -s for a plural (petit / petits; if the masculine already ends in -s or -x, like français or heureux, the plural adds nothing), and add -es for feminine plural (petites). If the masculine already ends in -e (rouge, calme), it stays the same for feminine. Listen for the difference: adding -e often makes a silent final consonant audible (petit 'peu-ti' becomes petite 'peu-tit').

examples.fr: un petit café, une petite maison
examples.en: a small cafe, a small house
examples.note: maison is feminine, so petit takes -e; you now hear the t at the end of petite.
Plural noun, so content takes -s, even though the adjective sits after être and the -s is silent.
Feminine plural: both endings stack, grand + e + s = grandes.

examples.fr: un pull rouge, une jupe rouge
examples.en: a red sweater, a red skirt
examples.note: rouge already ends in -e, so masculine and feminine look and sound the same.

contrast.note: Adjectives in -eux do not just add -e: -eux becomes -euse (heureux / heureuse). 'heureuxe' does not exist.
beau is irregular: its feminine is belle, not 'beaue'. Learn beau / belle, nouveau / nouvelle, vieux / vieille as pairs.
A mixed group takes the masculine plural: contents, not contentes, even with one man among many women.

teaching.commonMistake: English adjectives never change, so learners write 'une grand maison' or 'elles sont fatigué'; always check the noun's gender and number and adjust the ending (grande, fatiguées).

probes.ex: Ma voisine a une voiture verte.
probes.exEn: My neighbour has a green car.

probes.ex: Ils sont fatigués après le travail.
probes.exEn: They are tired after work.

probes.ex: Ma mère est très sérieuse.
probes.exEn: My mother is very serious.

items.note: Feminine of petit: add -e, and the final t, silent in petit, is now pronounced ('peu-tit').
items.ex: C'est une petite maison.
items.exEn: It's a small house.

items.note: After être the adjective still agrees with the subject: elle is feminine, so grand takes -e and you hear the d. For people grand means tall; for things it means big.
items.ex: Elle est grande.
items.exEn: She is tall.

items.note: Plural masculine: add -s to grand. The -s is silent, so grand and grands sound identical; only the article and verb show the plural.
items.ex: Les arbres sont grands.
items.exEn: The trees are big.

items.note: Feminine plural stacks both endings: vert + e + s = vertes; pommes is feminine and plural.
items.ex: Les pommes sont vertes.
items.exEn: The apples are green.

items.note: calme already ends in -e, so it does not change for a feminine noun; only the plural adds -s (calmes).
items.ex: Ma mère est très calme.
items.exEn: My mother is very calm.

items.note: Adjectives in -eux change to -euse for the feminine: heureux / heureuse. Listen for the new 'z' sound at the end.
items.ex: Ma sœur est heureuse.
items.exEn: My sister is happy.

items.note: Adjectives in -f change to -ve for the feminine: neuf / neuve; voiture is feminine.
items.ex: J'ai une voiture neuve.
items.exEn: I have a brand-new car.

items.note: beau is irregular: the feminine is belle, with a double l; maison is feminine.
items.ex: Quelle belle maison !
items.exEn: What a beautiful house!

items.note: blanc is irregular: the feminine is blanche, and the silent c turns into an audible 'sh' sound.
items.ex: Elle porte une chemise blanche.
items.exEn: She is wearing a white shirt.

items.note: bon doubles the n before adding -e: bonne. The nasal 'bon' becomes a clear 'bon-n' sound.
items.ex: C'est une bonne idée.
items.exEn: It's a good idea.

items.note: fatigué keeps its accent and adds -s for a plural subject; a group with at least one man uses this masculine plural form.
items.ex: Nous sommes fatigués.
items.exEn: We are tired.

items.note: Nationality adjectives agree too and are written with a small letter: français + e + s = françaises for a group of women.
items.ex: Elles sont françaises.
items.exEn: They (women) are French.

teaching.rule: In French most adjectives come AFTER the noun, the opposite of English: une voiture rouge (a red car), un film français. A small group of very common short adjectives come BEFORE the noun, as in English; remember them with BAGS: Beauty (beau, joli), Age (jeune, vieux, nouveau), Goodness (bon, mauvais), Size (grand, petit, gros). Colours and nationalities always go after. Wherever it sits, the adjective still agrees with the noun.

examples.note: Colour adjectives always follow the noun: say 'a shirt blue'.
petit is a Size adjective (BAGS), so it goes before the noun, as in English.
vieux is an Age adjective, so it comes first; it also takes the irregular feminine vieille.
Nationality adjectives follow the noun and are written with a small letter.

contrast.fr: un ancien collègue / un immeuble ancien
contrast.en: a former colleague / an old building
contrast.note: A few adjectives change meaning with position: ancien before the noun means 'former', after it means 'old'.
nouveau, beau and vieux take a special form (nouvel, bel, vieil) before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h, precisely because they come first.
Long adjectives (intéressant, important, difficile) go after the noun even when English puts them first.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers put every adjective before the noun ('une rouge voiture', 'un français film'); keep the English order only for the short BAGS adjectives and put everything else after the noun.

probes.en: correct: colour adjectives go after the noun
probes.ask: Is “une voiture rouge” right, and why?
probes.ex: Elle a acheté une voiture rouge.
probes.exEn: She bought a red car.
options: wrong: it should be une rouge voiture
correct: rouge is a BAGS adjective, so it can go anywhere
wrong: it should be une voiture rouges

probes.en: correct: vieux is an Age adjective (BAGS), so it goes before the noun
probes.ask: Is “un vieil homme” right, and why?
probes.ex: Un vieil homme attend le bus.
probes.exEn: An old man is waiting for the bus.
options: wrong: it should be un homme vieil
wrong: it should be un homme vieux
correct: every French adjective goes before the noun

probes.ex: Marc est un ancien ami de ma mère.
probes.exEn: Marc is a former friend of my mother's.

items.note: Default order: noun first, then the adjective. Colours always follow the noun; rouge already ends in -e so it does not change.
items.ex: Mon père a une voiture rouge.
items.exEn: My father has a red car.

items.note: beau is a Beauty adjective (BAGS), so it goes before the noun, as in English.
items.ex: Ils ont un beau chien.
items.exEn: They have a beautiful dog.

items.note: grand is a Size adjective, so it comes before the noun, and takes -e because maison is feminine.
items.ex: Nous habitons dans une grande maison.
items.exEn: We live in a big house.

items.note: petit (Size) goes before the noun; problème is masculine despite ending in -e, so no agreement change.
items.ex: J'ai un petit problème.
items.exEn: I have a small problem.

items.note: bon (Goodness) goes before the noun; its opposite mauvais does the same: un mauvais livre.
items.ex: C'est un bon livre.
items.exEn: It's a good book.

items.note: nouveau (Age: newness) goes first, and takes the irregular feminine nouvelle because idée is feminine.
items.ex: J'ai une nouvelle idée !
items.exEn: I have a new idea!

items.note: vieux (Age) goes before the noun and becomes vieil before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h, to avoid two vowels clashing.
items.ex: Je parle avec un vieil homme.
items.exEn: I'm talking with an old man.

items.note: jeune (Age) comes before the noun; it already ends in -e, so it is the same for masculine and feminine.
items.ex: Une jeune femme attend le bus.
items.exEn: A young woman is waiting for the bus.

items.note: Colour after the noun, and bleu takes -e to agree with the feminine robe.
items.ex: Elle porte une robe bleue.
items.exEn: She is wearing a blue dress.

items.note: Nationality adjectives always follow the noun and take a small letter, unlike English 'French'.
items.ex: On regarde un film français ce soir.
items.exEn: We're watching a French film tonight.

items.note: ancien before the noun means 'former, previous'; the position changes the meaning, not just the style.
items.ex: C'est un ancien ami de mon père.
items.exEn: He's a former friend of my father's.

items.note: ancien after the noun means 'old, historic'; compare un ancien ami (a former friend). Feminine maison gives ancienne with a double n.
items.ex: Ils habitent dans une maison ancienne.
items.exEn: They live in an old house.

teaching.rule: When you talk about SOME of something you cannot count (bread, water, music, time), French needs a small word before the noun where English can leave a gap: je mange du pain (I eat bread). Pick it by the noun's gender: du for masculine (du pain), de la for feminine (de la soupe), de l' before a vowel or silent h (de l'eau), and des for plurals (des fruits). After a negative (ne... pas, except after être: ce n'est pas du pain) and after quantity words (beaucoup, un peu, trop) all of these shrink to plain de: pas de pain, beaucoup de pain.

examples.note: pain is masculine, so 'some' is du (a contraction of de + le).
limonade is feminine, so 'some' is de la; English drops the word, French cannot.
Before a vowel de la and du both become de l'.

examples.fr: Je ne mange pas de viande.
examples.note: After ne... pas the partitive collapses to de: not 'pas de la viande'.

contrast.note: After aimer, adorer, détester and préférer use le / la / les (bread in general), not du: you like the whole category, not a portion.
un pain is one countable loaf; du pain is an unmeasured amount. Same noun, different article.
After a quantity word there is no article at all: beaucoup de, never 'beaucoup du'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers drop the article ('je mange pain', 'je bois eau') because English says 'I eat bread'; French always needs du / de la / de l' / des before an uncounted noun.

probes.ex: Il reste de la soupe dans la casserole.
probes.exEn: There is some soup left in the pan.

probes.fr: Je ne bois pas de lait.
probes.ex: Je ne bois pas de lait le matin.
probes.exEn: I don't drink milk in the morning.
options: I drink a lot of milk.

probes.en: some water (noun starts with a vowel)
probes.ex: Je bois de l'eau à chaque repas.
probes.exEn: I drink water at every meal.

items.note: pain is masculine, so 'some' is du, a contraction of de + le; French cannot drop the article the way English does.
items.ex: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: I'd like some bread, please.

items.note: soupe is feminine, so 'some' is de la, written as two words and never contracted.
items.ex: Ce soir, je mange de la soupe.
items.exEn: Tonight I'm eating soup.

items.note: eau starts with a vowel, so de la becomes de l' with an apostrophe, whatever the gender.
items.ex: Tu veux de l'eau ?
items.exEn: Do you want some water?

items.note: argent is masculine but starts with a vowel, so du becomes de l'; money is uncountable, hence the partitive.
items.ex: Tu as de l'argent sur toi ?
items.exEn: Do you have any money on you?

items.note: fromage is masculine (most -age nouns are), so du; English 'there is cheese' has no article, French must add one.
items.ex: Il y a du fromage dans le frigo.
items.exEn: There is cheese in the fridge.

items.note: confiture is feminine, so de la; you spread an amount of it, not one whole jam, so the partitive fits.
items.ex: Elle met de la confiture sur sa tartine.
items.exEn: She puts jam on her toast.

items.note: For plurals the 'some' word is des; French counts fruits in the plural where English says 'fruit'.
items.ex: J'achète des fruits au marché.
items.exEn: I'm buying fruit at the market.

items.note: After ne... pas every partitive shrinks to plain de: pas de sucre, never 'pas du sucre'.
items.ex: Je ne prends pas de sucre dans mon café.
items.exEn: I don't take sugar in my coffee.

items.note: After a quantity word (un peu, beaucoup, trop, assez) there is no article: just de + noun.
items.ex: Je mets un peu de lait dans mon thé.
items.exEn: I put a little milk in my tea.

items.note: Quantity word + plain de, whatever the gender or number of the noun that follows; 'beaucoup du' is wrong.
items.ex: Nous avons beaucoup de travail cette semaine.
items.exEn: We have a lot of work this week.

items.note: Activities use faire + partitive: faire du sport, faire de la natation, faire du piano. sport is masculine, so du.
items.ex: J'aime faire du sport le week-end.
items.exEn: I like doing sport at the weekend.

items.note: Abstract uncountables (music, patience, luck) take the partitive too; musique is feminine, so de la.
items.ex: J'écoute de la musique dans le bus.
items.exEn: I listen to music on the bus.

teaching.rule: To say what is about to happen or what you plan to do, French uses aller (to go) in the present plus the verb in its dictionary form (the infinitive, ending in -er, -ir or -re), exactly like English 'I am going to eat': je vais manger. Only aller changes with the person (je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont); the second verb never changes. To say something is NOT going to happen, wrap ne... pas around the aller part: je ne vais pas sortir. This is the everyday future in spoken French, so listen for vais / vas / va followed straight by another verb.

examples.note: vais (I go) + manger in its dictionary form: nothing else to conjugate.
Weather and predictions use the same pattern: va + infinitive.

examples.en: We're going to visit the museum.
examples.note: Only allons carries the person; visiter stays unchanged.

examples.fr: Je ne vais pas sortir ce soir.
examples.en: I'm not going to go out tonight.
examples.note: ne and pas surround vais, not the infinitive: 'je vais ne pas sortir' is wrong.

contrast.note: aller followed by a place (not a verb) is simple movement, not a future: to Paris is à Paris.
The plain present says what happens habitually; je vais manger says it is about to happen.
The verb after aller must be the dictionary form (manger), never a past participle (mangé) or a conjugated form (mange).

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers conjugate both verbs ('je vais mange') or drop aller and use the present for plans; keep aller conjugated and leave the second verb in its dictionary form: je vais manger.

probes.ex: Nous allons partir à huit heures.
probes.exEn: We're going to leave at eight.

probes.ex: Prends un parapluie, il va pleuvoir.
probes.exEn: Take an umbrella, it's going to rain.

probes.ex: Désolé, je ne vais pas venir ce soir.
probes.exEn: Sorry, I'm not going to come tonight.

items.note: vais is the je form of aller; the verb after it stays in its dictionary form (manger), whoever the subject is.
items.ex: Ce midi, je vais manger au restaurant.
items.exEn: At lunchtime I'm going to eat at the restaurant.

items.note: Same pattern with partir: vais + dictionary form; there is no need to learn a future tense for this.
items.ex: Je vais partir bientôt.
items.exEn: I'm going to leave soon.

items.note: vas is the tu form of aller; the final s is silent, so vais and vas sound almost the same, and the subject tells them apart.
items.ex: Tu vas voir, c'est facile.
items.exEn: You'll see, it's easy.

items.note: Weather uses il as a dummy subject, then va + dictionary form; pleuvoir only ever appears in the il form.
items.ex: Il va pleuvoir ce soir.
items.exEn: It's going to rain tonight.

items.note: allons is the nous form of aller (the s of nous links: 'nou-za-lon'); visiter stays unchanged.
items.ex: Nous allons visiter Paris demain.
items.exEn: We're going to visit Paris tomorrow.

items.note: allez is the vous form; a favourite phrase of French shopkeepers and waiters when recommending something.
items.ex: Vous allez adorer ce film.
items.exEn: You're going to love this film.

items.note: vont is the irregular ils form of aller; arriver stays in the dictionary form.
items.ex: Ils vont arriver dans dix minutes.
items.exEn: They're going to arrive in ten minutes.

items.en: I'm not going to go out
items.note: To negate, ne... pas wraps around the aller part only; the second verb sits outside, after pas.
items.ex: Je ne vais pas sortir ce soir.
items.exEn: I'm not going to go out tonight.

items.note: Time markers like ce soir, demain, ce week-end, bientôt usually accompany the near future to say when.
items.ex: Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ce soir ?
items.exEn: What are you going to do tonight?

items.en: let's get going (literally: we are going to go there)
items.note: on (we, informal) + va + y aller (go there); a very common spoken phrase to announce leaving.
items.ex: Allez, on va y aller.
items.exEn: Come on, let's get going.

items.en: what are you going to do?
items.note: In casual speech the question word quoi stays at the end; the standard version is Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ?
items.ex: Et toi, tu vas faire quoi ce week-end ?
items.exEn: And you, what are you going to do this weekend?

items.note: A reassuring set phrase: ça (it) + va + aller; literally 'it is going to go'.
items.ex: Ne t'inquiète pas, ça va aller.
items.exEn: Don't worry, it'll be okay.

teaching.rule: A reflexive verb is one where the action comes back onto the person doing it: se laver (to wash oneself), se lever (to get oneself up). In the dictionary it starts with se; in a sentence you swap se for a little pronoun that matches the subject: je me, tu te, il/elle/on se, nous nous, vous vous, ils/elles se. The pronoun sits right before the verb, and before a vowel me/te/se shrink to m'/t'/s' (je m'appelle). Many daily-routine verbs are reflexive in French even when English has no 'myself': getting up, going to bed, getting dressed, hurrying, having fun. In the negative, ne goes before the pronoun and pas after the verb: je ne me lève pas.

examples.fr: Je me lève à sept heures.
examples.note: se lever becomes me lève after je: the pronoun matches the subject.
With tu the pronoun is te, and the verb takes its usual tu ending -es.
se shrinks to s' before the vowel of appelle.
nous appears twice: once as subject, once as the reflexive pronoun; this is normal, not a typo.

examples.fr: Je ne me lève pas tôt.
examples.note: ne... pas wraps both the pronoun and the verb together.

contrast.note: NOT 'Je lave' on its own, which means you wash something else, like the car.
NOT 'Elle se habille': se must shrink to s' before a vowel.
NOT 'Je repose': French treats resting as something you do to yourself, so the pronoun is compulsory.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers drop the reflexive pronoun ('Je lève à sept heures') because English has no 'myself' there; always keep the matching pronoun before the verb (Je me lève).

probes.ex: Je me lève à sept heures.
probes.exEn: I get up at seven.

probes.ex: Elle s'appelle Léa.
probes.exEn: Her name is Léa.

probes.ex: Nous nous couchons tard le samedi.
probes.exEn: We go to bed late on Saturdays.

items.note: The pronoun tells you the washing lands on the subject; after je it becomes me lave.
items.ex: Je me lave les mains.
items.exEn: I wash my hands.

items.note: Literally 'to raise oneself'; the e of lever turns into è (lève) whenever the ending after it is silent: je me lève, but nous nous levons.
items.ex: Je me lève à sept heures.
items.exEn: I get up at seven.

items.note: French says 'I call myself' for names; m' replaces me because appelle starts with a vowel.
items.ex: Je m'appelle Marie.
items.exEn: My name is Marie.

items.note: With il the pronoun stays se; coucher alone means to put someone else to bed.
items.ex: Il se couche tard.
items.exEn: He goes to bed late.

items.note: Resting is reflexive in French; on takes se like il and elle.
items.ex: On se repose le dimanche.
items.exEn: We rest on Sundays.

items.note: Always reflexive; the command form drops the subject and puts toi after the verb: Dépêche-toi !
items.ex: Il se dépêche pour prendre le train.
items.exEn: He's hurrying to catch the train.

items.note: Literally 'to amuse oneself'; s' because amuser starts with a vowel, and ils takes the same se/s' as il.
items.ex: Les enfants s'amusent dans le jardin.
items.exEn: The children are having fun in the garden.

items.note: Waking up is reflexive; réveiller without the pronoun means to wake someone else.
items.ex: Je me réveille à six heures.
items.exEn: I wake up at six.

items.note: The h of habiller is silent, so se shrinks to s' just as before a vowel.
items.ex: Elle s'habille vite le matin.
items.exEn: She gets dressed quickly in the morning.

items.note: French uses the reflexive pronoun plus les dents instead of 'my/your teeth'; the pronoun already says whose.
items.ex: Tu te brosses les dents ?
items.exEn: Are you brushing your teeth?

items.note: The first nous is the subject, the second is the reflexive pronoun; saying nous only once is a mistake.
items.ex: Le samedi, nous nous levons tard.
items.exEn: On Saturdays we get up late.

items.note: In the negative, ne comes before the pronoun and pas after the verb, so the pronoun stays glued to the verb.
items.ex: Le dimanche, je ne me lève pas tôt.
items.exEn: On Sundays I don't get up early.

teaching.rule: Use the passé composé to say something happened and is over: 'I ate', 'she finished', 'we saw'. Build it from two words: the present tense of avoir (j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont) plus a fixed form of the verb called the past participle. To make the participle, cut the ending off the dictionary form and add -é for -er verbs (manger → mangé), -i for -ir verbs (finir → fini), -u for -re verbs (vendre → vendu). A handful of very common verbs have irregular participles you simply learn: fait, eu, vu, pris, été, compris. Listen for the little avoir word right before the verb; that is the signal you are hearing the past.

examples.note: j'ai (present of avoir) + mangé (manger with -er replaced by -é).
finir is an -ir verb, so its participle ends in -i: fini.
vendre is an -re verb, so its participle ends in -u: vendu.
prendre is irregular: the participle is pris, not 'prendu'.
The negative ne... pas wraps around the avoir word only; the participle stays outside.

contrast.note: NOT 'Je mangé': French needs the helper avoir; the participle alone is not a sentence.
NOT 'Elle est été': the verb être itself uses avoir in the past, with the participle été.
NOT 'Je vois un film hier': a finished action with 'yesterday' needs the past, not the present.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers drop the helper verb and say 'Je mangé' or 'Je vu'; always put the present of avoir first (J'ai mangé, J'ai vu), then the participle.

probes.ex: J'ai mangé une pizza hier soir.
probes.exEn: I ate a pizza last night.

probes.ex: Il a fini son travail à midi.
probes.exEn: He finished his work at noon.

probes.ex: J'ai pris le train ce matin.
probes.exEn: I took the train this morning.

items.note: j'ai is the present of avoir; mangé is manger with its -er ending swapped for -é, the pattern for all regular -er verbs.
items.ex: Hier soir, j'ai mangé une pizza.
items.exEn: Last night I ate a pizza.

items.note: tu as is the tu form of avoir; parlé follows the -er → -é pattern and never changes for the subject.
items.ex: Tu as parlé avec Marie ?
items.exEn: Did you speak with Marie?

items.note: finir is an -ir verb, so the participle drops -ir and adds -i: fini.
items.ex: Il a fini son travail.
items.exEn: He finished his work.

items.note: vendre is an -re verb, so the participle drops -re and adds -u: vendu.
items.ex: Nous avons vendu la voiture.
items.exEn: We sold the car.

items.note: vous avez is the vous form of avoir; visité is another regular -er participle, the same whether vous is one polite person or a group.
items.ex: Vous avez visité le Louvre ?
items.exEn: Did you visit the Louvre?

items.note: faire is irregular: its participle is fait, so it covers both 'did' and 'made'.
items.ex: J'ai fait du sport ce matin.
items.exEn: I did some exercise this morning.

items.note: avoir is its own helper here: j'ai + eu, the tiny irregular participle of avoir, pronounced like the u in 'tu'.
items.ex: J'ai eu de la chance.
items.exEn: I was lucky. (literally: I had luck)

items.note: voir is irregular: the participle is vu, one syllable, not 'voiré'.
items.ex: J'ai vu un bon film.
items.exEn: I saw a good film.

items.note: prendre is irregular: the participle is pris; the same form works for its cousins appris (learned) and compris (understood).
items.ex: J'ai pris le train.
items.exEn: I took the train.

items.note: Surprisingly, être takes avoir in the past: elle a + été, and été never changes to match the subject.
items.ex: Elle a été malade toute la semaine.
items.exEn: She was ill all week.

items.note: The negative wraps only the helper: n'ai pas, then the participle compris (from comprendre) sits after it.
items.ex: Désolé, je n'ai pas compris.
items.exEn: Sorry, I didn't understand.

items.note: A time word that signals a finished action, so the verb next to it goes into the passé composé, not the present.
items.ex: J'ai travaillé hier.
items.exEn: I worked yesterday.

teaching.rule: A small group of verbs about coming, going and changing state (aller, venir, revenir, partir, arriver, entrer, rentrer, sortir, monter, descendre, rester, tomber, naître, mourir, devenir, and all reflexive verbs, the ones with me/te/se before the verb, like se lever) build their past with être instead of avoir: je suis allé, elle est partie.
