With être, the participle behaves like an adjective and must match the subject: add -e for a woman or girl (allée), -s for a group (allés), -es for a group of women (allées). The extra letters are silent, so you see the difference only in writing. When you hear suis, es, est, sommes, êtes or sont before a participle, you are in this group.

examples.note: aller takes être (je suis); a male speaker writes allé.

examples.fr: Elle est allée à la plage.
examples.note: Same verb, female subject: allée gets a silent -e to match elle.

examples.fr: Nous sommes partis à huit heures.
examples.note: nous is a group, so partis takes -s; if everyone in the group is female, parties.
Every reflexive verb (se lever, se coucher...) takes être: me suis + levé.
The negative wraps être (ne suis pas); the participle follows outside.

contrast.note: NOT 'Elle a arrivé': arriver is a movement verb, so it needs être, and the participle agrees (arrivée).
NOT 'Il a venu': venir belongs to the être group; venu, not 'veni'.
NOT 'Je suis mangé': manger is not a movement or reflexive verb, so it stays with avoir.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers use avoir for every verb ('J'ai allé'); with movement, state-change and reflexive verbs switch to être (Je suis allé) and add -e / -s to the participle to match who did it.

probes.ex: Elle est allée à Paris hier.
probes.exEn: She went to Paris yesterday.

probes.ex: Marie est partie à huit heures.
probes.exEn: Marie left at eight.

probes.ex: Nous sommes rentrés tard hier soir.
probes.exEn: We came home late last night.

items.note: aller takes être (je suis) and allé matches the subject: a female speaker writes allée, sounding exactly the same.
items.ex: Je suis allé au cinéma.
items.exEn: I went to the cinema.

items.note: Because elle is feminine, the participle takes a silent -e: allée; the -e shows only in writing.
items.ex: Elle est allée à la plage.
items.exEn: She went to the beach.

items.note: partir takes être, and a group adds -s: partis (parties for an all-female group).
items.ex: Nous sommes partis à huit heures.
items.exEn: We left at eight o'clock.

items.note: venir is irregular (venu, not 'veni') and takes être; il is masculine singular, so no extra letter.
items.ex: Il est venu avec sa sœur.
items.exEn: He came with his sister.

items.note: arriver looks like a normal -er verb but it describes movement, so it takes être and agrees: arrivée for elle.
items.ex: Elle est arrivée en retard.
items.exEn: She arrived late.

items.note: naître (to be born) is a change of state, so être + né; a woman writes née.
items.ex: Je suis né en 1990.
items.exEn: I was born in 1990.

items.note: rentrer (to go back home) takes être; ils is plural, so rentrés ends in -s.
items.ex: Ils sont rentrés tard hier soir.
items.exEn: They came home late last night.

items.note: sortir takes être (tu es); write sortie if you are talking to a woman, same sound.
items.ex: Tu es sorti hier soir ?
items.exEn: Did you go out last night?

items.note: monter takes être; elles is feminine plural, so the participle gets both -e and -s: montées.
items.ex: Elles sont montées au premier étage.
items.exEn: They (the women) went up to the first floor.

items.note: tomber (to fall) is in the être group even though it is not really 'going' anywhere; learn it with the movement verbs.
items.ex: Il est tombé dans la rue.
items.exEn: He fell in the street.

items.note: All reflexive verbs take être: the reflexive pronoun me comes first, then suis, then the participle (levée for a woman).
items.ex: Je me suis levé à six heures.
items.exEn: I got up at six.

items.note: rester (to stay) takes être; ne... pas wraps suis only, and the participle resté (restée for a woman) comes after pas.
items.ex: Je ne suis pas resté longtemps.
items.exEn: I didn't stay long.

teaching.rule: The French word for 'in' or 'to' depends on what kind of place follows. Before a city use à (à Paris). Before a country it depends on the country's gender: en for feminine countries, which are nearly all those ending in -e (en France), au for masculine ones (au Canada), aux for plural ones (aux États-Unis). For someone's home or a professional's office use chez plus the person (chez moi, chez le médecin). To say where you come from, use de (je viens de Paris, de France), which fuses with le/les into du / des (du Canada, des États-Unis). For time: à for clock times (à midi), en for months and most seasons (en juillet), but au printemps for spring. Use depuis when something started in the past and is still going on, pendant for a finished stretch, dans for 'in X minutes from now', and jusqu'à for 'until'.

examples.note: Cities always take à, whatever their size or spelling.
France ends in -e, so it is feminine and takes en.
Canada does not end in -e, so it is masculine and takes au (à + le fused).
Clock times take à, like English 'at'.

examples.en: I've lived here for two years.
examples.note: The living started two years ago and continues now, so depuis with a present-tense verb.

contrast.note: NOT 'Je vais en Lyon': en is for feminine countries, never for cities.
NOT 'dans juillet': dans means 'inside' or 'X time from now', not 'in a month'.
NOT 'depuis le film': the sleeping is over, so pendant, not depuis.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers use one word for every 'in' ('dans Paris', 'dans France'); pick à for cities, en / au / aux for countries by gender, and keep dans for physical 'inside'.

probes.ex: J'habite à Paris depuis dix ans.
probes.exEn: I've lived in Paris for ten years.

probes.ex: Elle est en France pour le travail.
probes.exEn: She is in France for work.

probes.ex: J'apprends le français depuis un an.
probes.exEn: I've been learning French for a year.

items.note: A city takes à for both 'in' and 'to'; the accent on à is what separates it from a (has).
items.ex: J'habite à Paris.
items.exEn: I live in Paris.

items.note: France ends in -e, so it is feminine and takes en with no article; the same works for en Espagne, en Italie.
items.ex: Elle travaille en France.
items.exEn: She works in France.

items.note: Canada is masculine (no final -e), so à + le fuses into au; likewise au Japon, au Portugal.
items.ex: Mon frère vit au Canada.
items.exEn: My brother lives in Canada.

items.note: États-Unis is plural, so à + les fuses into aux; the x links to the vowel: o-zé-ta-zu-ni.
items.ex: Ils habitent aux États-Unis.
items.exEn: They live in the United States.

items.note: chez means 'at the home of' and is followed by a person or pronoun, never by a building word.
items.ex: On dîne chez moi ce soir.
items.exEn: We're having dinner at my place tonight.

items.note: de says where something or someone comes from; with a masculine or plural country it fuses: du Canada, des États-Unis, but de France.
items.ex: Je viens de Lyon.
items.exEn: I come from Lyon.

items.note: Clock times take à: à midi, à huit heures, à minuit.
items.ex: On mange à midi.
items.exEn: We eat at noon.

items.note: Months take en, with no article and a lowercase month name.
items.ex: Il fait chaud en juillet.
items.exEn: It's hot in July.

items.note: For the seasons, en goes with the three that start with a vowel (en été, en automne, en hiver) and au with printemps; months always take en, whatever letter they start with.
items.ex: Les fleurs poussent au printemps.
items.exEn: Flowers grow in spring.

items.note: The action started in the past and is still true now, so French uses the present tense with depuis where English says 'have been'.
items.ex: J'habite ici depuis deux ans.
items.exEn: I've lived here for two years.

items.note: A stretch of time that is finished or clearly bounded; it goes with the past tense, unlike depuis.
items.ex: J'ai dormi pendant le film.
items.exEn: I slept during the film.

items.note: With a length of time, dans means 'after that much time has passed', a false friend of 'inside'.
items.ex: Le film commence dans une heure.
items.exEn: The film starts in an hour.

items.note: jusque + à fuse with an apostrophe; before le it becomes jusqu'au (jusqu'au soir).
items.ex: Le magasin est ouvert jusqu'à vingt heures.
items.exEn: The shop is open until 8 pm.

teaching.rule: Many French words end in a written consonant that is normally silent (vous, les, petit, deux). When the next word starts with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u, or a silent h), that consonant wakes up and is pronounced as the first sound of the next word: vous avez sounds like 'vou-ZA-vé'. Written s and x link as a z sound, d links as a t sound, and n links as n while the vowel before it keeps its nasal ring. Listen for the linking sound: it is often the only thing that tells you a word is plural (les amis 'lé-ZA-mi').

examples.note: The silent s of vous becomes a z sound that starts avez: 'vou-ZA-vé'. Without it, a French ear hears two separate, clumsy words.
'lé-ZAN-fan': the linking z is the only audible plural marker, because the s of enfants is silent.
The silent t of petit is pronounced before ami: 'peu-ti-TA-mi'. Compare un petit chien, where the t stays silent.
A final d links as a t sound: 'gran-TÔ-tel'. The h of hôtel is silent, so liaison happens exactly as before a vowel.

contrast.note: Never link after et (and): say 'é An', not 'é-TAN'. Linking here would make it sound like est (is).
Some h-words (haricot, hors-d'oeuvre, huit) block liaison: 'lé a-ri-ko', with a tiny break instead of 'lé-ZA-ri-ko'.
No liaison before a consonant: the t of est stays silent because parti starts with p. Liaison only happens before a vowel sound.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers pronounce each word separately ('vous / avez', 'les / amis') so the plural and the flow disappear; carry the final consonant over as the first sound of the next vowel word: vou-za-vé, lé-za-mi.

probes.en: the s links as a z: 'vou-za-vé'
probes.ask: How is “vous avez” pronounced?
probes.ex: Vous avez des enfants ?
probes.exEn: Do you have children?
options: the s is pronounced as s: 'vou-sa-vé'
the v of avez is dropped: 'vou-zé'

probes.en: the d links as a t: 'gran-tô-tel'
probes.ask: How is “un grand hôtel” pronounced?
probes.ex: Ils travaillent dans un grand hôtel.
probes.exEn: They work in a big hotel.
options: the d links as a d: 'gran-dô-tel'

probes.ask: How is “Paul et Anne” pronounced?
probes.ex: Paul et Anne arrivent demain.
probes.exEn: Paul and Anne arrive tomorrow.
options: the t links as a d: 'é-dan'
et and Anne merge into one syllable

items.note: The silent s of vous is pronounced as a z that starts avez: 'vou-ZA-vé'; keep your tongue in the z position and slide straight into the a.
items.ex: Est-ce que vous avez un stylo ?
items.exEn: Do you have a pen?

items.note: Same z link as vous avez: 'nou-ZA-von'; the final -ons is a nasal 'on' with no n at the end.
items.ex: Ce soir, nous avons des invités.
items.exEn: Tonight we have guests.

items.note: 'lé-ZA-mi': the linking z is the only sound that tells you it is plural, since the s of amis is silent; without the z, nothing tells the listener there is more than one friend.
items.ex: Je dîne avec les amis de Marie.
items.exEn: I'm having dinner with Marie's friends.

items.note: The n of un links: 'un-NA-mi'. Keep the nasal 'un' sound, then add a clear n as the first sound of ami.
items.ex: Marc est un ami de mon frère.
items.exEn: Marc is a friend of my brother's.

items.note: The silent t of petit is pronounced before the vowel of ami: 'peu-ti-TA-mi'. Literally 'little friend', it is the everyday word for boyfriend.
items.ex: Je te présente mon petit ami.
items.exEn: Let me introduce my boyfriend.

items.en: it is a / he is a
items.note: The t of est links to un: 'sè-TUN'. This is one of the most frequent liaisons in French, so it is a great one to copy from day one.
items.ex: Oui, c'est un bon restaurant.
items.exEn: Yes, it's a good restaurant.

items.note: A final x links as a z sound: 'deu-ZEUR'. The h of heures is silent, so liaison behaves exactly as before a vowel.
items.ex: Il est deux heures.
items.exEn: It is two o'clock.

items.note: 'trwa-ZAN': the s of trois links as z, and ans keeps its nasal 'an' sound with no n pronounced at the end.
items.ex: Ma fille a trois ans.
items.exEn: My daughter is three.

items.note: A final d links as a t, not a d: 'gran-TÔ-tel'. The h of hôtel is a silent 'h muet', which allows the link.
items.ex: Nous dormons dans un grand hôtel.
items.exEn: We are sleeping in a big hotel.

items.note: The n of en links: 'an-NÉ-té'. Keep the nasal 'an' of en, then pronounce a real n to start été.
items.ex: Je vais à la plage en été.
items.exEn: I go to the beach in summer.

items.note: The silent s of très becomes z: 'trè-ZIM-por-tan'. Liaison after très, plus, and bien before a vowel is compulsory in careful speech.
items.ex: C'est très important pour moi.
items.exEn: It's very important to me.

items.note: A forbidden liaison: the t of et is never pronounced, so say 'é el' with a tiny break. Linking would make it sound like est (is).
items.ex: Lui et elle sont amis.
items.exEn: He and she are friends.

teaching.rule: Connectors are the small words that glue two ideas together so you can say more than one sentence at a time. Learn each one by its job: et joins (and), ou offers a choice (or), mais contrasts (but), parce que gives a reason (because), donc and alors give a result (so). To tell a story in order use d'abord (first), puis or ensuite (then / next) and enfin (finally). Most of them go exactly where the English word goes, so the hard part is just remembering the sound: et is said 'é' with a silent t, and parce que shrinks to parce qu' before a vowel.

examples.fr: Je prends du pain et du fromage.
examples.note: et links two items; its t is never pronounced, even before a vowel.
mais introduces the contrast, like English 'but'.

examples.fr: Je reste parce que je suis fatigué.
examples.note: parce que gives the reason and is two words, never 'pourquoi', which asks the question.

examples.fr: Il pleut, donc je prends un parapluie.
examples.en: It's raining, so I'm taking an umbrella.
examples.note: donc gives the logical result of the first half.

examples.fr: D'abord on mange, puis on sort.
examples.en: First we eat, then we go out.
examples.note: d'abord opens the sequence, puis moves to the next step.

contrast.note: NOT 'parce que il pleut': que loses its e before a vowel and becomes qu'.

contrast.fr: Pourquoi tu restes ? Parce que je suis fatigué.
contrast.en: Why are you staying? Because I'm tired.
contrast.note: pourquoi asks the question; parce que answers it. They are not interchangeable.
NOT 'où' with an accent: ou means 'or', où means 'where'; only the accent separates them.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'parce que il' or write 'ou' for 'where'; shrink parce que to parce qu' before a vowel, and remember ou = or, où = where.

probes.ex: C'est cher, mais c'est bon.
probes.exEn: It's expensive, but it's good.

probes.ex: Je reste parce qu'il pleut.
probes.exEn: I'm staying because it's raining.

probes.fr: ___ on mange, puis on sort, et enfin on rentre.
probes.ex: D'abord on mange, puis on sort, et enfin on rentre.
probes.exEn: First we eat, then we go out, and finally we go home.

items.note: Joins two words or ideas; pronounced 'é' with a silent t, and it never links to a following vowel.
items.ex: Je prends du pain et du fromage.
items.exEn: I'll have bread and cheese.

items.note: Introduces a contrast; in speech it often starts a reply ('Mais non !').
items.ex: C'est cher, mais c'est très bon.
items.exEn: It's expensive, but it's very good.

items.note: Offers a choice; no accent, unlike où (where).
items.ex: Tu veux du thé ou du café ?
items.exEn: Do you want tea or coffee?

items.note: Two words that give a reason; before a vowel que shrinks to qu' (parce qu'il).
items.ex: Je reste à la maison parce que je suis fatigué.
items.exEn: I'm staying home because I'm tired.

items.note: States a logical result; slightly more formal than alors, and the c is pronounced.
items.ex: Il pleut, donc je prends un parapluie.
items.exEn: It's raining, so I'm taking an umbrella.

items.note: The everyday spoken 'so': it can give a result or just open a sentence ('Alors, on y va ?').
items.ex: Je suis fatigué, alors je rentre.
items.exEn: I'm tired, so I'm going home.

items.note: Adds something to what was just said; in 'Moi aussi' it means 'me too'.
items.ex: Moi aussi, j'adore Paris.
items.exEn: I love Paris too.

items.note: Opens a sequence of steps; the d' is a shrunken de and is always attached.
items.ex: On prend d'abord un café.
items.exEn: First of all we have a coffee.

items.note: Moves the story to the next step; the s is silent.
items.ex: Je mange, puis je vais au travail.
items.exEn: I eat, then I go to work.

items.note: Same job as puis but a bit fuller; handy when you are listing several steps.
items.ex: On visite le musée, ensuite on déjeune.
items.exEn: We visit the museum, after that we have lunch.

items.note: Closes a sequence or shows relief that something has happened at last.
items.ex: Après deux heures de route, on arrive enfin !
items.exEn: After two hours on the road, we finally arrive!

items.note: Introduces an illustration of what you just said; the x of exemple is pronounced 'gz'.
items.ex: J'aime les fruits, par exemple les pommes.
items.exEn: I like fruit, for example apples.

teaching.rule: Regular -ir verbs like finir (to finish) and choisir (to choose) drop -ir and add -is, -is, -it, -issons, -issez, -issent: je finis, tu finis, il finit, nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent. The -iss- in the plural is the mark of this group. Regular -re verbs like vendre (to sell) and attendre (to wait for) drop -re and add -s, -s, nothing, -ons, -ez, -ent: je vends, tu vends, il vend, nous vendons, vous vendez, ils vendent. In the singular the endings are silent, so finis and finit sound the same, and so do vends and vend; in the plural you hear more: finissent ends in a clear 'ss' sound and vendent in a clear d.

examples.note: finir: stem fin- plus -is; the s is silent.
The plural of choisir inserts -iss-: choisissons.
-re verbs add nothing for il / elle / on; the final d is silent.
In the ils form the d is pronounced: 'a-tand'. attendre already means 'wait for'.

contrast.note: NOT 'nous finons': regular -ir verbs put -iss- before the plural endings (finissons, finissez, finissent).
NOT 'il vendt': -re verbs add no ending for il / elle / on; the d belongs to the stem and stays silent.
Not every -ir verb works like finir: partir, sortir and dormir drop a consonant in the singular (je pars, je sors, je dors) and never take -iss- (nous partons).
NOT 'J'attends pour le bus': attendre already contains the 'for'.

teaching.commonMistake: Learners drop the -iss- from the plural of finir-type verbs ('nous finons', 'ils choisent'); the plural is nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent, and the same for choisir: nous choisissons.

probes.ex: Nous finissons à six heures.
probes.exEn: We finish at six.

probes.ex: Il vend sa voiture.
probes.exEn: He's selling his car.

probes.ex: Ils choisissent un restaurant.
probes.exEn: They're choosing a restaurant.

items.note: finir: stem fin- plus -is for je; the s is silent, so it sounds like 'fi-ni'.
items.ex: Le vendredi, je finis à midi.
items.exEn: On Fridays I finish at noon.

items.note: choisir: stem chois- plus -is for tu; it looks and sounds exactly like je choisis.
items.ex: Ce soir, c'est ton tour : tu choisis le film.
items.exEn: Tonight it's your turn: you choose the film.

items.note: -it for il, elle and on; the t is silent, so elle finit sounds like je finis.
items.ex: D'habitude, elle finit tard.
items.exEn: She usually finishes late.

items.note: The plural of finir-type verbs inserts -iss- before -ons: fi-ni-SSON.
items.ex: Le jeudi, nous finissons à cinq heures.
items.exEn: On Thursdays we finish at five.

items.note: -iss- plus -ez for vous; the s between vowels sounds like z: choi-zi-SSÉ.
items.ex: Si vous choisissez cette option, votre billet coûte plus cher.
items.exEn: If you choose this option, your ticket costs more.

items.note: -iss- plus a silent -ent for ils and elles: you hear the 'ss', which tells ils choisissent apart from il choisit.
items.ex: Pour les vacances, ils choisissent toujours la mer.
items.exEn: For their holidays they always pick the seaside.

items.note: vendre: stem vend- plus -s for je; both the d and the s are silent.
items.ex: Si ça t'intéresse, je vends mon vélo.
items.exEn: If you're interested, I'm selling my bike.

items.note: -re verbs add no ending for il, elle and on: il vend, with a silent d.
items.ex: Au marché, il vend des fruits et des légumes.
items.exEn: At the market he sells fruit and vegetables.

items.note: Stem vend- plus -ons; the d is now pronounced: van-DON.
items.ex: Ici, nous vendons du pain bio.
items.exEn: Here we sell organic bread.

items.note: attendre starts with a vowel, so je becomes j'; attendre needs no word for 'for'.
items.ex: Pardon, j'attends quelqu'un.
items.exEn: Sorry, I'm waiting for someone.

items.note: Stem attend- plus -ez for vous; the d is pronounced: a-tan-DÉ.
items.ex: Bonjour, vous attendez le médecin ? Asseyez-vous, il arrive.
items.exEn: Hello, are you waiting for the doctor? Have a seat, he's on his way.

items.note: répondre follows vendre: stem répond- plus a silent -ent, so you hear the d: ré-POND.
items.ex: Quand je pose une question, ils répondent en anglais.
items.exEn: When I ask a question, they reply in English.

items.note: entendre (to hear) follows vendre: tu entends, with a silent -ds.
items.ex: Chut ! Écoute, tu entends ce bruit ?
items.exEn: Shh! Listen, can you hear that noise?

teaching.rule: The imperative gives orders, advice and invitations. It has three forms, taken from the present tense with the subject pronoun left out: the tu form (Regarde !), the nous form, which means 'let's' (Regardons !), and the vous form, for one person you call vous or for several people (Regardez !). For -er verbs, for aller and for verbs like ouvrir and offrir, the tu form loses its final s: tu manges becomes Mange !, tu vas becomes Va !, tu ouvres becomes Ouvre ! Most other verbs keep it: Finis ! Attends ! Viens ! Before y the s comes back: Vas-y ! To say 'don't', put ne... pas around the verb: Ne touche pas ! Être and avoir have their own forms: sois, soyons, soyez and aie, ayons, ayez.

examples.note: tu manges → Mange !: no subject, and the s of an -er verb disappears.
The nous form means 'let's'; y is 'there', joined to the verb by a hyphen.
The vous form, for one person you call vous or for a group.
ne and pas surround the verb, as in any negative.

contrast.note: With tu it is a statement. To make it an order, drop tu and the s: Regarde la télé !
NOT 'Regardes !': -er verbs (and aller: Va !) lose the s of the tu form in the imperative.
finir-type verbs and -re verbs keep their s: Attends ! Finis ! It is -er verbs and aller (Va !) that drop it.

teaching.commonMistake: Learners keep the s on -er verbs ('Regardes !', 'Manges !') or keep the pronoun ('Tu regarde !'); the tu imperative of an -er verb is the present form without tu and without the s: Regarde ! Mange !

probes.ex: Écoute, c'est important.
probes.exEn: Listen, it's important.

probes.ex: N'oublie pas ton billet, on part demain.
probes.exEn: Don't forget your ticket, we're leaving tomorrow.
options: You're not going to forget your ticket.

probes.ex: Il est tard, partons tout de suite.
probes.exEn: It's late, let's leave right away.

items.note: tu regardes → Regarde !: no pronoun, and an -er verb drops its s.
items.ex: Regarde, ton bus arrive !
items.exEn: Look, your bus is coming!

items.note: écouter is an -er verb, so tu écoutes becomes Écoute ! with no s.
items.ex: Écoute, j'ai une idée pour ton anniversaire.
items.exEn: Listen, I've got an idea for your birthday.

items.note: attendre is a -re verb, so the s stays: tu attends → Attends !
items.ex: Attends, tu as oublié ton sac !
items.exEn: Wait, you've forgotten your bag!

items.note: réfléchir is a finir-type verb, so the s stays: Réfléchis !
items.ex: Réfléchis bien avant de donner ta réponse.
items.exEn: Think carefully before you give your answer.

items.note: aller drops its s like an -er verb: tu vas → Va ! 'Go and get' is simply va chercher.
items.ex: Va chercher ton manteau, il fait froid.
items.exEn: Go and get your coat, it's cold.

items.note: ne... pas wraps around the verb; ne becomes n' before the vowel of oublie.
items.ex: N'oublie pas ton passeport !
items.exEn: Don't forget your passport!

items.note: être has its own imperative: sois (tu), soyons (nous), soyez (vous).
items.ex: Sois sage chez ta grand-mère !
items.exEn: Be good at your grandmother's!

items.note: avoir has its own imperative: aie, ayons, ayez. avoir peur is 'to be afraid'.
items.ex: N'aie pas peur, tu ne vas pas tomber.
items.exEn: Don't be scared, you're not going to fall.

items.note: The vous form is the present without vous: vous entrez → Entrez !
items.ex: Entrez, votre table est prête.
items.exEn: Come in, your table is ready.

items.note: faire is irregular in the present (vous faites) and the imperative keeps that form: Faites !
items.ex: Faites attention à vos affaires dans le métro.
items.exEn: Watch your belongings on the metro.

items.note: In the negative, ne and pas surround the verb: Ne touchez pas.
items.ex: Ne touchez pas, s'il vous plaît, c'est fragile.
items.exEn: Please don't touch, it's fragile.

items.note: The nous form means 'let's'; ne... pas around it means 'let's not'. perdre du temps is 'to waste time'.
items.ex: Ne perdons pas de temps, le train part dans dix minutes.
items.exEn: Let's not waste any time, the train leaves in ten minutes.

items.note: être in the nous imperative is soyons, a form learners have to memorise.
items.ex: Soyons honnêtes, ce n'est pas facile.
items.exEn: Let's be honest, it isn't easy.

teaching.rule: Pouvoir (can, to be able to, to be allowed to), vouloir (to want) and devoir (to have to, must) are irregular, and each is followed directly by a second verb in the infinitive: je peux venir, je veux partir, je dois travailler. Only the first verb changes: je peux, tu peux, il peut, nous pouvons, vous pouvez, ils peuvent; je veux, tu veux, il veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils veulent; je dois, tu dois, il doit, nous devons, vous devez, ils doivent. The stem changes again in the ils form (peuvent, veulent, doivent). In the negative, ne... pas goes around the first verb: je ne peux pas venir.

examples.note: peux + the infinitive aider, with no de or à in between; the object pronoun t' goes just before the infinitive.
English needs 'to'; French puts the infinitive straight after veut.

examples.fr: Nous devons partir à sept heures.
examples.en: We have to leave at seven.
examples.note: devons carries the person; partir stays in the infinitive.
ne... pas wraps around peuvent, not around venir.

contrast.note: NOT 'je veux de partir' or 'je veux à partir': the infinitive comes straight after the modal.

contrast.fr: Tu ne dois pas fumer ici.
contrast.note: ne... pas + devoir means 'must not', a prohibition, not 'don't have to'.
For a skill you have learned, French uses savoir, not pouvoir: je peux nager means you are able or allowed to right now.

teaching.commonMistake: Learners put de or à between the modal and the next verb ('je veux de manger') or conjugate both verbs ('je peux viens'); the second verb stays in the infinitive, directly after the modal: je veux manger, je peux venir.

probes.ex: Nous pouvons partir maintenant.
probes.exEn: We can leave now.

probes.ex: Ils veulent partir en vacances.
probes.exEn: They want to go on holiday.

probes.ex: Elle est fatiguée, elle veut dormir.
probes.exEn: She's tired, she wants to sleep.

items.note: pouvoir: je peux, with a silent x; the next verb stays in the infinitive.
items.ex: Demain, je peux venir à huit heures.
items.exEn: Tomorrow I can come at eight.

items.note: tu peux sounds exactly like je peux; only the pronoun tells them apart.
items.ex: Si tu veux, tu peux dormir ici.
items.exEn: If you like, you can sleep here.

items.note: In everyday speech on peut is the usual way to say 'we can'; on takes the il form, peut.
items.ex: On peut payer par carte ?
items.exEn: Can we pay by card?

items.note: pouvoir changes its stem in the nous and vous forms: vous pouvez.
items.ex: Vous pouvez laisser vos valises ici.
items.exEn: You can leave your suitcases here.

items.note: ne... pas goes around peux, and the infinitive follows pas.
items.ex: Samedi, je ne peux pas venir, je travaille.
items.exEn: I can't come on Saturday, I'm working.

items.note: vouloir: je veux, with a silent x; English 'to' has no French equivalent before the infinitive.
items.ex: Ce soir, je veux rester à la maison.
items.exEn: Tonight I want to stay home.

items.note: Tu veux + infinitive is the everyday way to offer or suggest something to a friend.
items.ex: Tu veux inviter ta sœur ?
items.exEn: Do you want to invite your sister?

items.note: il veut ends in t; je veux and tu veux end in x, but all three sound the same.
items.ex: Mon fils veut devenir pilote.
items.exEn: My son wants to become a pilot.

items.note: veulent goes back to the eu of je veux and il veut (unlike nous voulons) and adds an l; the -ent is silent.
items.ex: Mes voisins veulent vendre leur maison.
items.exEn: My neighbours want to sell their house.

items.note: devoir: je dois, with a silent s, then the infinitive.
items.ex: Désolé, je dois partir.
items.exEn: Sorry, I have to go.

items.note: devoir changes its stem in the nous and vous forms: nous devons.
items.ex: Nous devons trouver un hôtel ce soir.
items.exEn: We need to find a hotel tonight.

items.note: vous devez, then the infinitive: a common form on signs and in official instructions.
items.ex: Vous devez montrer votre passeport.
items.exEn: You must show your passport.

teaching.rule: Il faut says that something is necessary without saying who has to do it. Its il stands for nobody, so it never changes: there is no 'je faut' or 'on faut'. Follow it with an infinitive for an action, il faut partir, and English picks 'we', 'you' or 'one' from the situation. Follow it with a noun for what is needed or for how long something takes: il faut un passeport (you need a passport), il faut deux heures (it takes two hours). To say who needs a thing, put a pronoun before faut: il me faut un stylo (I need a pen). The negative il ne faut pas forbids (you mustn't); the future is il faudra. Il faut que + a full clause also exists, but it needs the subjunctive, which comes later.

examples.note: faut + infinitive, no de in between. The il is impersonal, and English chooses 'we' because of the situation.

examples.fr: Il faut deux heures en train.
examples.en: It takes two hours by train.
examples.note: With a length of time, il faut translates 'it takes'.

examples.fr: Il nous faut une plus grande table.
examples.note: A pronoun before faut (me, te, nous, vous) names who needs the thing.

contrast.fr: Il ne faut pas venir. / Tu n'as pas besoin de venir.
contrast.en: You mustn't come. / You don't have to come.
contrast.note: il ne faut pas forbids; it does not mean 'you don't have to'. For that, use pas besoin de or ce n'est pas la peine de.

contrast.fr: Il faut partir. / Il doit partir.
contrast.en: We have to leave. / He has to leave.
contrast.note: With devoir, il is a real person (he). With faut, il is nobody, and the person comes from the context.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers read il faut as 'he needs' or build 'je faut'; faut only ever takes impersonal il. They also use il ne faut pas for 'you don't have to', when it actually means 'you mustn't'.

probes.ex: Il ne faut pas courir dans le couloir.
probes.exEn: You mustn't run in the corridor.

probes.fr: Il faut dix minutes à pied.
probes.en: It takes ten minutes on foot.
probes.ex: Pour aller à la gare, il faut dix minutes à pied.
probes.exEn: It takes ten minutes on foot to get to the station.
options: He needs ten minutes on foot.

probes.ex: Pour ce gâteau, il me faut du sucre.
probes.exEn: I need some sugar for this cake.

items.note: il faut + infinitive: the il is nobody in particular, and English chooses 'we', 'you' or 'I' from the situation.
items.ex: Il est tard, il faut partir.
items.exEn: It's late, we have to leave.

items.note: No de and no que between faut and the infinitive: il faut réserver, not 'il faut de réserver'.
items.ex: Le restaurant est petit, il faut réserver.
items.exEn: The restaurant is small, you need to book.

items.note: ne and pas go around faut. This forbids something; it never means 'you don't have to'.
items.ex: Il ne faut pas fumer ici.
items.exEn: You mustn't smoke here.

items.note: With a length of time, il faut means 'it takes'. Ça prend deux heures is a more casual equivalent.
items.ex: D'ici, il faut deux heures en train.
items.exEn: From here, it takes two hours by train.

items.note: me before faut says who needs the thing. The il is still impersonal: il me faut never means 'he needs'.
items.ex: Il me faut un stylo, tu en as un ?
items.exEn: I need a pen, do you have one?

items.en: what do we need to bring?
items.note: qu'est-ce qu'il faut + infinitive asks what has to be done, without naming who does it.
items.ex: Pour le pique-nique, qu'est-ce qu'il faut apporter ?
items.exEn: What do we need to bring for the picnic?

items.note: être stays in the infinitive after faut: il faut être, never 'il faut est'.
items.ex: Avec les enfants, il faut être patient.
items.exEn: With children, you have to be patient.

items.note: il faut + a noun says what is needed, with its article: il faut un passeport, il faut du temps.
items.ex: Pour ce voyage, il faut un passeport.
items.exEn: You need a passport for this trip.

items.note: In conversation the question word can sit after faut. Combien de temps faut-il ? is the more formal order.
items.ex: Il faut combien de temps pour aller à la gare ?
items.exEn: How long does it take to get to the station?

items.note: nous before faut says who needs the thing; the il stays impersonal. Nous avons besoin de and on a besoin de say the same.
items.ex: Il nous faut deux chambres pour ce soir.
items.exEn: We need two rooms for tonight.

items.note: il faut + du temps: the partitive du because time is uncountable here. Ça prend du temps is a more casual equivalent.
items.ex: Pour apprendre une langue, il faut du temps.
items.exEn: Learning a language takes time.

teaching.rule: The simple future says what will happen: je parlerai (I will speak). For most verbs, take the whole infinitive and add the endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont: parler → je parlerai, tu parleras, il parlera, nous parlerons, vous parlerez, ils parleront. Verbs ending in -re drop their final e first: prendre → je prendrai. A small set of very common verbs have their own stem, but the endings never change: être → ser- (je serai), avoir → aur- (j'aurai), aller → ir- (j'irai), faire → fer- (je ferai), venir → viendr-, pouvoir → pourr-, voir → verr-, pleuvoir → pleuvr- (il pleuvra). Every future stem ends in r, so listen for an r just before the ending. In conversation, aller + infinitive (je vais manger) is the most common way to talk about the future, and the plain present often covers a fixed arrangement (je pars demain). The simple future is the natural choice for things further off or less certain (un jour, dans vingt ans), for predictions and forecasts, for promises, and in writing; often both futures are possible.

examples.fr: Un jour, je parlerai français couramment.
examples.en: One day I'll speak French fluently.
examples.note: A regular -er verb: the whole infinitive parler + -ai.

examples.fr: Demain, il fera beau dans tout le pays.
examples.en: Tomorrow it'll be sunny all over the country.
examples.note: Weather forecasts use the simple future; fera comes from the irregular stem fer- of faire.

examples.fr: Je t'attendrai devant la gare, promis.
examples.en: I'll wait for you outside the station, I promise.
examples.note: A promise, so the simple future; attendre drops its final e before the ending: attendr- + -ai.

examples.fr: Je ne serai pas là demain.
examples.note: ne and pas go around the single future verb: there is no helper word to wrap.

contrast.note: aller + infinitive: the near future, for something about to happen or already planned.
The simple future: one word, and the moment is less immediate.
NOT 'j'êtrai': être uses its own stem ser-; only the endings are regular.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers build the future on the present stem and lose the r ('je prendai'), keep the final e of -re verbs ('je prendrerai'), or apply the rule to être and avoir as written ('j'êtrai', 'j'avoirai'); start from the whole infinitive (parler-), the -re infinitive without its e (prendr-) or the irregular stem (ser-, aur-, ir-, fer-), then add -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont.

probes.ex: Un jour, je serai riche.
probes.exEn: One day I'll be rich.

probes.ex: L'année prochaine, nous irons au Japon.
probes.exEn: Next year we'll go to Japan.
options: We are going to Japan right now.

probes.ex: Demain, il fera beau.
probes.exEn: Tomorrow it'll be sunny.

items.note: Regular -er verbs keep the whole infinitive and add -ai: parler + ai.
items.ex: Un jour, je parlerai français couramment.
items.exEn: One day I'll speak French fluently.

items.note: être has its own future stem, ser-; the ending -ai is the regular one.
items.ex: Plus tard, je serai médecin.
items.exEn: Later on I'll be a doctor.

items.note: avoir has the future stem aur-; avoir froid (to be cold) keeps avoir in every tense.
items.ex: Prends un pull, sinon tu auras froid.
items.exEn: Take a jumper, or you'll be cold.

items.note: faire has the future stem fer-; il fera beau is also the standard phrase in a weather forecast.
items.ex: J'espère qu'il fera beau le jour de ton mariage.
items.exEn: I hope it'll be sunny on your wedding day.

items.note: pouvoir has the future stem pourr-, with a double r; it is the future of 'can'.
items.ex: Dans deux ans, je pourrai voter.
items.exEn: In two years I'll be able to vote.

items.note: avoir has the future stem aur-; the nous ending is -ons, as in the present.
items.ex: Dans dix ans, nous aurons une maison à la campagne.
items.exEn: In ten years we'll have a house in the countryside.

items.note: aller has the shortest future stem of all, ir-: j'irai, tu iras, nous irons.
items.ex: Ne t'inquiète pas, tu iras au Japon un jour.
items.exEn: Don't worry, you'll go to Japan one day.

items.note: -re verbs drop their final e before the ending: comprendre → comprendr- + -as.
items.ex: Tu es trop jeune, mais un jour tu comprendras.
items.exEn: You're too young, but one day you'll understand.

items.note: il y a becomes il y aura: avoir's future stem aur- + -a.
items.ex: Dans vingt ans, il y aura des voitures sans conducteur partout.
items.exEn: In twenty years there'll be driverless cars everywhere.

items.note: A set phrase and a promise, where the simple future is the natural choice; je vais faire de mon mieux is also heard.
items.ex: Je ne promets rien, mais je ferai de mon mieux.
items.exEn: I'm not promising anything, but I'll do my best.
alts: je vais faire de mon mieux

items.note: What a shopkeeper or waiter asks at the end of an order; ce sera is the future of c'est.
items.ex: Merci, madame. Ce sera tout ?
items.exEn: Thank you, madam. Will that be all?

teaching.rule: To say something has only just happened, French uses venir (to come) in the present, then de, then the verb in the infinitive: je viens de manger means 'I've just eaten'. Only venir changes with the person (je viens, tu viens, il vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils viennent); the second verb stays in the infinitive, and de becomes d' before a vowel: il vient d'arriver. There is no past tense in the sentence, yet it describes the very recent past. It is the mirror image of aller + infinitive, which looks just ahead.

examples.fr: Je viens de finir mon travail.
examples.note: viens + de + finir: the present of venir describes a past that is only moments old.
de becomes d' before a vowel.
A reflexive verb keeps its pronoun, matching the subject, just before the infinitive.
viennent is the ils form; partir stays in the infinitive.

contrast.note: venir de + a place says where you come from; only venir de + an infinitive means 'have just done'.
Without de, venir + infinitive means coming somewhere in order to do something.
aller + infinitive looks just ahead; venir de + infinitive looks just behind.

teaching.commonMistake: Learners translate 'I have just eaten' word for word with avoir ('j'ai juste mangé', which usually means 'all I did was eat') or drop the de ('je viens manger', which means 'I'm coming to eat'); use venir + de + infinitive: je viens de manger. You may hear juste added for emphasis (je viens juste de manger), but learn the plain form first.

probes.ex: Désolée, elle vient de partir.
probes.exEn: Sorry, she's just left.
options: She left a long time ago.

probes.ex: Merci, mais nous venons de déjeuner.
probes.exEn: Thanks, but we've just had lunch.

probes.ex: Ils viennent d'arriver.
probes.exEn: They've just arrived.

items.note: viens is the je form of venir; de and the infinitive manger stay the same for every subject.
items.ex: Non merci, je viens de manger.
items.exEn: No thanks, I've just eaten.

items.note: vient is the il / elle form; with a noun subject it works the same way.
items.ex: Trop tard, le train vient de partir !
items.exEn: Too late, the train has just left!

items.note: de becomes d' before the vowel of arriver; venons is the nous form.
items.ex: Nous venons d'arriver à l'hôtel.
items.exEn: We've only just got to the hotel.

items.note: rater is the everyday verb for missing a bus or a train; manquer also works.
items.ex: Tu viens de rater le bus, le prochain est dans dix minutes.
items.exEn: You've just missed the bus; the next one is in ten minutes.

items.note: venez is the vous form; the whole phrase still sits in the present tense.
items.ex: Vous venez de gagner un voyage à Rome !
items.exEn: You've just won a trip to Rome!

items.note: viennent is the ils / elles form, with a doubled n; finir stays in the infinitive.
items.ex: Les filles viennent de finir leurs devoirs.
items.exEn: The girls have just finished their homework.

items.note: A handy way to say something has only just begun: vient de commencer.
items.ex: Chut, le film vient de commencer !
items.exEn: Shh, the film has just started!

items.note: rentrer is to come back home; viens de rentrer says it happened moments ago.
items.ex: Je viens de rentrer du travail.
items.exEn: I've just got home from work.

items.note: de becomes d' before avoir; the recent past works with any verb.
items.ex: Ma cousine vient d'avoir un bébé.
items.exEn: My cousin has just had a baby.

items.note: With a reflexive verb, the pronoun (se for on) sits just before the infinitive.
items.ex: Non, on ne se connaît pas, on vient de se rencontrer.
items.exEn: No, we don't know each other, we've only just met.

items.note: recevoir stays in the infinitive after de; only venir carries the person.
items.ex: Je viens de recevoir ton message.
items.exEn: I've just received your message.

items.note: Weather verbs take il as a dummy subject, so the recent past is il vient de pleuvoir.
items.ex: Attention, la route est mouillée, il vient de pleuvoir.
items.exEn: Careful, the road is wet, it has just rained.

teaching.rule: French has no separate -ing tense. The ordinary present covers both 'I eat' and 'I am eating': je mange can mean either, and the context tells you which. When you want to insist that something is happening right now, at this very moment, use être en train de + infinitive: je suis en train de manger (I'm in the middle of eating). Only être changes with the person (je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont); the second verb stays in the infinitive, and de becomes d' before a vowel (en train d'écrire). It is often used to explain why you cannot do something else. Do not use it for states such as wearing, living or knowing, or for plans: English 'I'm leaving tomorrow' is just je pars demain. In the past, the same phrase with the imparfait (j'étais en train de) describes what was going on when something else happened.

examples.fr: Je ne peux pas te parler, je suis en train de travailler.
examples.en: I can't talk to you, I'm in the middle of working.
examples.note: en train de insists that the work is happening right now.
The plain present already means 'are you doing': no extra word is needed.

examples.fr: Elle est en train d'écrire un roman.
examples.note: de becomes d' before the vowel of écrire.

examples.fr: J'étais en train de dormir quand tu as appelé.
examples.en: I was sleeping when you called.
examples.note: With the imparfait of être, it sets the scene that the call interrupted.

contrast.note: The plain present covers both English forms.

contrast.fr: Je suis en train de manger.
contrast.en: I'm eating right now (I'm in the middle of it).
contrast.note: Only for insisting on the moment: 'je suis mangeant' does not exist.
An English -ing for a plan is the plain present in French, never en train de.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers translate every '-ing' with être, saying 'je suis mange' or 'je suis mangeant'; the plain present (je mange) is already 'I'm eating', and être en train de + infinitive is there only when you want to stress 'right now'.

probes.fr: Je suis en train de manger.
probes.ex: Je te rappelle, je suis en train de manger.
probes.exEn: I'll call you back, I'm eating right now.

probes.fr: Demain, je suis en train de partir.
probes.en: wrong: for a plan French uses the plain present (je pars demain)
probes.ask: Is “Demain, je suis en train de partir.” right?
probes.ex: Je pars demain.
probes.exEn: I'm leaving tomorrow.
options: correct: en train de translates every English -ing
correct: en train de turns a verb into the future
wrong: en train de must be followed by a noun

probes.fr: Nous sommes en train ___ regarder le match.
probes.ex: Nous sommes en train de regarder le match.
probes.exEn: We're watching the match right now.

items.fr: je suis en train de cuisiner
items.note: être en train de + infinitive stresses that the action is happening right now.
items.ex: Je suis en train de cuisiner, je te rappelle.
items.exEn: I'm busy cooking, I'll call you back.

items.fr: il est en train de dormir
items.note: Only être changes with the person: il est; dormir stays in the infinitive.
items.ex: Chut, il est en train de dormir.
items.exEn: Shh, he's asleep right now.

items.fr: nous sommes en train de manger
items.en: we're in the middle of eating
items.note: sommes is the nous form of être; the phrase explains why now is a bad moment.
items.ex: Rappelle plus tard, nous sommes en train de manger.
items.exEn: Call back later, we're in the middle of eating.
alts: on est en train de manger

items.fr: ils sont en train de travailler
items.note: sont is the ils form of être; travailler stays in the infinitive.
items.ex: Ne les dérange pas, ils sont en train de travailler.
items.exEn: Don't disturb them, they're busy working.

items.note: de becomes d' before a vowel: en train d'écrire, en train d'attendre.
items.ex: Elle est en train d'écrire un roman.
items.exEn: She's writing a novel.

items.fr: je ne suis pas en train de dormir
items.note: ne ... pas goes around être, the only conjugated verb in the phrase.
items.ex: Je ne suis pas en train de dormir, je réfléchis !
items.exEn: I'm not asleep, I'm thinking!

items.note: The plain present already means 'are you doing'; tu fais quoi ? is the casual spoken version.
items.ex: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? On t'attend !
items.exEn: What are you doing? We're waiting for you!

items.note: The plain present covers English '-ing': je regarde is 'I watch' and 'I'm watching'.
items.ex: Je ne peux pas sortir, je regarde un film.
items.exEn: I can't go out, I'm watching a film.
alts: je suis en train de regarder un film

items.note: Wearing is a state, not an activity in progress, so French uses the plain present, not en train de.
items.ex: Il fait froid, alors je porte un manteau.
items.exEn: It's cold, so I'm wearing a coat.

items.note: English uses '-ing' for plans; French uses the plain present, never en train de.
items.ex: Je pars demain matin pour Rome.
items.exEn: I'm leaving for Rome tomorrow morning.

items.note: With the plain present, en ce moment does the job of English '-ing' for something going on these days.
items.ex: Je lis un livre passionnant en ce moment.
items.exEn: I'm reading a gripping book at the moment.

teaching.rule: on is one of the most frequent words in spoken French. In conversation it usually means 'we' and replaces nous: on part (we're leaving) is what people say, nous partons sounds formal or written. It also means 'people' or 'you' in general (en France, on dit bonjour en entrant dans un magasin), and 'someone' when you do not know or do not say who (on frappe à la porte). Whatever it means, on always takes the same verb form as il and elle: on est, on a, on fait, on va, never 'on sommes' or 'on avons'. In speech, nous often comes first for emphasis, then on carries the verb: nous, on préfère la mer. To say 'we' in writing or formal French, use nous with its own verb form.

examples.note: Spoken 'we': on + the il form of the verb (part), never 'on partons'.

examples.fr: En France, on dit bonjour en entrant dans un magasin.
examples.en: In France, people say hello when they walk into a shop.
examples.note: on as 'people in general': a habit or rule that applies to everyone.

examples.en: Somebody rang the bell, go and open the door.
examples.note: on as 'someone': the speaker does not know who it is.

examples.en: As for us, we prefer the seaside.
examples.note: nous first for emphasis, then on with the verb: very common in speech.

contrast.note: Spoken French: on + a (the il form of avoir).
Written or formal French: nous + avons; the meaning is the same.
il is one person; on part demain is 'we're leaving tomorrow', with the same verb form.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers hear on as 'we' and give it the nous verb ('on sommes', 'on allons'); on always takes the il / elle form: on est, on va.

probes.ex: On part demain matin, très tôt.
probes.exEn: We're leaving tomorrow morning, very early.

probes.fr: En France, on mange du pain tous les jours.
probes.en: In France, people eat bread every day.
probes.ex: En France, on mange du pain tous les jours.
probes.exEn: In France, people eat bread every day.
options: In France, he eats bread every day.
In France, you must eat bread every day.
In France, nobody eats bread any more.

probes.fr: Nous, on ___ du sport le samedi.
probes.ex: Nous, on fait du sport le samedi.
probes.exEn: We do sport on Saturdays.

items.note: Spoken 'we': on takes the il form of the verb, so part, not partons.
items.ex: On part dans dix minutes, tu es prêt ?
items.exEn: We're leaving in ten minutes, are you ready?

items.note: on + est (the il form of être); nous sommes en retard says the same in writing.
items.ex: Dépêche-toi, on est en retard !
items.exEn: Hurry up, we're late!

items.note: The passé composé of on uses a, the il form of avoir: on a gagné, never 'on avons gagné'.
items.ex: On a gagné le match !
items.exEn: We won the match!

items.note: peut is the il form of pouvoir; a polite, everyday way to ask for permission for a group.
items.ex: Bonjour, on peut entrer ?
items.exEn: Hello, can we come in?

items.note: A fixed phrase for putting off a decision: on means 'we', and verra is the future of voir in the il form.
items.ex: Je ne sais pas encore, on verra.
items.exEn: I don't know yet, we'll see.

items.note: Literally 'we see each other tomorrow': spoken 'we' is on, and the verb after se stays in the il form (voit).
items.ex: Bon, on se voit demain au bureau.
items.exEn: Right, see you tomorrow at the office.

items.note: nous in front adds emphasis; on still carries the verb, in the il form.
items.ex: Nous, on préfère la montagne.
items.exEn: As for us, we prefer the mountains.

items.note: on as 'people in general': a rumour or a reputation, with no one in particular behind it.
items.ex: On dit que ce restaurant est très bon.
items.exEn: People say this restaurant is very good.

items.note: on as 'people in general' for the language spoken somewhere.
items.ex: Au Québec, on parle français.
items.exEn: In Quebec, people speak French.

items.note: on is the general 'you' here: it applies to anybody.
items.ex: Prends un parapluie, on ne sait jamais.
items.exEn: Take an umbrella, you never know.

items.note: on as 'someone': the speaker does not know who it is.
items.ex: Chut, on frappe à la porte.
items.exEn: Shh, someone's knocking at the door.

items.note: on as 'someone' after a past verb: English often turns this into a passive.
items.ex: On m'a dit que le musée était fermé.
items.exEn: I was told the museum was closed.

teaching.rule: French has a second set of 'me, you, him' words, the stressed pronouns: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux (them, masculine or mixed) and elles (them, all female). Use them after a preposition (avec moi, chez toi, pour eux), after c'est (c'est lui), after que in a comparison (plus grand que toi), on their own as a short answer (Qui veut du café ? — Moi !), with aussi (moi aussi), and in front of the subject to stress it (Moi, je reste ici). The subject forms je, tu, il and ils can never stand alone or follow a preposition. Elle, nous, vous and elles look the same in both sets; only moi, toi, lui and eux are new.

examples.note: After a preposition such as avec, pour, chez or sans, 'me' is moi.
A one-word answer has no verb, so only the stressed form can stand there.
Moi in front of je adds emphasis or contrast, the way English leans on 'I' with the voice.
eux is 'them' for a masculine or mixed group; for a group of women it is elles.

contrast.note: NOT 'C'est il': after c'est, use the stressed form.
NOT 'avec ils' or 'avec les': after a preposition, 'them' is eux (or elles for an all-female group).
NOT 'Je aussi': je can never stand without its verb.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers reach for the subject form everywhere ('avec je', 'C'est il', 'Je aussi'); after a preposition, after c'est and in a short answer with no verb, use moi, toi, lui, eux: avec moi, c'est lui, moi aussi.

probes.ex: Paul ? Je pars avec lui demain.
probes.exEn: Paul? I'm leaving with him tomorrow.

probes.ex: Ce café est pour toi ?
probes.exEn: Is this coffee for you?

probes.fr: Je n'aime pas le café. — ___ non plus.
probes.ex: Je n'aime pas le café. — Moi non plus.
probes.exEn: I don't like coffee. — Me neither.

items.note: After a preposition, 'me' is moi, never je or me.
items.ex: Tu veux venir avec moi ?
items.exEn: Do you want to come with me?

items.note: chez + toi means at your home; with someone you call vous it is chez vous.
items.ex: Tu es malade ? Reste chez toi aujourd'hui.
items.exEn: Are you ill? Stay at home today.

items.note: lui is the stressed form of il; it follows prepositions like pour.
items.ex: Ce cadeau est pour lui.
items.exEn: This present is for him.

items.note: nous is the same in both sets, so after a preposition it simply stays nous.
items.ex: Vous venez avec nous ?
items.exEn: Are you coming with us?

items.note: vous also stays vous after a preposition; Madame shows this is the polite vous.
items.ex: Madame, il y a un message pour vous.
items.exEn: Madam, there's a message for you.

items.note: eux replaces ils after a preposition; cousins is masculine, so eux, not elles.
items.ex: Mes cousins sont là ; je sors avec eux ce soir.
items.exEn: My cousins are here; I'm going out with them tonight.

items.note: elles is 'them' for an all-female group; tantes is feminine, so chez elles.
items.ex: Mes tantes nous invitent chez elles dimanche.
items.exEn: My aunts are inviting us to their place on Sunday.

items.note: With no verb after it, 'you' must be the stressed toi; with someone you call vous, ask Et vous ?
items.ex: Salut Léa ! Moi, ça va. Et toi ?
items.exEn: Hi Léa! I'm fine. And you?

items.note: After c'est, French uses the stressed form: c'est elle, c'est lui, c'est moi.
items.ex: Regarde, c'est elle, la nouvelle voisine.
items.exEn: Look, that's her, the new neighbour.

items.note: After que in a comparison, use the stressed form: que toi, never que tu.
items.ex: Ton petit frère est déjà plus grand que toi !
items.exEn: Your little brother is already taller than you!

items.note: With no verb, je becomes moi; the negative answer is moi non plus.
items.ex: J'ai faim. — Moi aussi !
items.exEn: I'm hungry. — Me too!

items.note: être à + stressed pronoun says who something belongs to: c'est à moi, c'est à lui.
items.ex: Ce stylo est à moi.
items.exEn: This pen is mine.

items.note: With no verb after it, il becomes lui: lui aussi, like moi aussi; for a woman it is elle aussi.
items.ex: Marie est fatiguée, et Paul ? — Lui aussi !
items.exEn: Marie is tired. And Paul? — He is too!

teaching.rule: Whenever à or de comes right before the article le or les, the two words must fuse: à + le = au, à + les = aux, de + le = du, de + les = des. Nothing fuses with la or l': à la, à l', de la, de l' stay as two words. The fusion happens wherever à or de is needed: after verbs built with à or de (jouer au foot but jouer du piano, parler du film, penser aux vacances), inside place phrases ending in de (à côté du cinéma, près des magasins), in dish names built with à (une tarte aux pommes) and in time phrases (au début du mois). Before a vowel or silent h, l' blocks the fusion: à l'hôpital, not au hôpital. Only the articles fuse: when le or les means 'it' or 'them', it stays apart (je commence à les comprendre, I'm starting to understand them).

examples.note: jouer à + a sport or game: à + le tennis fuses into au.
jouer de + an instrument: de + le violon fuses into du.

examples.fr: La pharmacie est près des magasins.
examples.en: The chemist's is near the shops.
examples.note: près de + les magasins fuses into des; here des means 'of the', not 'some'.
banque is feminine: à la never fuses.

contrast.note: NOT 'au hôpital': before a vowel or silent h the article is l', and à l' never fuses.

contrast.fr: Je joue au foot. / Je joue du piano.
contrast.en: I play football. / I play the piano.
contrast.note: Same verb, different little word: jouer à for sports and games, jouer de for instruments.
NOT 'de le directeur': de + le is always du.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers translate word by word and leave the pieces apart ('à le cinéma', 'de les enfants'), or fuse where they shouldn't ('au hôpital'); fuse only à or de with le and les: au cinéma, des enfants, but à l'hôpital, de la gare.

probes.ex: Il joue de la guitare dans un groupe.
probes.exEn: He plays the guitar in a band.

probes.ex: Il téléphone au médecin pour prendre rendez-vous.
probes.exEn: He's phoning the doctor to make an appointment.

probes.ex: Je n'ai pas compris la fin du film.
probes.exEn: I didn't understand the end of the film.

items.note: jouer à + a sport: à + le foot fuses into au.
items.ex: Le samedi, je joue au foot avec mes amis.
items.exEn: On Saturdays I play football with my friends.

items.note: jouer de + an instrument: de + le piano fuses into du.
items.ex: Ma fille joue du piano depuis deux ans.
items.exEn: My daughter has been playing the piano for two years.

items.note: parler de means to talk about; de + le film fuses into du.
items.ex: On parle du film après la séance ?
items.exEn: Shall we talk about the film after the screening?

items.note: à côté de ends in de, so de + le cinéma fuses into du.
items.ex: La boulangerie est à côté du cinéma.
items.exEn: The bakery is next to the cinema.

items.note: gare is feminine: de la stays as two words, there is nothing to fuse.
items.ex: L'hôtel est en face de la gare.
items.exEn: The hotel is opposite the station.

items.note: toilettes is plural in French, so à + les fuses into aux.
items.ex: Excusez-moi, je dois aller aux toilettes.
items.exEn: Excuse me, I need to go to the toilet.

items.note: Dish names use à for the main ingredient; à + les pommes fuses into aux.
items.ex: Ma grand-mère fait une tarte aux pommes le dimanche.
items.exEn: My grandmother makes an apple tart on Sundays.

items.note: vanille is feminine: à la never fuses.
items.ex: Je voudrais une glace à la vanille, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: I'd like a vanilla ice cream, please.

items.note: rentrer de + le travail fuses into du; here du means 'from the', not 'some'.
items.ex: Il rentre du travail vers dix-neuf heures.
items.exEn: He gets home from work at around seven p.m.

items.en: at the beginning of the month
items.note: Two fusions in one phrase: à + le début gives au, de + le mois gives du.
items.ex: Je suis payé au début du mois.
items.exEn: I get paid at the beginning of the month.

items.note: demander à quelqu'un: à + les enfants fuses into aux, with a z sound before the vowel.
items.ex: Demande aux enfants s'ils ont faim.
items.exEn: Ask the children if they're hungry.

items.note: de + les billets fuses into des; this des means 'of the', not 'some'.
items.ex: Le prix des billets a encore augmenté.
items.exEn: The price of the tickets has gone up again.

items.en: to the hospital / at the hospital
items.note: hôpital starts with a silent h, so the article is l' and à l' never fuses: not au hôpital.
items.ex: Ma sœur travaille à l'hôpital.
items.exEn: My sister works at the hospital.

teaching.rule: The change you met after pas also happens after ne... plus and ne... jamais: the articles un, une, du, de la, de l' and des become plain de (d' before a vowel), as in il n'y a plus de lait and il ne prend jamais de dessert. It still happens when the noun belongs to a second verb: je ne veux pas acheter de fleurs. Two things never change: le, la, l' and les (je n'aime pas les tomates), and the article after être (ce n'est pas une erreur). Keep the ne: without it, plus de means 'more', not 'no more'.

examples.fr: Il n'y a plus de lait dans le frigo.
examples.en: There's no milk left in the fridge.
examples.note: du lait becomes de lait after ne... plus, just as after pas.

examples.fr: Il ne prend jamais de dessert.
examples.note: un dessert becomes de dessert after ne... jamais.

examples.fr: Je ne veux pas acheter de fleurs.
examples.en: I don't want to buy flowers.
examples.note: The noun belongs to acheter, but the negative on veux still turns des into de.

contrast.note: NOT 'pas de tomates' here: les means tomatoes in general, and le, la, l' and les never change after a negative.
NOT 'ce n'est pas d'erreur': after être the article stays.

contrast.fr: Je ne veux plus de pain. / Je veux plus de pain.
contrast.en: I don't want any more bread. / I want more bread.
contrast.note: With ne, plus de means 'no more'; without ne, it means 'more'. Always write the ne.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers keep the positive article after plus and jamais or when a second verb follows ('je ne veux pas acheter des fleurs'), or change the articles that must stay ('je n'aime pas de tomates', 'ce n'est pas d'erreur'); say de after the negative, but leave le, la, les and the article after être alone.

probes.fr: Mon père ne boit jamais ___ alcool.
probes.ex: Mon père ne boit jamais d'alcool.
probes.exEn: My father never drinks alcohol.

probes.ex: Ce n'est pas un restaurant cher.
probes.exEn: It's not an expensive restaurant.

probes.ex: Nous n'avons plus de sucre, je vais en acheter.
probes.exEn: We have no sugar left; I'll go and buy some.

items.note: des frères becomes de frères after pas.
items.ex: Je n'ai pas de frères, mais j'ai une sœur.
items.exEn: I don't have any brothers, but I have a sister.

items.note: de l'argent becomes d'argent after pas: de shrinks to d' before the vowel.
items.ex: Désolé, je n'ai pas d'argent sur moi.
items.exEn: Sorry, I don't have any money on me.

items.fr: il n'y a plus de pain
items.note: du pain becomes de pain after ne... plus; keep the ne, because plus de pain on its own can mean 'more bread'.
items.ex: Il n'y a plus de pain à la boulangerie.
items.exEn: There's no bread left at the bakery.

items.note: du vin becomes de vin after ne... jamais.
items.ex: Elle ne boit jamais de vin.
items.exEn: She never drinks wine.

items.note: des animaux becomes d'animaux after pas, because animaux starts with a vowel.
items.ex: Nous n'avons pas d'animaux à la maison.
items.exEn: We don't have any animals at home.

items.fr: je ne bois plus de café
items.en: I don't drink coffee any more
items.note: du café becomes de café after ne... plus.
items.ex: Je ne bois plus de café le soir.
items.exEn: I don't drink coffee in the evening any more.

items.note: Short for il n'y a pas de problème, so de, as after any pas; compare ce n'est pas un problème, where être keeps un.
items.ex: Tu peux m'aider ? — Pas de problème !
items.exEn: Can you help me? — No problem!

items.note: faire du bruit becomes ne pas faire de bruit: ne pas sits together in front of an infinitive, and the article still becomes de.
items.ex: Fais attention à ne pas faire de bruit, le bébé dort.
items.exEn: Be careful not to make any noise; the baby's asleep.

items.fr: il n'a pas trouvé de travail
items.note: In the passé composé the rule still applies: du travail becomes de travail after pas.
items.ex: Mon cousin n'a pas encore trouvé de travail.
items.exEn: My cousin hasn't found work yet.

items.fr: ce n'est pas une bonne idée
items.note: After être the article stays: une, not de.
items.ex: Partir maintenant, ce n'est pas une bonne idée.
items.exEn: Leaving now isn't a good idea.

items.fr: ce ne sont pas des touristes
items.note: After être the plural article des stays too; de would be wrong here.
items.ex: Ce ne sont pas des touristes, ils habitent ici.
items.exEn: They're not tourists; they live here.

items.note: le, la and les never change after a negative: only un, une and the partitives become de.
items.ex: Mon fils n'aime pas le fromage, mais il adore les yaourts.
items.exEn: My son doesn't like cheese, but he loves yoghurts.

teaching.rule: After a word that measures an amount - beaucoup (a lot), peu (little / few), un peu (a little), trop (too much / too many), assez (enough), plus (more), moins (less / fewer) - or a container or measure such as une bouteille, un kilo or une tasse, French uses plain de, not du, de la or des, when the noun is meant in general: beaucoup de livres, une bouteille de lait. Before a vowel or a silent h, de becomes d': assez d'argent. The noun keeps its own number: things you count stay plural (trop de voitures), things you don't stay singular (trop de bruit). Two exceptions: la plupart (most) takes des (la plupart des gens), and plusieurs (several) and quelques (a few) take no de at all (plusieurs fois, quelques amis).

examples.fr: Elle a trop de devoirs ce soir.
examples.en: She has too much homework tonight.
examples.note: trop de + plain de; devoirs is plural in French, and it stays plural after de.
A container or measure works like a quantity word: paquet de, whatever the gender or number of what is inside.
peu de means 'few / not much'; de becomes d' before the vowel of amis.
Measures take plain de: un litre de lait, never 'un litre du lait'.

contrast.note: NOT 'trop du bruit': once a quantity word is there, du, de la and des normally shrink to plain de.

contrast.fr: un peu de sucre / peu de sucre
contrast.en: a little sugar / not much sugar
contrast.note: un peu de is positive (some, a bit); peu de without un is negative (hardly any). One small word flips the meaning.
The exception: la plupart takes des, not de, and the verb after it is plural (la plupart des étudiants travaillent).
NOT 'quelques d'amis': quelques and plusieurs go straight before the noun, with no de.

teaching.commonMistake: Learners carry the partitive over after a quantity word ('beaucoup des gens', 'un kilo des pommes'); as soon as an amount is named, the article normally drops to plain de: beaucoup de gens, un kilo de pommes.

probes.fr: Il y a trop ___ voitures en ville.
probes.ex: Il y a trop de voitures en ville.
probes.exEn: There are too many cars in town.

probes.fr: La plupart ___ élèves sont déjà là.
probes.ex: La plupart des élèves sont déjà là.
probes.exEn: Most of the pupils are already here.

probes.ex: J'ai peu de temps aujourd'hui.
probes.exEn: I don't have much time today.

items.note: trop (too much / too many) + plain de: trop de sel, never 'trop du sel'.
items.ex: Il y a trop de sel dans cette soupe.
items.exEn: There's too much salt in this soup.

items.note: assez (enough) + de, and de becomes d' before the vowel of argent.
items.ex: Tu as assez d'argent pour le billet ?
items.exEn: Do you have enough money for the ticket?

items.note: peu de without un means 'few / not many', a negative idea; touristes stays plural after de.
items.ex: En novembre, il y a peu de touristes.
items.exEn: In November there are few tourists.

items.note: un peu de means 'a little, some' and goes with things you don't count, like patience or sugar.
items.ex: Avec un peu de patience, tu vas y arriver.
items.exEn: With a little patience, you'll get there.

items.note: A measure + plain de: un morceau de fromage. Without a measure word it would be du fromage (some cheese).
items.ex: Je mange un morceau de fromage avec mon pain.
items.exEn: I'm eating a piece of cheese with my bread.

items.note: A container + de: une bouteille d'eau, not 'une bouteille de l'eau'; de becomes d' before the vowel.
items.ex: Je prends une bouteille d'eau pour le voyage.
items.exEn: I'm taking a bottle of water for the trip.

items.note: Weights take plain de, and the fruit stays plural: un kilo de pommes, never 'un kilo des pommes'.
items.ex: Je voudrais un kilo de pommes, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: I'd like a kilo of apples, please.

items.note: douzaine needs de where English says just 'a dozen eggs'; de becomes d' before œufs.
items.ex: J'achète une douzaine d'œufs au marché.
items.exEn: I'm buying a dozen eggs at the market.

items.note: moins de means 'less' (or 'fewer' with a plural); like every quantity word it takes plain de.
items.ex: Je mets moins de sucre dans mon café maintenant.
items.exEn: I put less sugar in my coffee now.

items.note: plus de means 'more' of something; plain de, never 'plus du temps'. davantage de means the same, in a slightly more formal style.
items.ex: J'aimerais avoir plus de temps pour lire.
items.exEn: I'd like to have more time to read.

items.note: The exception: la plupart (most) takes des, not de, and the verb that follows is plural.
items.ex: Au bureau, la plupart des gens arrivent à neuf heures.
items.exEn: At the office, most people arrive at nine.

items.note: plusieurs (several) goes straight before the noun with no de at all; it never changes for gender.
items.ex: J'ai vu ce film plusieurs fois.
items.exEn: I've seen this film several times.

teaching.rule: To point at one particular thing, French uses a word that agrees with the noun: ce before a masculine singular noun (ce livre), cet before a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or a silent h (cet ami, cet hôtel), cette before any feminine singular noun, vowel or not (cette maison, cette école), and ces before any plural (ces livres, ces maisons). Each form can mean 'this' or 'that' ('these' or 'those' for ces). To make the difference clear, add -ci (here) or -là (there) to the noun: ce pull-ci, ce pull-là. Cet and cette sound exactly the same, so the noun's gender decides the spelling.

examples.note: livre is masculine and starts with a consonant, so ce.
ami is masculine but starts with a vowel, so ce becomes cet and the t links on: 'sè-ta-mi'.
Every feminine singular noun takes cette.
Plurals take ces for both genders; before a vowel the s links as a z: 'sé-za-mi'.

contrast.note: NOT 'cet école': cet is only for masculine nouns; école is feminine, so cette, even before a vowel.
-ci points to what is near, -là to what is further away; without them, ce pull can mean either.

contrast.en: these books / his or her books
contrast.note: ces and ses sound the same: ces points at the books, ses says whose they are.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'ce ami' or 'cet école', or look for separate words for 'this' and 'that'; choose by the noun's gender and first sound (ce livre, cet ami, cette école, ces livres) and add -ci or -là only when you need the contrast.

probes.ex: Cet arbre a cent ans.
probes.exEn: This tree is a hundred years old.

probes.ex: Cette idée me plaît beaucoup.
probes.exEn: I really like this idea.

probes.ex: Ces questions sont difficiles.
probes.exEn: These questions are difficult.

items.note: livre is masculine and starts with a consonant, so ce; ce can mean 'this' or 'that'.
items.ex: Tu as déjà lu ce livre ?
items.exEn: Have you already read this book?

items.note: rue is feminine, so cette.
items.ex: J'habite dans cette rue.
items.exEn: I live in this street.

items.note: Any plural takes ces, whatever the gender.
items.ex: Combien coûtent ces chaussures ?
items.exEn: How much are these shoes?

items.note: The h of hôtel is silent, so the noun starts with a vowel sound and ce becomes cet.
items.ex: Nous restons dans cet hôtel trois nuits.
items.exEn: We're staying in this hotel for three nights.

items.note: école starts with a vowel but is feminine, so cette; cet is for masculine nouns only.
items.ex: Mes enfants vont dans cette école.
items.exEn: My children go to this school.

items.note: amie is feminine, so cette; cet ami and cette amie sound the same, only the spelling shows the gender.
items.ex: Tu connais cette amie de Paul ?
items.exEn: Do you know this friend of Paul's?

items.note: ces before a vowel links with a z sound: 'sé-zan-fan'.
items.ex: Qui sont ces enfants ?
items.exEn: Who are these children?

items.note: week-end is masculine and starts with a consonant sound, so ce.
items.ex: Je reste à la maison ce week-end.
items.exEn: I'm staying at home this weekend.

items.note: With a time word, ce means the one we are in now or the nearest one: ce matin, this morning.
items.ex: Je suis très fatigué ce matin.
items.exEn: I'm very tired this morning.

items.note: semaine is feminine, so cette.
items.ex: J'ai beaucoup de travail cette semaine.
items.exEn: I have a lot of work this week.

items.note: été is masculine and starts with a vowel, so cet.
items.ex: On part en Bretagne cet été.
items.exEn: We're going to Brittany this summer.

items.note: fois is feminine, so cette; -ci adds 'this one, now', and cette fois on its own means the same.
items.ex: Cette fois-ci, on prend le train.
items.exEn: This time, we're taking the train.

teaching.rule: To compare two things, put plus (more), moins (less) or aussi (as) before the adjective and que (than / as) after it: plus grand que, moins cher que, aussi rapide que. The adjective still agrees with what it describes (ma sœur est plus grande que moi), and a pronoun standing alone after que is moi, toi, lui or elle, not je or tu. For the top or the bottom of a group, add le, la or les: le plus grand, la moins chère. When the adjective normally follows the noun, the article appears twice: le restaurant le plus cher. 'In' after a superlative is normally de: le plus grand parc de la ville. Exceptions to know now: 'better' is meilleur, never 'plus bon', and with a verb it is mieux, never 'plus bien'.

examples.fr: Le train est plus rapide que le bus.
examples.en: The train is faster than the bus.
examples.note: plus + adjective + que: the basic 'more ... than' pattern.

examples.fr: Cette jupe est moins chère que la robe.
examples.en: This skirt is cheaper than the dress.
examples.note: moins ... que means 'less ... than'; chère agrees with jupe, which is feminine.

examples.fr: Il est aussi grand que son père.
examples.en: He's as tall as his father.
examples.note: aussi ... que means 'as ... as'; the second 'as' is que, not comme.

examples.fr: C'est le film le plus drôle de l'année.
examples.en: It's the funniest film of the year.
examples.note: drôle comes after the noun, so le appears twice; 'of the year' after a superlative is de.

contrast.fr: Elle est plus grande que moi.
contrast.note: NOT 'plus grande que je': after que, use the stressed pronoun moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux.

contrast.fr: le plus grand musée de la ville
contrast.en: the biggest museum in the city
contrast.note: Say de, not dans: after a superlative, 'in' is normally de.
Keep both articles: without the second le, the phrase no longer means 'the most expensive'.

teaching.commonMistake: Learners say 'plus grand de moi' or, following English, 'le plus grand dans le monde'; after an adjective, 'than' is que (plus grand que moi), and 'in' after a superlative is normally de (le plus grand du monde).

probes.ex: Paul est plus grand que Marc.
probes.exEn: Paul is taller than Marc.

probes.fr: C'est la ville la plus calme ___ la région.
probes.ex: C'est la ville la plus calme de la région.
probes.exEn: It's the quietest town in the region.

probes.fr: Elle est aussi grande que moi.
probes.en: She is as tall as me.
probes.ex: Elle est aussi grande que moi, maintenant.
probes.exEn: She's as tall as me now.

items.note: plus + adjective + que is 'more ... than'; for people grand means tall. After que, use moi, not je.
items.ex: Mon frère est plus grand que moi.
items.exEn: My brother is taller than me.

items.note: moins + adjective + que is 'less ... than'; it is the everyday way to say 'cheaper than'.
items.ex: Le train est moins cher que l'avion.
items.exEn: The train is less expensive than the plane.

items.note: aussi + adjective + que is 'as ... as'; both 'as' words change: aussi first, que second.
items.ex: Ce livre est aussi intéressant que le film.
items.exEn: This book is as interesting as the film.

items.note: The adjective still agrees: chambre is feminine, so petit becomes petite inside the comparison.
items.ex: Ma chambre est plus petite que la tienne.
items.exEn: My bedroom is smaller than yours.

items.note: For people, plus âgé que is the neutral way to say 'older than'; plus vieux que is also common.
items.ex: Paul est plus âgé que sa sœur.
items.exEn: Paul is older than his sister.

items.note: moins ... que with a feminine subject: sportif becomes sportive, then the comparison wraps around it.
items.ex: Ma sœur est moins sportive que moi.
items.exEn: My sister is less sporty than me.

items.note: Adverbs compare the same way: il court plus vite que moi. vite is an adverb, so it never agrees. One exception: with a verb, 'better' is mieux, never 'plus bien'.
items.ex: Il court plus vite que moi.
items.exEn: He runs faster than me.

items.note: le / la / les + plus + adjective names the top of a group; grand means big for things and tall for people. grand comes before the noun, so there is only one le.
items.ex: C'est le plus grand parc de la ville.
items.exEn: It's the biggest park in the city.

items.note: belle sits before the noun, so the superlative goes there too: la plus belle plage.
items.ex: C'est la plus belle plage de la région.
items.exEn: It's the most beautiful beach in the region.

items.note: cher follows the noun, so the article is repeated: le menu le moins cher. 'The cheapest' is literally 'the least expensive'.
items.ex: Je prends le menu le moins cher.
items.exEn: I'll take the cheapest set menu.

items.note: Plural noun, so les and chers: les hôtels les plus chers, with the article twice because cher follows the noun.
items.ex: Ce sont les hôtels les plus chers de la ville.
items.exEn: These are the most expensive hotels in the city.
