items.fr: la plus grande de la classe
items.note: After a superlative, 'in' is normally de: la plus grande de la classe, rather than dans la classe.
items.ex: Léa est la plus grande de la classe.
items.exEn: Léa is the tallest in the class.

teaching.rule: Many English adverbs end in -ly; the French ones often end in -ment. Start from the FEMININE form of the adjective and add -ment: lent → lente → lentement (slowly), heureux → heureuse → heureusement (fortunately). If the masculine adjective already ends in a vowel, add -ment to it directly: vrai → vraiment, poli → poliment. Adjectives of more than one syllable ending in -ant or -ent change to -amment and -emment, which are pronounced the same way: courant → couramment, récent → récemment (the one-syllable lent follows the first rule: lentement). A few are irregular: gentil → gentiment, bon → bien, mauvais → mal. With a one-word verb the adverb goes right after it (il parle lentement). In the passé composé, bien, mal and vraiment go between avoir or être and the past participle (j'ai bien dormi); many other -ment adverbs can go either there or after the participle (il a répondu poliment, il a poliment répondu).

examples.note: lent → feminine lente → lentement; the adverb comes right after the verb.
calme already ends in -e, so it just adds -ment: calmement.
courant ends in -ant, so the adverb ends in -amment: couramment.
bien is the adverb of bon; in the passé composé it goes between avoir and the participle.

contrast.note: NOT 'sérieuxment': build from the feminine sérieuse, then add -ment.
NOT 'j'ai aimé vraiment ce livre': vraiment, like bien and mal, sits between avoir and the participle.
NOT 'elle parle bon': bon is the adjective (good); with a verb you need the adverb bien (well).

teaching.commonMistake: Learners build the adverb from the masculine form ('heureuxment', 'sérieuxment'); start from the feminine (heureuse → heureusement) unless the masculine already ends in a vowel (vrai → vraiment).

probes.ex: Il demande poliment l'addition.
probes.exEn: He politely asks for the bill.

probes.ex: Elle sourit gentiment à l'enfant.
probes.exEn: She smiles kindly at the child.

probes.en: correct: bien goes between avoir and the past participle
probes.ask: Is “J'ai bien dormi” right, and why?
probes.ex: J'ai bien dormi, merci.
probes.exEn: I slept well, thanks.
options: wrong: bien goes after the past participle (j'ai dormi bien)
wrong: the adjective bon is needed here (j'ai bon dormi)
correct: a French adverb can go anywhere in the sentence

items.note: lent → feminine lente → lentement: the feminine form plus -ment.
items.ex: Le temps passe lentement quand on attend.
items.exEn: Time passes slowly when you're waiting.

items.note: rapide already ends in -e, so it just adds -ment. vite means the same and is just as common.
items.ex: Les enfants apprennent rapidement.
items.exEn: Children learn quickly.

items.note: heureux → feminine heureuse → heureusement; it means 'luckily', not 'happily'.
items.ex: Le train est en retard, mais heureusement nous avons le temps.
items.exEn: The train is late, but fortunately we have time.

items.note: vrai ends in a vowel, so -ment goes straight onto the masculine: vraiment, not 'vraiement'.
items.ex: Ce gâteau est vraiment bon.
items.exEn: This cake is really good.

items.note: poli ends in a vowel, so -ment is added to the masculine: poliment.
items.ex: Le serveur nous salue poliment.
items.exEn: The waiter greets us politely.

items.note: facile already ends in -e, so it just adds -ment: facilement.
items.ex: Mon frère se fâche facilement.
items.exEn: My brother gets angry easily.

items.note: courant ends in -ant, so the adverb ends in -amment: couramment. It is the usual word for speaking a language fluently.
items.ex: Après deux ans, elle parle couramment.
items.exEn: After two years, she speaks fluently.

items.note: récent ends in -ent, so the adverb ends in -emment, pronounced just like -amment. dernièrement means the same.
items.ex: Ils ont déménagé récemment, donc ils ne connaissent personne ici.
items.exEn: They moved recently, so they don't know anyone here.

items.note: Irregular: gentil → gentiment, with one l and no extra e.
items.ex: Elle me répond gentiment.
items.exEn: She answers me kindly.

items.note: bien is the adverb of bon: bon describes a noun, bien describes how something is done. In the passé composé it goes between avoir and the participle.
items.ex: Tu as bien dormi ?
items.exEn: Did you sleep well?

items.note: mal is the adverb of mauvais; like bien, it sits between avoir and the participle.
items.ex: J'ai mal dormi cette nuit.
items.exEn: I slept badly last night.

items.note: complet → feminine complète → complètement; the grave accent of the feminine stays.
items.ex: La salle est complètement vide.
items.exEn: The room is completely empty.

items.note: patient ends in -ent, so the adverb ends in -emment: patiemment.
items.ex: Mon chien attend patiemment.
items.exEn: My dog waits patiently.

teaching.rule: Countries and continents have a gender, and the word for 'in' or 'to' follows it. Feminine names - nearly every one ending in -e, and all the continents - take en: en Italie, en Belgique, en Europe. Masculine names take au: au Japon, au Portugal, au Brésil, except that a masculine name starting with a vowel takes en, for the sound: en Iran. Plural names take aux: aux Pays-Bas. Cities take à, with no article (à Rome), unless the article is part of the name: Le Caire gives au Caire. A few island countries also take plain à: à Cuba. For 'from', use de (d' before a vowel) for feminine countries and for cities, du for masculine countries (but d'Iran, as with en Iran), des for plural ones: d'Espagne, du Brésil, des États-Unis. Watch the exceptions to the -e rule: le Mexique and le Cambodge are masculine, so au Mexique.

examples.note: Irlande ends in -e, so it is feminine and takes en.

examples.fr: On part au Maroc cet hiver.
examples.en: We're going to Morocco this winter.
examples.note: le Maroc is masculine, so 'to' is au; the same word means 'in'.
A plural country name takes aux, like aux États-Unis.
'From' + a masculine country is du (de + le).

contrast.note: NOT 'en Mexique': it ends in -e but le Mexique is masculine, one of the few exceptions.
NOT 'au Afghanistan': a masculine country starting with a vowel takes en.
NOT 'en Rome': cities take à, whatever their gender.
With a feminine country, 'from' is plain de with no article: de Grèce, d'Italie.

teaching.commonMistake: Learners use en for every country ('en Japon', 'en Portugal') or keep the article after de ('je viens de la Suisse'); check the gender first: au Japon, au Portugal, je viens de Suisse.

probes.ex: Ils vivent au Danemark depuis deux ans.
probes.exEn: They've been living in Denmark for two years.

probes.ex: Je viens de Suisse, mais j'habite à Lyon.
probes.exEn: I'm from Switzerland, but I live in Lyon.

probes.ex: Il revient du Canada ce soir.
probes.exEn: He's coming back from Canada tonight.

items.note: le Japon is masculine (it doesn't end in -e), so 'in' or 'to' is au.
items.ex: Mon cousin habite au Japon.
items.exEn: My cousin lives in Japan.

items.note: l'Italie ends in -e, so it is feminine and takes en.
items.ex: Nous passons nos vacances en Italie.
items.exEn: We're spending our holidays in Italy.

items.note: le Portugal is masculine; au means both 'to' and 'in', so the verb tells you which.
items.ex: Cet été, je vais au Portugal.
items.exEn: This summer I'm going to Portugal.

items.note: la Belgique ends in -e, so en; there is no article after en.
items.ex: On parle français en Belgique.
items.exEn: People speak French in Belgium.

items.note: An exception: le Mexique ends in -e but is masculine, so au, not en.
items.ex: Ma sœur travaille au Mexique.
items.exEn: My sister works in Mexico.

items.note: l'Iran is masculine, but it starts with a vowel, so it takes en instead of au.
items.ex: Ma collègue est née en Iran.
items.exEn: My colleague was born in Iran.

items.note: les Pays-Bas is plural, so 'in' or 'to' is aux.
items.ex: Mon frère étudie aux Pays-Bas.
items.exEn: My brother is studying in the Netherlands.

items.note: 'From' + a masculine country: de + le fuses into du.
items.ex: Ce café vient du Brésil.
items.exEn: This coffee comes from Brazil.

items.note: 'From' + a feminine country is plain de, with no article, and de becomes d' before the vowel: d'Espagne.
items.ex: Je rentre d'Espagne demain.
items.exEn: I'm coming back from Spain tomorrow.

items.note: 'From' + a plural country: de + les fuses into des.
items.ex: Ils reviennent des États-Unis la semaine prochaine.
items.exEn: They're coming back from the United States next week.

items.note: Cities take à, but Le Caire keeps its article, so à + le fuses into au.
items.ex: Ma tante habite au Caire.
items.exEn: My aunt lives in Cairo.

items.note: Some island countries behave like cities and take plain à with no article: à Cuba.
items.ex: Ils partent en vacances à Cuba.
items.exEn: They're going on holiday to Cuba.

items.note: All the continents are feminine, so they take en: en Europe, en Asie, en Afrique.
items.ex: Il voyage en Europe tout l'été.
items.exEn: He's travelling in Europe all summer.

teaching.rule: Three small words answer 'how long?' and 'when?'. depuis is for something that started in the past and is still going on, and the verb stays in the PRESENT where English says 'have been': je suis à Paris depuis trois jours (I've been in Paris for three days). depuis works with a length of time (depuis trois jours) and with a starting point (depuis lundi, since Monday). ça fait + time + que says the same thing with the length up front: ça fait trois jours que je suis à Paris. pendant gives the length of a stretch seen as a whole, with an end: one that is over (j'ai attendu pendant deux heures), planned (je serai là pendant une semaine) or repeated (je marche pendant une heure tous les jours); it never means 'and still going on'. With an event or a period, pendant means 'during': pendant les vacances. il y a + time means 'ago' and points to a moment in the past, so it goes with a past verb: je suis arrivé il y a dix minutes. To ask, use depuis combien de temps ? (casually, depuis quand ?) for something still going on, and pendant combien de temps ? for a stretch with an end.

examples.fr: J'apprends le français depuis six mois.
examples.en: I've been learning French for six months.
examples.note: Still learning now, so depuis takes the present where English says 'have been learning'.
depuis + a starting point means 'since'; the verb is still in the present.

examples.fr: Ça fait une heure que je t'attends !
examples.en: I've been waiting for you for an hour!
examples.note: ça fait ... que puts the length first; the verb is still in the present.

examples.fr: J'ai habité à Rome pendant trois ans.
examples.en: I lived in Rome for three years.
examples.note: Finished: the person no longer lives there, so pendant + passé composé.

examples.fr: Nous sommes arrivés il y a une semaine.
examples.note: il y a + time = 'ago': it points to one moment in the past.

contrast.fr: J'habite à Lyon depuis cinq ans.
contrast.en: I've lived in Lyon for five years (and still do).
contrast.note: depuis + present: the situation continues today.

contrast.fr: J'ai habité à Lyon pendant cinq ans.
contrast.en: I lived in Lyon for five years (and then left).
contrast.note: pendant + past: the five years are over.

contrast.fr: J'ai quitté Lyon il y a cinq ans.
contrast.en: I left Lyon five years ago.
contrast.note: il y a dates a moment in the past; it says nothing about how long anything lasted.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers copy 'have been' and say 'j'ai été à Paris depuis trois jours'; when the situation is still going on, French keeps the present: je suis à Paris depuis trois jours.

probes.fr: J'habite à Nantes depuis trois ans.
probes.en: I've lived in Nantes for three years (and still do).
probes.ex: J'habite à Nantes depuis trois ans et j'adore cette ville.
probes.exEn: I've lived in Nantes for three years and I love this city.
options: I lived in Nantes for three years (and then left).
I'll live in Nantes for three years.
I lived in Nantes three years ago.

probes.fr: Je suis arrivé il y a dix minutes.
probes.ex: Ne t'inquiète pas, je suis arrivé il y a dix minutes.
probes.exEn: Don't worry, I arrived ten minutes ago.
options: I waited ten minutes before arriving.

probes.fr: J'ai travaillé à Londres ___ cinq ans, puis je suis rentré en France.
probes.ex: J'ai travaillé à Londres pendant cinq ans, puis je suis rentré en France.
probes.exEn: I worked in London for five years, then I came back to France.

items.note: Still true today, so depuis + a present-tense verb, where English says 'have been'.
items.ex: Je travaille ici depuis deux ans.
items.exEn: I've been working here for two years.

items.note: depuis + a starting point means 'since'; the verb stays in the present because it is still happening.
items.ex: Il pleut depuis lundi.
items.exEn: It's been raining since Monday.

items.note: The same depuis + present pattern with a time of day as the starting point.
items.ex: Elle est malade depuis ce matin.
items.exEn: She's been ill since this morning.

items.note: Literally 'since always': for something that has always been true and still is.
items.ex: Je connais Paul depuis toujours.
items.exEn: I've always known Paul.

items.note: The question for something still going on; the answer uses depuis and the verb stays in the present.
items.ex: Vous attendez depuis combien de temps ?
items.exEn: How long have you been waiting?

items.note: ça fait + a length of time + que + present: the same meaning as depuis, with the length placed first.
items.ex: Ça fait une heure que je t'attends !
items.exEn: I've been waiting for you for an hour!

items.note: pendant gives the length of a stretch with an end; this wait is over, so the verb is in the past.
items.ex: J'ai attendu pendant deux heures.
items.exEn: I waited for two hours.

items.note: pendant + an event or a period means 'during'; here with a present for something that happens every holiday.
items.ex: Je lis beaucoup pendant les vacances.
items.exEn: I read a lot during the holidays.

items.note: The question for a stretch that is over or planned as a whole; compare depuis combien de temps ? for something still going on.
items.ex: Tu as vécu à Londres pendant combien de temps ?
items.exEn: How long did you live in London?

items.note: il y a + a length of time means 'ago' and goes with a past verb; here it has nothing to do with 'there is'.
items.ex: Je l'ai vu il y a deux jours.
items.exEn: I saw him two days ago.

items.note: il y a + longtemps: a moment far back in the past.
items.ex: J'ai lu ce livre il y a longtemps.
items.exEn: I read this book a long time ago.

teaching.rule: In a shop you need three verbs: coûter (to cost: Ça coûte combien ?), payer (to pay) and essayer (to try on). You pay par carte (by card) or en espèces (in cash): the little words par and en are fixed. When the cashier gives the total, you hear ça fait + the amount: Ça fait douze euros. Watch the false friend la monnaie: it means change (coins, or the money handed back to you), while money in general is l'argent. Food shopping is faire les courses; going round the shops for fun is faire les magasins.

examples.note: The everyday way to ask a price; Combien ça coûte ? means the same.
par carte for a card, but en espèces for cash.

examples.fr: Ça fait douze euros, s'il vous plaît.
examples.en: That comes to twelve euros, please.
examples.note: What the cashier says when giving the total: ça fait + the amount.

examples.fr: Je fais les courses au supermarché le samedi.
examples.en: I do the food shopping at the supermarket on Saturdays.
examples.note: faire les courses is buying food and everyday things, not shopping for fun.

contrast.note: Not 'I have no money': for that, say Je n'ai pas d'argent.
With no article it is par carte; with an article or a possessive, avec ma carte or avec la carte also works.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers use la monnaie for 'money'; la monnaie is change, and money in general is l'argent: Je n'ai pas d'argent (I have no money) but Je n'ai pas de monnaie (I have no change).

probes.ex: Ce sac est joli, ça coûte combien ?
probes.exEn: This bag is pretty, how much does it cost?

probes.ex: Désolé, je n'ai pas de monnaie, seulement un billet de cinquante euros.
probes.exEn: Sorry, I don't have any change, only a fifty-euro note.

probes.ex: Cette veste me plaît, je peux l'essayer ?
probes.exEn: I like this jacket, can I try it on?

items.note: Masculine; the final x is silent, and the word does not change in the plural (les prix).
items.ex: Je regarde toujours le prix avant d'acheter.
items.exEn: I always look at the price before buying.

items.note: Written with û (ça coûte, ils coûtent); ask a price with Ça coûte combien ?
items.ex: Combien coûte ce pull ?
items.exEn: How much does this sweater cost?

items.note: Pay FOR something takes no extra word in French: payer le pain, not payer pour le pain.
items.ex: Je peux payer par carte ?
items.exEn: Can I pay by card?

items.note: Fixed phrase with en; en liquide means the same and is a little more casual.
items.ex: Je préfère payer en espèces.
items.exEn: I prefer to pay in cash.

items.note: Feminine; pay with it par carte, and at the till you often hear just la carte or la carte bleue.
items.ex: J'ai oublié ma carte bancaire à la maison.
items.exEn: I left my bank card at home.

items.note: Feminine; a false friend: it is the coins or the money handed back, not money in general (l'argent).
items.ex: Vous avez de la monnaie ?
items.exEn: Do you have any change?

items.note: Feminine; the person working there is le caissier or la caissière.
items.ex: Il y a beaucoup de monde à la caisse.
items.exEn: There are a lot of people at the checkout.

items.note: Feminine; it is used for clothes, while shoe size is la pointure.
items.ex: Cette robe est trop petite, il me faut la taille au-dessus.
items.exEn: This dress is too small, I need the next size up.

items.note: Also means 'to try' in general; in a shop it is what you do in the fitting room before buying.
items.ex: Je peux essayer cette veste ?
items.exEn: Can I try on this jacket?

items.note: Masculine plural in this sense (les soldes d'été); in France the main sales run at set dates in winter and in summer.
items.ex: J'ai acheté ce manteau pendant les soldes.
items.exEn: I bought this coat in the sales.

items.note: Buying food and everyday things; going round shops for fun is faire les magasins.
items.ex: Je fais les courses le samedi matin.
items.exEn: I do the shopping on Saturday mornings.

items.note: Masculine; short for distributeur de billets, the machine you take money out of.
items.ex: Il y a un distributeur près d'ici ?
items.exEn: Is there a cash machine near here?

teaching.rule: To say how you travel, French uses en when you sit inside the vehicle (en train, en voiture, en avion, en bus, en métro) and à when you ride on it or walk (à vélo, à pied). The verb for taking transport is prendre: je prends le bus, on prend le métro. A ticket for a train or a plane is un billet, while for the metro or a city bus it is usually un ticket. At the station you wait sur le quai, and if the train leaves without you, you have raté (missed) it.

examples.fr: Je vais à Lyon en train.
examples.en: I'm going to Lyon by train.
examples.note: You sit inside the train, so it takes en.

examples.fr: Elle va au travail à vélo.
examples.en: She goes to work by bike.
examples.note: You ride on a bike, not inside it, so it takes à.

examples.fr: On prend le bus ou le métro ?
examples.en: Shall we take the bus or the metro?
examples.note: prendre is the verb for using any kind of transport.

examples.fr: Un billet pour Marseille, s'il vous plaît.
examples.note: billet is the word for a train or plane ticket; pour gives the destination.

contrast.note: Walking takes à, like à vélo; en is only for vehicles you sit inside (en voiture).
For the metro and city buses it is un ticket; for trains and planes it is un billet.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers translate 'by car' or 'by train' with par or avec; French says en voiture, en train, and à pied, à vélo for walking and cycling.

probes.ex: Il y a beaucoup de monde sur le quai.
probes.exEn: There are a lot of people on the platform.

probes.ex: Le train est en retard, on va attendre un peu.
probes.exEn: The train is late, we'll wait a bit.

probes.ex: J'ai raté mon train, je vais prendre le suivant.
probes.exEn: I missed my train, I'll take the next one.

items.note: Masculine; used for trains, planes and concerts (a metro or bus ticket is usually un ticket), and it also means a banknote: un billet de dix euros.
items.ex: J'ai acheté un billet de train pour Bordeaux.
items.exEn: I bought a train ticket to Bordeaux.

items.note: Masculine; the qu sounds like k, and you wait sur le quai (on the platform).
items.ex: Je vous attends sur le quai.
items.exEn: I'll wait for you on the platform.

items.note: Feminine; faire sa valise means to pack your suitcase.
items.ex: Je fais ma valise ce soir.
items.exEn: I'm packing my suitcase tonight.

items.note: Masculine; vol also means a theft, but in travel talk it is a flight.
items.ex: Notre vol a deux heures de retard.
items.exEn: Our flight is two hours late.

items.note: Often with être (je suis en retard) or arriver (arriver en retard); the opposite is en avance (early).
items.ex: Désolé, je suis en retard à cause des bouchons.
items.exEn: Sorry, I'm late because of the traffic jams.

items.note: Masculine (un arrêt); the vowel start makes le shrink to l'.
items.ex: On se retrouve à l'arrêt de bus.
items.exEn: We'll meet at the bus stop.

items.note: Masculine; short for le métropolitain, and you go en métro or prendre le métro.
items.ex: Pour aller au musée, c'est plus rapide en métro.
items.exEn: To get to the museum, it's quicker by underground.

items.note: Walking takes à, never en: aller à pied means to walk somewhere.
items.ex: J'y vais à pied, c'est tout près.
items.exEn: I'm going on foot, it's very close.

items.note: Inside a vehicle takes en: en voiture, en train, en avion.
items.ex: Nous partons en vacances en voiture.
items.exEn: We are going on holiday by car.

items.note: Masculine; the counter where you buy tickets or ask for information.
items.ex: Vous pouvez acheter votre billet au guichet.
items.exEn: You can buy your ticket at the ticket office.

items.note: Feminine; the train or bus you change to on the way, and the time you have to catch it.
items.ex: À Lyon, nous avons une correspondance de vingt minutes.
items.exEn: In Lyon, we have a twenty-minute connection.

items.note: Everyday verb; manquer means the same and is a little more formal.
items.ex: Dépêche-toi, on va rater le bus !
items.exEn: Hurry up, we're going to miss the bus!

teaching.rule: At the doctor's or the pharmacy, most illnesses are nouns used with avoir: avoir de la fièvre (to have a temperature), avoir un rhume (to have a cold), avoir la grippe (to have the flu). To say how you feel, use se sentir (je me sens fatigué) or aller (je vais mieux). You prendre rendez-vous (make an appointment) chez le médecin, and he or she gives you an ordonnance (prescription) to take to the pharmacy. Watch the false friend: un médicament is a medicine you take, while la médecine is the science doctors study.

examples.fr: J'ai de la fièvre depuis deux jours.
examples.en: I've had a temperature for two days.
examples.note: fièvre is feminine, so 'some fever' is de la; depuis + present for something still going on.

examples.fr: Je ne me sens pas bien.
examples.note: se sentir is reflexive, so ne... pas wraps me sens.

examples.fr: Prenez un comprimé le matin et le soir.
examples.en: Take one tablet in the morning and one in the evening.
examples.note: prendre is the verb for taking medicine, as in English.

examples.fr: Elle a pris rendez-vous chez le médecin.
examples.en: She made an appointment at the doctor's.
examples.note: prendre rendez-vous is the fixed way to say 'make an appointment'; chez means 'at the place of'.

contrast.note: La médecine is the science: elle fait des études de médecine (she is studying medicine).
malade is an adjective used with être, but the illness itself is a noun used with avoir: j'ai un rhume, j'ai la grippe.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers call the pills or syrup they take 'une médecine'; what you take is un médicament, and la médecine is the field doctors study.

probes.ex: J'ai de la fièvre et mal à la gorge.
probes.exEn: I have a temperature and a sore throat.

probes.en: I'd like to make an appointment.
probes.ex: Bonjour, je voudrais prendre rendez-vous avec le docteur Martin.
probes.exEn: Hello, I'd like to make an appointment with Dr Martin.
options: I'd like to cancel an appointment.
I'd like to buy some medicine.
I'd like to see the pharmacist.

probes.fr: Vous avez quelque chose contre la toux ?
probes.en: Do you have anything for a cough?
probes.ex: Bonjour, vous avez quelque chose contre la toux, s'il vous plaît ?
probes.exEn: Hello, do you have anything for a cough, please?
options: Do you have anything for a headache?
Do you have anything for a fever?
Do you have anything for a sore throat?

items.note: Masculine, with a hyphen; prendre rendez-vous means to make an appointment.
items.ex: J'ai pris rendez-vous chez le dentiste pour lundi.
items.exEn: I've made an appointment at the dentist's for Monday.

items.note: Feminine; French says avoir de la fièvre where English says 'have a fever' or 'have a temperature'.
items.ex: Mon fils a de la fièvre depuis hier soir.
items.exEn: My son has had a fever since last night.

items.note: Masculine; avoir un rhume is to have a cold, while froid is cold as a temperature.
items.ex: J'ai un rhume, je reste à la maison.
items.exEn: I've got a cold, I'm staying at home.

items.note: Feminine; French says avoir la grippe, with la, just like 'have the flu'.
items.ex: Elle a la grippe, elle ne vient pas au bureau.
items.exEn: She has the flu, she isn't coming to the office.

items.note: Regular -er verb with a double s; the noun is la toux (a cough).
items.ex: Il tousse beaucoup la nuit.
items.exEn: He coughs a lot at night.

items.note: Adjective used with être; the same form for masculine and feminine (il est malade, elle est malade).
items.ex: Je ne vais pas à l'école, je suis malade.
items.exEn: I'm not going to school, I'm ill.

items.note: Masculine; a false friend: la médecine is the science, not the pills you take.
items.ex: Prenez ce médicament trois fois par jour.
items.exEn: Take this medicine three times a day.

items.note: Feminine (une ordonnance); the doctor writes it and you take it to the pharmacy.
items.ex: Le médecin m'a donné une ordonnance.
items.exEn: The doctor gave me a prescription.

items.note: Masculine; a woman is la pharmacienne, and you can ask them for advice about small health problems.
items.ex: Demandez conseil au pharmacien.
items.exEn: Ask the pharmacist for advice.

items.note: Reflexive: je me sens, tu te sens, il se sent; follow it with bien, mal or an adjective.
items.ex: Je ne me sens pas très bien ce matin.
items.exEn: I don't feel very well this morning.

items.note: Uses aller, not être: je vais mieux (I'm better), ça va mieux (things are better).
items.ex: Merci, je vais mieux aujourd'hui.
items.exEn: Thanks, I'm better today.

items.note: Always plural in this sense; aller aux urgences is to go to A&E.
items.ex: On l'a emmené aux urgences hier soir.
items.exEn: They took him to A&E last night.

teaching.rule: An ordinary day in French is told mostly with reflexive verbs in the present: je me réveille, je me douche, je me prépare, je pars au travail, je rentre, je me couche, je m'endors. Keep apart the pairs English blurs: se réveiller (to wake up) is not se lever (to get up), and se coucher (to go to bed) is not s'endormir (to fall asleep). The same verb without the pronoun acts on someone or something else: je me réveille (I wake up) but je réveille mon fils (I wake my son). Chores use faire: faire la vaisselle, faire le ménage.

examples.fr: Je me réveille à six heures, mais je me lève à six heures et quart.
examples.en: I wake up at six, but I get up at a quarter past six.
examples.note: Two different moments: se réveiller is opening your eyes, se lever is getting out of bed.

examples.fr: Je me douche, je me prépare et je pars au travail.
examples.en: I shower, get ready and leave for work.
examples.note: A routine is a chain of present-tense verbs; only the reflexive ones carry me.

examples.fr: Le soir, je me lave les cheveux.
examples.en: In the evening, I wash my hair.
examples.note: With a body part, French says les, not mes: me already shows whose hair it is.

examples.fr: Je me couche à onze heures, mais je m'endors vers minuit.
examples.en: I go to bed at eleven, but I fall asleep around midnight.
examples.note: se coucher is lying down in bed; s'endormir is actually falling asleep.

contrast.fr: Je réveille mon fils à sept heures.
contrast.en: I wake my son up at seven.
contrast.note: Without me, réveiller acts on someone else; je me réveille is waking yourself.
me already says whose hair it is, so the body part takes les: je me lave les cheveux.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers drop the reflexive pronoun ('je douche à sept heures') because English says 'I shower' with no 'myself'; keep it in every routine verb that has one: je me douche, je me prépare, je m'endors.

probes.ex: Le week-end, je m'endors tard.
probes.exEn: At the weekend, I fall asleep late.

probes.ex: Elle se maquille avant de sortir.
probes.exEn: She puts on her make-up before going out.

probes.ex: Ce soir, c'est toi qui fais la vaisselle.
probes.exEn: Tonight, you're the one doing the dishes.

items.note: Masculine; it comes from se réveiller (to wake up), and it sonne (rings) in the morning.
items.ex: Mon réveil sonne à six heures et demie.
items.exEn: My alarm clock goes off at half past six.

items.note: Reflexive: je me douche, tu te douches; prendre une douche (to take a shower) is just as common.
items.ex: Je me douche avant le petit-déjeuner.
items.exEn: I shower before breakfast.

items.note: Reflexive: il se rase; without se, raser means to shave someone or something else.
items.ex: Mon père se rase tous les jours.
items.exEn: My father shaves every day.

items.note: Reflexive: elle se maquille; le maquillage is the make-up itself.
items.ex: Elle se maquille devant le miroir.
items.exEn: She puts on her make-up in front of the mirror.

items.note: Reflexive: je me prépare; préparer without me means to prepare something, like a meal.
items.ex: Je me prépare en dix minutes.
items.exEn: I get ready in ten minutes.

items.note: Reflexive and irregular like dormir: je m'endors, il s'endort; se coucher is only going to bed.
items.ex: Le soir, je m'endors très vite.
items.exEn: In the evening, I fall asleep very quickly.

items.note: partir is irregular: je pars, tu pars, il part; it is not reflexive.
items.ex: Je pars au travail à huit heures.
items.exEn: I leave for work at eight o'clock.

items.note: Here rentrer means going back to where you live, like rentrer chez soi; it is not reflexive.
items.ex: Le soir, je rentre à la maison vers sept heures.
items.exEn: In the evening, I go home at about seven.

items.note: A short sleep after lunch, a habit many people keep at the weekend; faire une sieste is just as correct.
items.ex: Après le déjeuner, mon grand-père fait la sieste.
items.exEn: After lunch, my grandfather has a nap.

items.note: Cleaning the home (dusting, hoovering); not to be confused with faire la vaisselle (doing the dishes).
items.ex: Le samedi, nous faisons le ménage.
items.exEn: On Saturdays, we do the housework.

items.note: la vaisselle is the dishes themselves; you do it after the meal.
items.ex: Après le dîner, je fais la vaisselle.
items.exEn: After dinner, I do the dishes.

items.note: tous les + plural for a habit: tous les matins, tous les soirs.
items.ex: Je bois un café tous les matins.
items.exEn: I drink a coffee every morning.

teaching.rule: Most hobbies hang on three verbs. jouer à + a sport or game: jouer au tennis, jouer aux cartes. jouer de + a musical instrument: jouer de la guitare, jouer du violon. faire de + an activity: faire du vélo, faire de la natation, faire de la randonnée, with du, de la, de l' or des matching the noun. To say what you like, use aimer + le / la + the noun (j'aime la lecture) or + an infinitive (j'aime nager). To say what you did at the weekend, put the same verbs in the passé composé: j'ai joué au tennis, j'ai fait du vélo, je suis allé au cinéma.

examples.fr: Je joue au tennis le samedi.
examples.note: A sport or game takes jouer à, and à + le contracts to au.
An instrument takes jouer de: de la guitare, du violon.

examples.fr: Tu fais du sport ? — Oui, je fais de la natation.
examples.en: Do you do any sport? — Yes, I swim.
examples.note: faire de + the activity is the default way to talk about a sport you do, even where English says 'go' or 'do'.

examples.fr: Ce week-end, j'ai fait du vélo et je suis allé au cinéma.
examples.en: This weekend, I went cycling and went to the cinema.
examples.note: The weekend story goes in the passé composé: avoir with faire, être with aller.

contrast.fr: Je vais au travail à vélo.
contrast.en: I go to work by bike.
contrast.note: To get somewhere by bike is aller à vélo; faire du vélo is cycling as an activity in its own right.
natation is feminine, so the little word is de la: je fais de la natation.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers use one verb for everything ('play football', 'play the guitar', 'go cycling'); French says jouer à for a sport, jouer de for an instrument, and faire de for an activity: le samedi, je fais du vélo. aller à vélo only says how you get somewhere.

probes.ex: On va à la piscine samedi ?
probes.exEn: Shall we go to the pool on Saturday?

probes.ex: Tu fais du sport en ce moment ?
probes.exEn: Are you doing any sport at the moment?
options: Are you going to the gym?

probes.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ce week-end ?
probes.en: What did you do at the weekend?
probes.ex: Salut ! Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ce week-end ?
probes.exEn: Hi! What did you do at the weekend?
options: What are you doing this weekend?
What do you do at weekends?
Where did you go last week?

items.note: Masculine plural (un loisir); the everyday word, in conversation and on forms, for what you do in your free time.
items.ex: Quels sont tes loisirs ?
items.exEn: What are your hobbies?

items.note: Masculine; libre means free as in available, not free of charge, which is gratuit.
items.ex: Qu'est-ce que tu fais pendant ton temps libre ?
items.exEn: What do you do in your free time?

items.note: faire du + a masculine activity: cycling for its own sake. To get somewhere by bike is aller à vélo; the bike itself is un vélo.
items.ex: Le samedi matin, je fais du vélo avec mon père.
items.exEn: On Saturday mornings, I go cycling with my dad.

items.note: Feminine, so faire de la natation; the verb is nager (je nage) and the pool is la piscine.
items.ex: Je fais de la natation le mardi.
items.exEn: I go swimming on Tuesdays.

items.note: randonnée is feminine, so de la; in casual speech people shorten it to faire de la rando.
items.ex: J'aime faire de la randonnée en montagne.
items.exEn: I like hiking in the mountains.

items.note: Irregular: je cours, tu cours, il court, nous courons; the past participle is couru (j'ai couru).
items.ex: Je cours deux fois par semaine.
items.exEn: I run twice a week.

items.note: Masculine, plural les matchs; any competitive game between two sides: un match de foot, un match de tennis.
items.ex: On regarde le match ce soir ?
items.exEn: Shall we watch the game tonight?

items.note: Feminine (une équipe), even for a men's team; because it starts with a vowel, 'my team' is mon équipe.
items.ex: Mon équipe a gagné samedi.
items.exEn: My team won on Saturday.

items.note: Regular -er verb that also means to earn (gagner de l'argent); the opposite is perdre, to lose.
items.ex: Lyon a gagné deux à zéro.
items.exEn: Lyon won two-nil.

items.note: vidéo never takes an s here: un jeu vidéo, des jeux vidéo; you play them with jouer à, so jouer aux jeux vidéo.
items.ex: Mon frère joue aux jeux vidéo le soir.
items.exEn: My brother plays video games in the evening.

items.note: Feminine; a false friend: it means reading, not a lecture, which is un cours or une conférence.
items.ex: J'adore la lecture et le cinéma.
items.exEn: I love reading and films.

items.note: Reflexive: je me promène (è before a silent ending), nous nous promenons; the noun is une promenade, and se balader is a casual equivalent.
items.ex: Il fait beau, on va se promener ?
items.exEn: It's nice out, shall we go for a walk?

teaching.rule: Describe someone's build and character with être + adjective (il est mince, elle est timide) and their features with avoir + les + the feature + adjective: il a les cheveux courts, elle a les yeux verts. For what a person has on their face or wears, say avoir une barbe and porter des lunettes. Every adjective agrees with the person: -eux becomes -euse (paresseux, paresseuse), many adjectives in -eur become -euse (travailleur, travailleuse), and some change more (gentil, gentille; roux, rousse). To compare someone with a relative, use ressembler à: il ressemble à sa mère.

examples.fr: Elle a les yeux verts et les cheveux longs.
examples.en: She has green eyes and long hair.
examples.note: avoir + les + feature + adjective: the colour or length comes after the noun.

examples.fr: Mon père est grand et il porte des lunettes.
examples.en: My father is tall and wears glasses.
examples.note: être for what he is, porter for what he wears.

examples.fr: Ma cousine est drôle mais un peu paresseuse.
examples.en: My cousin is funny but a bit lazy.
examples.note: drôle already ends in -e, so it does not change for a woman; paresseux becomes paresseuse.
ressembler is always followed by à before the person.

contrast.fr: Il est petit. (not Il est court.)
contrast.note: court is for length (hair, a film, a skirt); a short person is petit.

contrast.fr: Elle ressemble à sa mère. (not Elle ressemble sa mère.)
contrast.note: ressembler needs à before the person it compares with.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers leave the adjective in its dictionary form whoever they describe ('ma sœur est paresseux'); when the person is a woman the adjective changes too: paresseuse, gentille, rousse, bavarde.

probes.ex: Elle est mince et elle a les cheveux longs.
probes.exEn: She is slim and has long hair.

probes.ex: Il ressemble à son père : même nez, même sourire.
probes.exEn: He looks like his father: same nose, same smile.
options: He is waiting for his father.
He is talking to his father.

probes.en: wrong: it should be bavarde, because sœur is feminine
probes.ask: Is “Ma sœur est bavard.” right?
probes.ex: Ma sœur est bavarde.
probes.exEn: My sister is chatty.
options: correct: adjectives after être never agree

items.note: Same form for both genders because it already ends in -e; the neutral, polite word for a slim build.
items.ex: Elle est grande et mince.
items.exEn: She is tall and slim.

items.note: Feminine rousse, plural roux; natural red hair is roux, not rouge: il a les cheveux roux.
items.ex: Sa fille est rousse, comme sa mère.
items.exEn: His daughter has red hair, like her mother.

items.note: Feminine courte; it is for length (hair, a film, a skirt), while a short person is petit.
items.ex: Il a les cheveux courts.
items.exEn: He has short hair.

items.note: Always feminine plural, even for one pair; sunglasses are des lunettes de soleil, and you porter des lunettes.
items.ex: Mon père porte des lunettes.
items.exEn: My father wears glasses.

items.note: Feminine; une moustache is feminine too, and 'he has a beard' is il a une barbe or il porte la barbe.
items.ex: Mon oncle a une barbe grise.
items.exEn: My uncle has a grey beard.

items.note: Feminine gentille, with a double l; the everyday word for a kind, considerate person.
items.ex: Ma grand-mère est très gentille.
items.exEn: My grandmother is very kind.

items.note: Same form for both genders; before a noun, un drôle de... means an odd... (un drôle de type, an odd guy).
items.ex: Ton copain est vraiment drôle !
items.exEn: Your friend is really funny!

items.note: Same form for both genders; the opposite is sociable (outgoing).
items.ex: Au début, il est un peu timide.
items.exEn: At first, he's a bit shy.

items.note: Feminine bavarde; related to the verb bavarder, to chat.
items.ex: Ma voisine est très bavarde.
items.exEn: My neighbour is very chatty.

items.note: -eux becomes -euse in the feminine (paresseuse); the final x is silent.
items.ex: Mon colocataire est paresseux : il ne fait jamais la vaisselle.
items.exEn: My flatmate is lazy: he never does the washing-up.

items.note: As an adjective it means hard-working; feminine travailleuse, the same -eur / -euse pattern as serveur / serveuse.
items.ex: C'est une étudiante très travailleuse.
items.exEn: She's a very hard-working student.

items.note: Always followed by à, which contracts with le: elle ressemble à sa mère, il ressemble au voisin.
items.ex: Tu ressembles beaucoup à ta mère.
items.exEn: You look a lot like your mother.

teaching.rule: Feelings are mostly être + an adjective that agrees with the person who feels them: il est content, elle est contente, ils sont déçus. Give the cause with de + a noun or an infinitive (content de mon travail, fier de toi, triste de partir) or with parce que + a whole clause. To say how someone looks from the outside, use avoir l'air + adjective: tu as l'air triste. Moods take de: être de bonne humeur, de mauvaise humeur. A few feelings are verbs rather than adjectives: s'ennuyer (to be bored), s'inquiéter (to worry).

examples.fr: Elle est contente de son nouvel appartement.
examples.en: She is pleased with her new flat.
examples.note: contente takes -e for a woman, and de introduces what pleases her.

examples.fr: Nous sommes très fiers de toi.
examples.en: We are very proud of you.
examples.note: Plural subject, so fiers with -s; de + the person you are proud of.

examples.fr: Tu as l'air triste, qu'est-ce qui se passe ?
examples.en: You look sad, what's going on?
examples.note: avoir l'air + adjective says how someone seems to others, not how they say they feel.

examples.fr: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout va bien.
examples.note: s'inquiéter is the verb behind inquiet; this is the everyday way to reassure someone.

contrast.note: je suis ennuyé means I'm bothered or in an awkward position; to say you are bored use the reflexive verb s'ennuyer.

contrast.fr: Il est énervé. (not Il est nerveux.)
contrast.note: énervé means irritated or worked up; nerveux describes a tense, jumpy person and is not the word for being annoyed.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers read énervé as 'nervous' and déçu as 'deceived'; énervé means annoyed and déçu means disappointed, so before an exam say je suis stressé, not je suis énervé.

probes.ex: Je suis déçu, on a perdu le match.
probes.exEn: I'm disappointed, we lost the match.

probes.ex: Elle est inquiète pour son fils.
probes.exEn: She is worried about her son.

probes.ex: Ne lui parle pas, il est de mauvaise humeur.
probes.exEn: Don't talk to him, he's in a bad mood.
options: He has a bad sense of humour.

items.note: Feminine contente; the everyday word for being happy or pleased about something, with de + what pleases you. heureux is the warmer, deeper word.
items.ex: Je suis très content de te voir !
items.exEn: I'm really happy to see you!

items.note: Same form for both genders; the noun is la tristesse.
items.ex: Elle est triste parce que son chat est malade.
items.exEn: She is sad because her cat is ill.

items.note: Feminine inquiète, with a grave accent; the verb is s'inquiéter, as in ne t'inquiète pas (don't worry).
items.ex: Ma mère est inquiète : il est minuit et mon frère n'est pas rentré.
items.exEn: My mother is worried: it's midnight and my brother isn't home.

items.note: A false friend: énervé means irritated or worked up, not nervous (for nerves before an exam say stressé); much stronger is en colère, angry.
items.ex: Il est énervé parce que son train est en retard.
items.exEn: He's annoyed because his train is late.

items.note: Past participle of décevoir, feminine déçue; a false friend, it never means deceived.
items.ex: Je suis déçu : le concert est annulé.
items.exEn: I'm disappointed: the concert has been cancelled.

items.note: Feminine surprise, where the s is now sounded; surpris de + infinitive: surpris de te voir.
items.ex: Elle a été très surprise de me voir.
items.exEn: She was very surprised to see me.

items.note: The final r is pronounced; feminine fière, with a grave accent. fier de + the person or thing.
items.ex: Je suis fier de toi !
items.exEn: I'm proud of you!

items.note: Feminine jalouse; jaloux de + the person you envy.
items.ex: Il est jaloux de son grand frère.
items.exEn: He's jealous of his big brother.

items.note: humeur is feminine, hence bonne; the phrase is être de bonne humeur, with de, never dans.
items.ex: Aujourd'hui, Paul est de bonne humeur.
items.exEn: Paul is in a good mood today.

items.note: The opposite of de bonne humeur; mauvais becomes mauvaise because humeur is feminine.
items.ex: Le matin, je suis souvent de mauvaise humeur.
items.exEn: In the morning, I'm often in a bad mood.

items.note: French says it with a reflexive verb: je m'ennuie, tu t'ennuies; je suis ennuyé means I'm bothered, not bored.
items.ex: Je m'ennuie, il n'y a rien à faire.
items.exEn: I'm bored, there's nothing to do.

items.note: avoir l'air + adjective describes how someone seems from the outside; conjugate avoir: elle a l'air, ils ont l'air. To say who someone looks like, use ressembler à.
items.ex: Tu as l'air fatigué, ça va ?
items.exEn: You look tired, are you OK?

items.note: Feminine soulagée; it comes from soulager, to relieve.
items.ex: Je suis soulagé : l'examen est fini.
items.exEn: I'm relieved: the exam is over.

teaching.rule: The unaccented e of little words (je, me, te, se, le, de, ne) and inside many words is a soft 'uh' called the e muet. At the end of a word it is silent (une table). Elsewhere it often disappears in everyday speech when only one consonant sound comes before it: samedi sounds 'sam-DI', un petit chat 'un p'tit chat', je te vois 'j'te vois'. It stays when dropping it would jam three consonants together (vendredi), and in a run of e's only one of two neighbours can go. The full form is never wrong: it is more common in careful speech and in the south of France.

examples.note: In everyday speech the middle e drops: sam'di (sam-DI), two syllables instead of three.
The e of je drops: j'te vois (zhteu-VWA). Only one of the two e's goes.
petit loses its e: un p'tit chat (un-PTI-sha).

contrast.note: In samedi only m comes before the e, so it can drop (sam'di). In vendredi, dropping the e would jam d, r and d together, so it stays: van-dreu-DI.
Two e's in a row: one of them goes, never both. Say j'me lève or je m'lève.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say every e as a full vowel ('suh-MEN', 'puh-TEE'), which sounds stilted in conversation; let the e go when a single consonant comes before it. Don't overdo it: dropping two e's in a row, or the e of vendredi, makes the word hard to recognise.

probes.ask: How is “à demain” usually said in everyday speech?
probes.ex: Bonne soirée, à demain !
probes.exEn: Have a good evening, see you tomorrow!

probes.en: no: it keeps d, r and d apart, so it stays
probes.ask: Can the e of “vendredi” drop in everyday speech?
probes.ex: Le marché a lieu le vendredi.
probes.exEn: The market is on Fridays.
options: no, because the e of a weekday name never drops
it is silent, like a final e

probes.ask: How is “la semaine” usually said in everyday speech?
probes.ex: Je travaille toute la semaine.
probes.exEn: I work all week.

items.note: The e of se- drops in everyday speech: la s'maine (la-SMÈN), two syllables.
items.ex: La semaine prochaine, je suis en vacances.
items.exEn: Next week I'm on holiday.

items.note: After a vowel, as in à demain, the e drops: à d'main, ending on the nasal 'in' sound.
items.ex: À demain !
items.exEn: See you tomorrow!

items.note: The middle e drops: app'ler (a-PLÉ), two syllables rather than three.
items.ex: Je vais appeler ma mère.
items.exEn: I'm going to call my mother.

items.note: de loses its e, and its d, now touching the s of suite, hardens into a t sound: tout d'suite sounds 'toot-SWEET'.
items.ex: Je reviens tout de suite.
items.exEn: I'll be right back.

items.note: After a vowel the e of che- drops: à ch'val (a-SHVAL). In le cheval only one of the two e's can go: le ch'val.
items.ex: Elle monte à cheval.
items.exEn: She rides horses.

items.note: Two e's in a row, and only one can drop: on its own it is usually rev'nir (reuv-NIR). Dropping both would jam r, v and n together.
items.ex: Je vais revenir plus tard.
items.exEn: I'll come back later.

items.note: After a vowel the e of ge- drops: au g'nou (o-JNOU). In le genou the two e's sit side by side, so only one can go: le g'nou.
items.ex: J'ai mal au genou.
items.exEn: My knee hurts.

items.note: The e between c and r drops: épic'rie (é-pis-RI), three syllables instead of four. Only the s sound comes before it, so the rule lets it go.
items.ex: Il y a une épicerie au coin de la rue.
items.exEn: There's a grocer's on the corner.

items.note: The e of re- drops after a vowel: tu veux r'garder (r-gar-DÉ).
items.ex: Tu veux regarder la télé ?
items.exEn: Do you want to watch TV?

items.note: The e before -ment is silent even in careful speech: douss-MAN, two syllables.
items.ex: Doucement, c'est fragile !
items.exEn: Gently, it's fragile!

items.note: petit loses its e: un p'tit peu (un-PTI-peu). The same happens in un p'tit café.
items.ex: Je parle un petit peu français.
items.exEn: I speak a little bit of French.

items.note: After a vowel the e of de- drops: mes d'voirs (mé-DVWAR). Homework in general is plural in French: faire ses devoirs.
items.ex: Je fais mes devoirs.
items.exEn: I'm doing my homework.

teaching.rule: French has two pairs of vowels that English speakers tend to merge. First, u and ou: for u (tu, vue, sûr) say 'ee', then round and push your lips forward as for 'oo' while your tongue stays forward; for ou (tout, vous, roue) the tongue pulls back and you get a short, tense 'oo' as in 'food'. Second, é and è: é (café, léger, fermé) is a closed 'ay' held steady with no glide at the end; è (mère, fête, règle) is the open e of English 'bed'. The e sound is always open (è) when its syllable ends in a pronounced consonant, which is why premier ends in é with a silent r, but première ends in è followed by a sounded r. Swapping u and ou changes the word: tu / tout, rue / roue, dessus / dessous.

examples.note: The French u: say 'ee', then round and push your lips forward as for 'oo' without moving your tongue back. English has no such vowel.
The French ou: the 'oo' of English 'food', but shorter, with well-rounded lips and the tongue pulled back; the s is silent.
é is a closed, steady 'ay' with no glide at the end: ka-FÉ, not English 'ka-FAY-ee'. Smile slightly and hold the sound still.
è is the open e of English 'bed': MÈR. It is open here because the syllable ends in a pronounced r.

contrast.note: Only the vowel changes: tongue forward for u (de-SÜ), tongue back for ou (de-SOO). Mix them up and you say the opposite.
Both end in a vowel, since the t of tout is silent, so the vowel alone tells the two words apart.
The masculine ends in closed é with a silent r (pruh-MYÉ); the feminine ends in open è followed by a sounded r (pruh-MYÈR).

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers replace u with ou, so tu sounds like tout and la rue like la roue, and they let é slide into the English diphthong 'ay-ee'. Keep the tongue forward and the lips rounded for u, and hold é perfectly still.

probes.en: only the vowel: tongue forward for rue, pulled back for roue
probes.ask: What tells “la rue” (the street) apart from “la roue” (the wheel) when you say them?
probes.ex: J'ai trouvé une roue de vélo dans la rue.
probes.exEn: I found a bike wheel in the street.
options: the r: rolled in rue, silent in roue
the final e: sounded in roue, silent in rue
nothing: the two words sound exactly the same

probes.en: on a steady closed é with no glide: ka-FÉ
probes.ask: How does “café” end?
probes.ex: Un café, s'il vous plaît.
probes.exEn: A coffee, please.
options: on a glide, as in English 'day': ka-FAY-ee
on the open è of mère: ka-FÈ

probes.en: with the open è of mère and a sounded r: pruh-MYÈR
probes.ask: How does “première” end?
probes.ex: C'est la première fois.
probes.exEn: It's the first time.
options: with the closed é of café and a silent r: pruh-MYÉ

items.note: The ou vowel: a short, tense 'oo' as in 'food', lips well rounded, tongue back (TOO); the t is silent. Keep it apart from tu (you), whose vowel is made with the tongue forward.
items.ex: Tout va bien.
items.exEn: Everything is fine.

items.note: Rounded 'oo' with the tongue back (DOO), and the x is silent. It must not sound like du (some, of the), where the tongue stays forward for u.
items.ex: Ce pull est très doux.
items.exEn: This jumper is very soft.

items.note: The ou vowel with rounded lips (ROO). Compare la rue (the street): the two words differ only in this vowel.
items.ex: Une voiture a quatre roues.
items.exEn: A car has four wheels.

items.note: The u vowel: say 'ee', then round your lips without moving your tongue (VÜ). With ou it would sound like vous (you).
items.ex: Cette chambre a une belle vue.
items.exEn: This room has a lovely view.

items.note: The u vowel with the tongue forward and the lips rounded (ZHÜ); the s is silent. Said with ou, it becomes joue (cheek; plays).
items.ex: Un jus d'orange, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: An orange juice, please.

items.note: The u vowel followed by a sounded r (SÜR). The circumflex changes nothing in speech, so sûr sounds exactly like sur (on); with ou it would become sourd (deaf).
items.ex: Tu es sûr ?
items.exEn: Are you sure?

items.note: Two closed é sounds, lé-JÉ: the final -er is said é and its r is silent. The feminine légère ends in open è plus a sounded r: lé-JÈR.
items.ex: Ce sac est léger.
items.exEn: This bag is light.

items.note: Open è twice, with both r's sounded: dèr-NYÈR. The masculine dernier ends in closed é with a silent r: dèr-NYÉ.
items.ex: C'est la dernière question.
items.exEn: That's the last question.

items.note: ê is the open è of English 'bed' (FÈT), and the t is pronounced because an -e follows it. Do not close it to é. Faire la fête means to party.
items.ex: On fait la fête ce soir !
items.exEn: We're partying tonight!

items.note: Both kinds of e in one word: closed é first, then open è before the v: é-LÈV. The final -e is silent.
items.ex: Cet élève travaille bien.
items.exEn: This pupil works well.

items.note: Open è, then closed é: fèr-MÉ. The first e is open because its syllable ends in r. Without the accent, ferme (farm; closes) ends on the open sound: FÈRM.
items.ex: Le magasin est fermé le dimanche.
items.exEn: The shop is closed on Sundays.

items.note: è before two consonants is open: RÈGL, with the final -e silent. Règle also means a ruler for drawing lines.
items.ex: Quelle est la règle ?
items.exEn: What's the rule?

teaching.rule: English stresses one syllable inside each word (ba-NA-na, PHAR-ma-cy, IN-ter-est-ing) and shrinks the others to 'uh'. French does not. Every syllable gets about the same length and a full vowel (the one exception is the light e of je, le or ne, which is often dropped in speech), and only the last pronounced syllable of a group of words is lengthened: cho-co-LA, un-ca-FÉ. A group is a chunk said in one breath, usually a noun with its article and adjectives, or a short verb phrase, so the stress moves to the end as the group grows: un café, then un café CRÈME. A final silent -e does not count, so in banane the stress falls on -nane. The stressed syllable is mostly longer, not louder: keep the syllables before it full and even instead of swallowing them.

examples.note: Three even beats, the last one longer: cho-co-LA, with the t silent. English squeezes the word into CHOC-lit.
One group said as one smooth stream, ja-bi-ta-pa-RI: no word inside it gets its own stress, only the very last syllable.
Four words, one group, one stress at the end, on vin. Verre sits in the middle of the group, so it stays light.

contrast.note: English says PA-ris; French says pa-RI, with even syllables and the weight on the last one. The s is silent.
On its own, café takes the stress on -fé; add crème and the group gets longer, so the stress moves to crème and -fé goes light.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers stress words near the front (PHAR-ma-cie, IN-té-res-sant) and reduce the other vowels to 'uh'; keep every syllable even and full, except the light e of je, le or ne, and lean only on the last syllable of the group.

probes.ask: Where does the stress fall in “Paris”, said on its own?
probes.ex: J'habite à Paris depuis deux ans.
probes.exEn: I've lived in Paris for two years.
options: on the first syllable, with the s pronounced: PA-riss
on the last syllable, with the s pronounced: pa-RISS

probes.ask: Where does the stress fall in “Je ne comprends pas”?
probes.ex: Pardon, je ne comprends pas.
probes.exEn: Sorry, I don't understand.

probes.en: on crème, the end of the group
probes.ask: In “un café crème”, which part carries the stress?
probes.ex: Je voudrais un café crème.
probes.exEn: I'd like a white coffee.
options: on ca-, the start of café

items.note: On its own, chocolat is stressed on -lat; add chaud and the group gets longer, so the stress moves to the end: cho-co-la-CHO, with -lat now light.
items.ex: Je voudrais un chocolat chaud.
items.exEn: I'd like a hot chocolate.

items.note: Two syllables, ba-NANN: the final -e is silent, so the stress lands on -nane. Both a's are the same open 'a', never the 'buh' of English 'banana'.
items.ex: Je mange une banane.
items.exEn: I'm eating a banana.

items.note: Four even beats, in-té-ré-SAN, with only the last one lengthened. English stresses the first syllable of 'interesting'; in French in- stays light.
items.ex: Ce livre est très intéressant.
items.exEn: This book is very interesting.

items.note: Four even syllables with the weight on the final nasal: ab-so-lu-MAN. Do not lean on ab- as in English 'AB-solutely'.
items.ex: Tu es d'accord ? — Absolument.
items.exEn: Do you agree? — Absolutely.

items.note: Three even beats, dik-syo-NÈR, with the stress on the last one and the final -e silent. English stresses DIC-tionary.
items.ex: Tu as un dictionnaire ?
items.exEn: Do you have a dictionary?

items.note: One group, one stress at the end: un-nor-di-na-teur-por-TABL. Said alone, ordinateur ends on -teur; inside this group -teur goes light and the stress moves to -table.
items.ex: Mon ordinateur portable est trop lent.
items.exEn: My laptop is too slow.

items.note: Said in four beats because the e before -ment drops: ma-leu-reuz-MAN, with the stress at the very end. The h is silent.
items.ex: Malheureusement, le magasin est fermé.
items.exEn: Unfortunately, the shop is closed.

items.note: far-ma-SI: three even syllables, the last one lengthened. English puts the weight on PHAR-; French keeps it light. In la pharmacie de la gare the stress moves on to gare, and -cie goes light.
items.ex: Il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?
items.exEn: Is there a chemist's near here?

items.note: Four even beats, la-ni-vèr-SÈR: the stress is on -saire, and the final -e is silent. In l'anniversaire de Paul the group grows and the stress moves to Paul.
items.ex: Samedi, c'est mon anniversaire.
items.exEn: Saturday is my birthday.

items.note: é-vi-da-MAN: the -emment ending is said like -amment, and the stress sits on the last syllable only.
items.ex: Tu viens ? — Évidemment !
items.exEn: Are you coming? — Obviously!

items.note: Three words, one rhythm group, one stress at the end: un-vèr-DO. Verre is in the middle of the group, so it is not stressed.
items.ex: Je voudrais un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: I'd like a glass of water, please.

items.note: su-pèr-mar-CHÉ: four even beats. English stresses SU-permarket; French leans only on the final -ché. In le supermarché du coin the group grows, so the stress moves to coin.
items.ex: Je fais les courses au supermarché.
items.exEn: I do the shopping at the supermarket.

teaching.rule: Shops, cafés and ticket windows run on a handful of fixed lines, and knowing both sides lets you follow the exchange. You say bonjour, then je voudrais... or je vais prendre..., c'est combien ? for the price, c'est tout when you have everything, and l'addition, s'il vous plaît in a restaurant. The staff say Et avec ceci ? (anything else?), Sur place ou à emporter ? and Vous payez comment ?, which you answer with par carte or en espèces. At the station ask for un aller simple or un aller-retour pour + the town. Leave with merci, au revoir.

examples.fr: — Bonjour, deux croissants, s'il vous plaît. — Et avec ceci ? — C'est tout, merci.
examples.en: — Hello, two croissants, please. — Anything else? — That's all, thanks.
examples.note: The bakery exchange in three lines: your request, the assistant's 'anything else?', and your 'that's all'.

examples.fr: Je vais prendre le menu du jour.
examples.en: I'll have the set menu of the day.
examples.note: Ordering in a restaurant: le menu is a fixed-price set meal, while the full list of dishes is la carte.

examples.en: — How are you paying? — By card.
examples.note: par carte and en espèces are the two answers you need at the till.

examples.fr: Un aller-retour pour Marseille, s'il vous plaît.
examples.note: At a ticket window, name the kind of ticket, then pour + the destination.

contrast.fr: un billet de train (not un ticket de train)
contrast.note: For trains, planes and concerts the word is un billet; un ticket is for the metro or the bus, and un ticket de caisse is a till receipt.
la carte is the standard word for the full list of dishes; le menu strictly means a fixed-price set meal, though many people also use it loosely for the list.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers wait for the bill to arrive on its own; in a French café or restaurant the waiter usually brings l'addition only when you ask for it, so catch their eye and say l'addition, s'il vous plaît.

probes.ex: — Ça fait douze euros. Vous payez comment ? — Par carte.
probes.exEn: — That's twelve euros. How are you paying? — By card.

probes.ex: — Vous voulez le ticket ? — Non merci, ça va.
probes.exEn: — Do you want the receipt? — No thanks, I'm fine.

probes.ex: Bonsoir, vous avez choisi ?
probes.exEn: Good evening, are you ready to order?

items.en: How much is it? / How much does it cost?
items.note: The simplest way to ask a price; name or point at the thing first: ce pull, c'est combien ? At the till, ça fait combien ? asks for the total.
items.ex: Excusez-moi, ce pull, c'est combien ?
items.exEn: Excuse me, how much is this jumper?

items.note: The usual way to order in a café or restaurant, followed by the dish or drink; je prends is just as common.
items.ex: Pour moi, je vais prendre une salade niçoise.
items.exEn: For me, I'll have a salade niçoise.

items.note: Feminine; in a café or restaurant you ask for it when you are ready to pay. In a hotel the bill is la note.
items.ex: On peut avoir l'addition, s'il vous plaît ?
items.exEn: Can we have the bill, please?

items.note: What a bakery or fast-food counter asks you; answer sur place (to eat here) or à emporter (to take with you).
items.ex: Bonjour ! Sur place ou à emporter ?
items.exEn: Hello! Eat in or take away?

items.note: The usual opening line in a shop once you have said bonjour; chercher takes a direct object, with no word for 'for'.
items.ex: Bonjour, je cherche un cadeau pour ma mère.
items.exEn: Hello, I'm looking for a present for my mother.

items.note: How you ask for a table on arrival at a restaurant; give the number of people after pour.
items.ex: Bonsoir, une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: Good evening, a table for two, please.

items.note: The shop assistant's line after you have asked for something; Et avec ça ? is the same, a little more casual.
items.ex: — Une baguette, s'il vous plaît. — Et avec ceci ?
items.exEn: — A baguette, please. — Anything else?

items.note: The answer to Et avec ceci ? once you have everything; add merci: c'est tout, merci.
items.ex: Non merci, c'est tout.
items.exEn: No thanks, that's all.

items.note: Masculine; un aller is the outward journey, so simple means one way only.
items.ex: Un aller simple pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: A single to Lyon, please.

items.en: a return ticket / a round trip
items.note: Masculine, with a hyphen: there and back; the plural is des allers-retours.
items.ex: Je voudrais un aller-retour pour Bordeaux.
items.exEn: I'd like a return ticket to Bordeaux.

items.note: The polite way to answer a shop assistant's Je peux vous aider ? when you only want to browse; je regarde seulement means the same.
items.ex: — Je peux vous aider ? — Non merci, je regarde.
items.exEn: — Can I help you? — No thanks, I'm just looking.

items.note: la monnaie is the change you get back (or coins in general); gardez is the vous command of garder, to keep.
items.ex: Voilà vingt euros, gardez la monnaie.
items.exEn: Here's twenty euros, keep the change.

items.note: The usual answer to Vous payez comment ?; the other one is en espèces, in cash.
items.ex: — Vous payez comment ? — Par carte, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: — How are you paying? — By card, please.

teaching.rule: French softens a request in three layers you can stack. First, the conditional: je voudrais instead of je veux, est-ce que je pourrais instead of je peux, vous pourriez instead of vous pouvez. Second, a question instead of an order: Vous pourriez fermer la porte ? rather than Fermez la porte ! Third, a cushion around it: excusez-moi before, s'il vous plaît, si possible or merci d'avance after. The more you ask of a stranger, the more layers you add, and a negative question (vous n'auriez pas... ?) is softer still. The same conditional softens a request among friends: tu pourrais m'aider ?

examples.fr: Je voudrais deux baguettes, s'il vous plaît.
examples.note: Conditional plus s'il vous plaît: the everyday shop request.

examples.en: Could you call me a taxi?
examples.note: Statement word order with a rising voice: the usual spoken way to ask a stranger to do something.

examples.fr: Est-ce que je pourrais vous poser une question ?
examples.en: Could I ask you a question?
examples.note: Asking permission: est-ce que + je pourrais + an infinitive.

examples.fr: Tu pourrais me passer le sel ?
examples.en: Could you pass me the salt?
examples.note: Among friends the conditional still softens: tu pourrais sounds warmer than tu peux.

contrast.fr: Fermez la porte, s'il vous plaît.
contrast.note: An instruction made polite by s'il vous plaît: fine from a teacher or on a sign, but to a stranger Vous pourriez fermer la porte ? sounds less like an order.

contrast.fr: Est-ce que je pourrais avoir de l'eau ? (softer than Je peux avoir de l'eau ?)
contrast.note: Both are correct; the conditional pourrais adds the distance English gets from 'could'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers lean on 'please' and put s'il vous plaît after a bare command ('Répétez, s'il vous plaît'); to a stranger that still sounds like an instruction, so turn it into a question in the conditional: Vous pourriez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

probes.fr: Je voudrais deux billets pour ce soir.
probes.en: polite and normal: je voudrais is the standard way to ask
probes.ask: How does “Je voudrais deux billets pour ce soir.” sound at a ticket office?
probes.ex: Bonjour, je voudrais deux billets pour ce soir.
probes.exEn: Hello, I'd like two tickets for tonight.
options: old-fashioned: people now just say je veux
too formal: je voudrais belongs in letters and emails
abrupt: it needs est-ce que to be polite

probes.en: an order: a request would be Vous pourriez fermer la porte ?
probes.ask: Said to a stranger, what is “Fermez la porte !”?
probes.ex: Fermez la porte !
probes.exEn: Close the door!
options: a polite request: the vous form is enough to make it polite
a soft request: the imperative is gentler than a question
a question: it asks whether the door is shut

probes.fr: Ça vous dérange si je m'assois ici ?
probes.en: Do you mind if I sit here?
probes.ex: Pardon, ça vous dérange si je m'assois ici ?
probes.exEn: Excuse me, do you mind if I sit here?
options: Would you like to sit here?

items.note: The conditional of vouloir: it turns 'I want' into a polite 'I would like', the default for ordering and asking.
items.ex: Je voudrais un renseignement, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: I'd like some information, please.

items.note: The conditional of pouvoir asks permission gently, with an infinitive after it; say it with a rising voice, after est-ce que, or more formally as pourrais-je.
items.ex: Bonjour, est-ce que je pourrais parler à Madame Martin ?
items.exEn: Hello, could I speak to Madame Martin?

items.note: The spoken polite request: statement word order with a rising voice; pourriez-vous, verb first, is the more formal version, and tu pourrais is the same request to a friend.
items.ex: Pardon, vous pourriez parler plus lentement ?
items.exEn: Sorry, could you speak more slowly?

items.note: déranger means to disturb; ça vous gêne si and ça vous ennuie si mean the same. If you don't mind, answer non, pas du tout (no, not at all).
items.ex: Ça vous dérange si j'ouvre la fenêtre ?
items.exEn: Do you mind if I open the window?

items.note: A negative question in the conditional is one of the softest ways to ask for something, because it is easy to say no to.
items.ex: Excusez-moi, vous n'auriez pas l'heure ?
items.exEn: Excuse me, would you happen to have the time?

items.note: Added at the end, it turns a wish into a gentle request that leaves the other person room to refuse.
items.ex: Une table près de la fenêtre, si possible.
items.exEn: A table by the window, if possible.

items.note: demander un service is to ask a favour, and rendre service à quelqu'un is to do someone one.
items.ex: Je pourrais vous demander un service ?
items.exEn: Could I ask you a favour?

items.note: A polite frame for asking for information; the question after it starts with si (if), où, quand..., with no est-ce que.
items.ex: Je voudrais savoir si le musée est ouvert lundi.
items.exEn: I'd like to know if the museum is open on Monday.

items.note: Closes a request politely, especially at the end of a message or an email; merci par avance means the same.
items.ex: Merci d'avance pour votre aide.
items.exEn: Thanks in advance for your help.

items.note: A warm yes to an offer or an invitation; avec plaisir means much the same.
items.ex: — Vous voulez un café ? — Volontiers, merci.
items.exEn: — Would you like a coffee? — Gladly, thank you.

items.note: The conditional of être turns c'est possible into a gentle request; follow it with de + an infinitive. In casual speech you also hear ça serait possible.
items.ex: Ce serait possible de changer de chambre ?
items.exEn: Would it be possible to change rooms?

items.note: Thanks someone for a favour or an offer; add très and de votre part for more warmth: c'est très gentil de votre part. c'est très aimable is a slightly more formal way to say it.
items.ex: — Je vous aide avec votre valise ? — Oh merci, c'est gentil !
items.exEn: — Shall I help you with your suitcase? — Oh thank you, that's kind of you!

teaching.rule: The imparfait is the past tense for how things WERE: descriptions (it was sunny, I was tired), habits (we used to go every summer), and actions that were going on in the background (I was reading). To form it, take the 'nous' form of the present, drop -ons, and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient: nous parlons gives je parlais, tu parlais, il parlait, nous parlions, vous parliez, ils parlaient. The only irregular stem is être: ét- (j'étais). Listen for the '-ai' sound at the end of the verb; the je, tu, il and ils forms all sound the same.

examples.fr: Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais à Lyon.
examples.en: When I was little, I lived in Lyon.
examples.note: A description of a past situation, not a single event: both verbs are imparfait.

examples.fr: Il faisait beau et les enfants jouaient dehors.
examples.en: The weather was nice and the children were playing outside.
examples.note: Scene-setting: weather and an ongoing activity. Faire gives fais- from nous faisons.

examples.fr: Chaque été, on allait à la mer.
examples.en: Every summer we used to go to the sea.
examples.note: A repeated habit ('used to') takes the imparfait; the stem all- comes from nous allons.

examples.fr: Nous finissions nos devoirs à 18 h.
examples.en: We used to finish our homework at 6 pm.
examples.note: -ir verbs like finir have a long stem finiss- from nous finissons.

contrast.note: One completed event that happened once is passé composé, not imparfait.
Present tense; the imparfait version is j'étais fatigué, 'I was tired'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers build the imparfait from the je form of the present (giving forms like 'je finais'); always start from the nous form minus -ons (nous finissons gives je finissais).

probes.ex: Nous étions en vacances.
probes.exEn: We were on holiday.

probes.ex: Elle chantait sous la douche.
probes.exEn: She was singing in the shower.

probes.ex: Quand j'étais petit, j'adorais le chocolat.
probes.exEn: When I was little, I loved chocolate.

items.note: Être is the one verb with an irregular imparfait stem, ét-; it describes a past state, not an event.
items.ex: Hier, j'étais très fatigué.
items.exEn: Yesterday I was very tired.

items.note: The imparfait of c'est; the go-to way to describe or judge something in the past ('it was great').
items.ex: C'était une belle journée.
items.exEn: It was a beautiful day.

items.note: Il y a in the past: avoir gives av- from nous avons, plus -ait; it also means 'there were', as it never changes for plural.
items.ex: Il y avait beaucoup de monde.
items.exEn: There were a lot of people.

items.note: Weather in the past is almost always imparfait because it describes the background; the stem fais- comes from nous faisons.
items.ex: Hier, il faisait beau et chaud.
items.exEn: Yesterday the weather was nice and hot.

items.note: Pleuvoir only exists in the il form; pleuv- plus -ait paints the rainy background of a story.
items.ex: Il pleuvait quand nous sommes sortis.
items.exEn: It was raining when we went out.

items.note: Avoir: av- plus -ions; the nous and vous endings are -ions and -iez, with a clear 'y' sound.
items.ex: À l'époque, nous avions un chien.
items.exEn: Back then, we had a dog.

items.note: Regular -er verb: parl- from nous parlons plus -ais; it describes what was in progress when something else happened.
items.ex: Je parlais avec Marc quand tu as appelé.
items.exEn: I was talking with Marc when you called.

items.note: The ils ending -aient looks long but sounds exactly like -ais and -ait; only the spelling shows the plural.
items.ex: Les enfants jouaient dans le jardin.
items.exEn: The children were playing in the garden.

items.note: Vouloir: voul- from nous voulons plus -iez; wanting is a state, so past 'wanted' is usually imparfait.
items.ex: Vous vouliez me voir ?
items.exEn: You wanted to see me?

items.note: Aller: all- from nous allons plus -ait; with a time phrase like le dimanche or chaque été the imparfait means 'used to'.
items.ex: Le dimanche, on allait chez ma grand-mère.
items.exEn: On Sundays we used to go to my grandmother's.

items.note: Manger keeps its extra -e only before a and o (je mangeais, nous mangeons); before -ions it drops it: mangions.
items.ex: Nous mangions quand il est arrivé.
items.exEn: We were eating when he arrived.

items.note: Regular -ir verbs take the long stem from nous finissons: finiss- plus -ais.
items.ex: Je finissais mes devoirs quand tu es rentré.
items.exEn: I was finishing my homework when you came home.

teaching.rule: When you tell a story about the past, use the passé composé for the EVENTS, the things that happened and moved the story forward (the phone rang, I fell, she left), and the imparfait for the BACKGROUND, how things were and what was going on (it was raining, I was sleeping, we used to go). Time words help you choose: 'tout à coup', 'soudain', 'un jour', 'ce jour-là' point to a passé composé event; 'd'habitude', 'tous les jours', 'à l'époque', 'pendant que' point to imparfait background ('hier' alone can open either). A single sentence often has both: 'Je dormais (background) quand le téléphone a sonné (event).'

examples.fr: Je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné.
examples.en: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
examples.note: Sleeping is the ongoing background (imparfait); the ring is the sudden event (passé composé).

examples.fr: D'habitude, je prenais le bus, mais ce jour-là j'ai pris un taxi.
examples.en: Usually I took the bus, but that day I took a taxi.
examples.note: Habit = imparfait; the one-off exception on a specific day = passé composé.

examples.fr: Il faisait froid, alors j'ai fermé la fenêtre.
examples.en: It was cold, so I closed the window.
examples.note: The cold is a description (imparfait); closing the window is what I did about it (passé composé).

examples.fr: Elle avait 20 ans quand elle a rencontré Marc.
examples.en: She was 20 when she met Marc.
examples.note: Age is a state (imparfait); the meeting is a datable event (passé composé).

contrast.fr: Hier, il pleuvait toute la journée. / Hier, il a plu toute la journée.
contrast.en: Yesterday it was raining all day. / Yesterday it rained all day.
contrast.note: Both are correct: the imparfait paints the scene, the passé composé reports the day's rain as a finished fact.
'Soudain' announces an event, so French wants the passé composé: Soudain, il a commencé à pleuvoir.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers use the passé composé for everything in the past because English 'I did' covers both; ask 'did it happen once, or was it the situation?' and give the situation the imparfait.

probes.fr: Je lisais quand elle est arrivée.
probes.en: I was reading when she arrived.
probes.ex: Je lisais quand elle est arrivée.
probes.exEn: I was reading when she arrived.
options: I had read before she arrived.

probes.ex: Soudain, il a commencé à pleuvoir.
probes.exEn: Suddenly it started to rain.

probes.ex: Il faisait beau, alors nous sommes sortis.
probes.exEn: The weather was nice, so we went out.

items.note: Signals a sudden event, so the verb that follows is in the passé composé.
items.ex: Tout à coup, la lumière s'est éteinte.
items.exEn: Suddenly, the light went out.

items.note: Introduces the moment something happened in a story; the verb after it is passé composé.
items.ex: Un jour, elle a décidé de partir.
items.exEn: One day, she decided to leave.

items.note: Points to one specific day, so it goes with a passé composé event; the -là is attached with a hyphen.
items.ex: Ce jour-là, j'ai rencontré ma femme.
items.exEn: That day, I met my wife.

items.note: Announces a habit, so the past verb after it is imparfait ('used to').
items.ex: D'habitude, je prenais le bus.
items.exEn: Usually, I took the bus.
